Separately, the surviving daemon was parented to init, so killing the harness handle kills the privilege wrapper rather than the daemon: restart tests add daemons instead of replacing them, and a later one rebinds the broker socket then exits, leaving the live daemon's broker path dead. After any daemon-restart test no agent can check in again.

cargo fmt only resolves through the pinned toolchain when run from inside the workspace directory, because the toolchain file lives there. Invoking it from the repository root with a manifest path fails claiming cargo-fmt is not installed, which misreads as a broken toolchain rather than a working-directory problem.

The collision fix is confirmed working on positive evidence rather than absence: the cap signature appears zero times in both the pytest and daemon logs, the daemon logged its name-reclaim path forty-three times, and twenty-five tests newly pass - every one a parametrization that previously died on the cap. The fix's own new error paths fired zero times, so it traded no new failure mode for the one it removed.

The triage model's causal half held and its forecast half did not: non-passing went from a hundred and twenty-three to a hundred and nine, not to the predicted forty-nine. The cap failures were MASKING other failures rather than substituting for passes. Agent-caused went from a predicted twenty-nine to fifty-two because every later test now reports the agent error instead of the cap, and independent defects went from twenty to forty-one because tests that used to die at create now reach their assertions and fail there. Roughly half the cap failures were concealing independent defects.

Near-deterministic corroboration of the agent-wedge hypothesis: the daemon brokered exactly the same number of guest socat streams in both runs before the agent went silent, the same integer to the unit. That is what an output pipe filling to a fixed capacity looks like, and it is strong evidence for the unread-stdout-pipe cause over anything load- or timing-dependent. The broker-side symptom differed between runs, so the visible error is a downstream consequence rather than the cause.

An unpredicted mid-run event cost sixteen failures: the gateway VM's docker daemon stalled on its own, the monitor hit its failure threshold and force-restarted the VM, recovering in about fifty seconds, but seventeen test positions drained through the roughly three-second window where the socket was absent. Every test that regressed against the previous run falls inside that window. The inferred trigger is the orphaned-gateway-container crash loop already identified, accumulating inside a memory-constrained VM.

The cleanup was not disabled, it was inert, and the distinction changes the fix. The destructive preflight sweep WAS deliberately removed, for a reason that still stands: it wiped every sandbox-prefixed VM, container and network on the host, destroying the operator's production sessions and golden image. That was correctly left removed. The separate teardown sweep was never switched off - it shells out to bare docker, which on macOS reaches the host's Docker rather than the gateway VM's, where session and gateway containers actually live behind a socket the operator cannot open. The sweep found nothing and reported success.

Re-enabling the gateway-VM sweep does not reinstate the hazard that got the preflight removed, because the sudo pivot the socket's ownership forces is itself the scoping: the VM belongs to the test daemon's own uid and production's gateway VM lives under a different uid's state tree. The reaper only removes resources whose session id the daemon does not recognize AND which are not running, and does nothing at all when the daemon cannot be asked, rather than reading silence as an absence of live work.

The agent wedge is fixed with decisive evidence rather than an absence of symptoms: the daemon brokered a hundred and ninety-six guest socat streams against a wedge point of a hundred and nine that had been identical across two prior runs, and the agent's log reached about one and a half times the pipe capacity that used to block it while the agent stayed responsive throughout. Roughly three log lines per stream, matching the earlier estimate.

Measured detail the earlier analysis missed: the privilege wrapper does forward a termination signal, so only the forced-kill path orphaned a daemon. That explains why teardown appeared to work while restart tests silently accumulated daemons - the two paths used different signals. The restart helper now finds the real daemon by owning uid and staged binary path, escalates only after a grace period, and collects any earlier orphan too.

PRODUCTION CRASH, not a test defect: the daemon panics at startup with a nested-runtime error whenever the session store already holds Lima rows and the daemon uid differs from the operator uid - which is the normal macOS deployment. Startup reconciliation is called bare from the async main, and on a populated store it reaches an executor that blocks on the current runtime handle, whose own doc-comment says callers must be inside a blocking task. A fresh daemon on an empty store is fine; every restart on a populated one dies. Accounted for ninety-eight of a hundred and twenty-three failures, five panicking directly and ninety-three refused connections behind them.

The crash was invisible until the harness was fixed, and the harness defect is what hid it: restart tests killed the privilege wrapper rather than the daemon, so the original daemon kept serving the socket while its replacement panicked unnoticed. A defect in the test harness was masking a production crash for months. The call site dates to April and the three harness commits touch only the e2e directory.

The headline counts of the first and third runs are identical at thirty-six passed and a hundred and twenty-three failed, and mean entirely different things: the third run died at position sixty-three of a hundred and sixty. Over the comparable region that both runs reached in byte-identical order, passes went from twenty-five to thirty-six with six fewer failures, five fewer errors, eleven newly passing and none regressed. Every apparent regression sits beyond the point this run never reached. Comparing headline totals across runs of different reach would have read real progress as a total reversal.

All three harness fixes are confirmed on the full run: the agent brokered a hundred and fifty streams against the old wall of a hundred and nine with zero agent-death failures where the previous run had fifty-two, it outlived the daemon and re-checked in to restarted ones, the gateway VM's docker never stalled where the previous run lost sixteen tests to an outage, and the run ended clean with nothing leaked and nothing needing manual cleanup for the first time in three attempts.

The runtime-handle call appears exactly once in workspace production code, which turns the sweep for sibling nested-runtime panics from a best-effort search into a closed question. Every other blocking-on-a-runtime call in the tree is either a top-level runtime in a binary's main, a test, or a deliberate own-thread-own-runtime construction carrying its own explanatory comment. That single sink is reachable through exactly three executor call sites, and the transitive graph through them resolves to nineteen entry points and forty-six call sites, of which precisely one was unwrapped.

The fix was measured by A/B against real residue rather than a synthetic fixture: the e2e store was already sitting in the exact failing state, holding a running Lima row under a daemon uid different from the operator's, left by the run that first hit the crash. Two binaries built from trees identical but for the wrapper - the unfixed one panicked at the production line with the documented exit status, the fixed one came up, served health and session reads, and shut down cleanly. The regression guard was proven to bite by re-injecting the bare call and watching it panic at the same line.

The macOS full backend has no working egress at all: the Lima guest never receives its gateway default route, measured directly as an empty result from a route query inside the guest while the daemon side reports the gateway address, components ready and firewall rules installed. Twenty-four failures run-wide trace to it. The decisive corroboration is the pass pattern rather than the error text - every Lima test asserting traffic is blocked passes, and not one requiring working egress does. The backend is failing closed: the core promise holds, and the backend is unusable.

Ruled out by measurement rather than reasoning for the missing-route defect: the permission-denied class appears only three times run-wide, and the Linux route-installation path is never reached on macOS at all, with zero mentions of its transport in the entire log. Before fixing, establish whether any macOS path is even meant to install that route - a wrong route and no such code are different defects with different fixes, and a second crop of failures should be expected behind whichever it is.

The suite now reaches its own end: seventy-four passed against eighty-five failed with no errors, from thirty-six passed at the start of this session, with zero regressions at any position across all four runs and test order verified byte-identical between them. The region measured before the panic fix reproduced exactly, so the whole gain is in territory never previously executed. Thirty-eight tests newly pass against the run immediately before.

A daemon-side signature appeared that no test reports: a bridge listener error spinning about twelve times a second for four minutes, over three thousand occurrences. It is strictly downstream of the workspace-sync defect, with an exact eleven-of-eleven intersection between affected sessions and zero on either side alone. One fix serves both, but the listener should back off regardless rather than spin on a failure it cannot resolve.

log.title: Slot identity stops being positional or guessed
log.summary:
Slot identity now comes from the slot, never from position or a guess. The NIC parser claimed to build a slot-to-interface map and actually built a position-to-interface one, and several call sites fell back to guessing an interface name or defaulting a slot index to zero - which can attach a session to the wrong layer-two segment, meaning its egress policy is enforced on someone else's network. Silent, and a security consequence rather than an inconvenience.

The silent guess turned out to exist at five sites, not the three the spec names. The two extra were missed because the spec's file table uses the word restart for two different functions, one of which claims a FRESH slot before guessing - making it create-shaped, where falling back on the persisted name points at the previously held slot and is actively wrong rather than conservatively stale. They landed in a separately revertable commit so the spec-mandated three stay attributable alone.

Fail-closed was resolved at the map level rather than at discovery, which avoided a silent availability regression: failing discovery would have made the daemon refuse to start on a reduced pool, and that would have made both degraded arms of the pool-resize decision unreachable - the arms that exist precisely for that condition. The spec's own wording asks for a refused create, not a refused startup. The invariant that makes it airtight is that guest-reported output can only withhold a map entry, never manufacture one, so operator-influenced input cannot forge a mapping; matching is on exact name, so a zero-padded spelling cannot stand in.

One site deliberately keeps a fallback: the persisted interface name was written at create time from the verified map and is what the session's existing interface is actually parented on, and the map is legitimately absent before readiness completes. Precedence is record wins, map fills only a blank record, disagreement refuses. A reviewer walked all seven combinations and found no ordering producing a silent wrong answer.

The version floor was declined rather than skipped: a floor asserts which version first honours the interface key, that boundary is unmeasured from a single data point, and it is enforced at instance creation so the cost would land on hosts that work today. The shipped verification backstop covers the same hazard, asserted directly.

Making the refusal observable exposed a third, independent defect: the per-session gateway monitor had no backend filter, so an unhealthy lite gateway was being re-created by the full-backend macvlan setup on a guessed interface. Guarded by backend, which is a real behaviour change - macOS lite sessions now get no per-session gateway re-create from that loop, having previously got one that was doubly wrong. A correct lite re-create is tracked, not claimed.

Single-operator behaviour proven unchanged by byte diff of the rendered template rather than argued from inputs: exactly N added interface lines, empty diff once stripped, and those are the names the platform would have chosen positionally anyway. Independently reproduced by the reviewer with its own binary.

Three commits, 18 new tests (2216 passing, 179 skipped), clippy -D warnings and fmt clean, five spec amendments framed as amendments against a smaller measured set, all commits reviewed and approved.
decisions: The remaining macOS e2e debt becomes its own milestone rather than expanding this one, on the user's call. The reasoning that makes this safe: a suite does not need to be green to be useful, it needs to be deterministic and understood. This one now reproduces position for position across runs with a catalogued failure set and zero regressions, so later sessions can use it as a regression instrument by comparing against the recorded baseline. The ownership arc is therefore not blocked on fixing eighty-five tests.

The silent slot-index guess exists at five sites, not the three the spec names. The two extra ones were missed because the file table uses the word restart for two different functions: one of them claims a FRESH slot and then guesses the interface name, which makes it create-shaped rather than restart-shaped, so falling back on the persisted name would point at the previously held slot and be actively wrong rather than conservatively stale. Both extra sites are being fixed in a second, separately revertable commit so the spec-mandated three stay attributable on their own.

The fail-closed requirement for the interface map is resolved at the map level rather than at discovery, which avoids a silent availability regression. Failing at discovery would make the daemon refuse to start on a reduced pool, and that in turn would make both degraded arms of the pool-resize decision unreachable - the arms that exist precisely for that condition. The spec's own wording asks for a refused create, not a refused startup. The property that makes this airtight is that guest-reported output can only withhold a map entry, never manufacture one, so operator-controlled input cannot forge a mapping.

The Lima version floor was deliberately NOT raised. Fix 2's verification backstop shipped instead, with a test asserting the hazard directly: given a non-contiguous slot set and a guest reporting positional interface names, nothing maps and every session claiming one is refused. The floor was declined rather than skipped, because a floor is a claim about which version FIRST honours the interface key and that boundary is unmeasured - the evidence is a single version. Any floor set from one data point is either an over-restriction or a guess at the boundary, and it would be enforced at instance creation, so the cost would land on hosts that work today.

The restart site keeps its persisted fallback while the other four refuse outright, and the precedence is record wins, map fills only a blank record, disagreement refuses. The justification is that the persisted interface name was written at create time from the verified map and is what the session's existing virtual interface is actually parented on, so reading it is correct rather than coincidental - and the map is legitimately absent before readiness completes, so an empty map there means not-yet-known rather than wrong. Refusing on it would break restore for something that is not a fault, which is the regression the exit criteria warn about.

Slot identity approved on independent review. The reviewer walked all seven combinations of the restart site's precedence and found no ordering producing a silent wrong answer - the structural property being that the disagreement check binds only when the map holds the slot, so a map miss falls through to the record rather than refusing. It also confirmed the guest can suppress a map entry but never inject one, because the map is built by iterating the daemon's own slot list and using guest output solely for containment, with exact-name matching so a zero-padded spelling cannot stand in.

Guarding that monitor arm by backend is a real behaviour change, not a message change: macOS lite sessions now receive no per-session gateway re-create from that loop. They previously received one that was wrong in two independent ways - the wrong setup function and a guessed interface - so this removes a defect rather than a working capability, but it is recorded as a behaviour change so nobody has to infer it from a diff. A correct lite re-create is separate work and was not attempted or claimed.

The observability follow-up is approved. The backend guard cannot filter the wrong way because the enum has two variants and the comparison passes the intended one through, and it is consistent with two existing filters on adjacent paths. The degraded marking clears on every path that resolves the condition, and the one case where it persists indefinitely is correct - the gateway really is down and the status says so. The adjacent stale-status gap was confirmed as genuinely separate work rather than something to fold in, because mixing it here would make a revert of the guard carry an unrelated change with it.
discoveries: The entire defect catalogue and the run history live only in untracked files - the handoff directory and the tracker state are both gitignored - so a session's worth of measurement across four full runs was one deletion away from being lost. Durable findings must be written into a tracked surface at the time they are produced, not left in coordination artifacts, and that surface has to be self-contained because it cannot reference the ephemeral files it came from.

Failing closed and failing silently are a bad pairing. One of the guessed-interface sites sits in a continue-on-error monitor loop, so refusing there means logging and skipping, which does stop traffic but leaves an operator with a session that looks healthy and has no gateway. A refusal that protects the invariant still has to be observable, otherwise the safety property is bought with a diagnosability loss.

A defect label was reused for two different defects across the investigation series, and the final document applied the reassignment retroactively to its own comparison table. Anyone reading the series in order would silently conflate the two. The durable record keeps the final numbering, states the reuse explicitly, and notes which labels are retired so the gaps read as intentional rather than as lost entries. Ad-hoc identifiers coined mid-investigation need a stated meaning at the point they stop being obvious.

The strongest evidence that a generator change is behaviour-preserving is a byte diff of its rendered output, not an argument about its inputs. Rendering the template before and after for the single-operator case produced exactly eight added interface lines and an otherwise identical file; stripping those eight lines left an empty diff. Those names are also the ones the platform would have chosen positionally for a contiguous zero-based set, so the machine comes up on the same interfaces and the same sockets.

A refusal that leaves work undone must be observable at a level operators actually watch, and the reason is that this particular skip is not self-clearing: the interface map only changes when the gateway machine restarts, so a warning-level line can sit unnoticed indefinitely by anyone alerting on errors. The remedy pairs an error-level log with a degraded marking on the session's own status surface, so the condition is visible where an operator already looks rather than only in a log they might grep.

The per-session gateway monitor iterated every running session with no backend filter, while the instance-recovery path next to it does filter. Because lite and full-backend gateway containers share a naming scheme, the health probe cannot tell them apart, so an unhealthy lite gateway was being re-created by the full-backend macvlan setup on a guessed interface - a defect entirely independent of the slot work, found only because making the refusal observable forced someone to check whether the tag would surface for the sessions reaching that arm.

A degraded marking is only meaningful if the path that resolves the condition also clears it. This one borrows an existing status value rather than defining a new one, and the recovery paths remove the entry both on success and after marking a session failed, so the tag lives exactly as long as the condition. The reason this arm needs the marking while the adjacent failure arm does not is that the adjacent one retries every tick, whereas this refusal cannot change until the gateway machine restarts.

log.title: Per-operator socket groups at enrollment and de-enrollment
log.summary:
Shipped the independently-shippable half of the cross-operator slot fix: per-operator groups, range assignment at enrollment, and de-enrollment. The defect it addresses is active and was recorded only in the spec - every enrolled operator sits in the single group owning every slot socket, so slot partitioning currently enforces nothing. Enforcement, moving the sockets onto these groups, is deliberately a later session, because until virtual-machine ownership flips the daemon's own gateway must open every slot.

De-enrollment shipped with enrollment rather than after it, because reclaiming a range without revoking membership recreates the defect exactly and nothing at any layer would detect it. Revoke-before-reassign is enforced in code rather than documented: a range recorded against another group cannot be handed out. Two-member fail-closed is preserved rather than resolved - a group holding more than one operator is refused and named, never settled by picking one. A half-done de-enrollment leaves zero operator members with the range still recorded, which surfaces as lost capacity and blocks reuse; all three partial-failure paths were traced and every one fails in the safe direction.

Where the range lives was an open question the spec leaves to phase one, and it was settled on four measured properties rather than convenience. It is not operator-writable: six paths were attempted as the real second operator against its real group - overwrite, change, append, minting a fresh group, deleting its own group, and editing membership - and all refused, with an authentication-only control proving the boundary is authorization rather than a wrong password. Testing the mint and delete paths mattered as much as the overwrite, since widening is not the only way to obtain slots one was not given. The unprivileged daemon can read everything the next session's derivation needs. The later phase stops reading it rather than converting it, so there is no flag day. And an absent value now refuses instead of defaulting - which was a real defect, not a hypothetical: an absent range was surfacing as the whole pool in two places.

The reusable finding is that reading a directory attribute prints a not-found message and still exits zero, so exit status cannot distinguish absent from present and only the text can. The same class bit twice: native attributes also read back with a type prefix ahead of the key, caught only because enrollment verifies a write by reading it back rather than trusting the writing command's status.

Two existing guards were touched. The emitter-equivalence checker fired on this change and was extended rather than routed around, preserving its force - it still fails on any hardcoded literal, which is how the created account and the plist-named account came apart before. The uninstaller knew nothing about these groups, so a leftover would have made the next install skip creation and inherit a stale range; it now revokes then deletes, in the same order as enrollment reversal.

The enrollment-ordering failure was re-measured first-hand with a positive control rather than cited from the earlier session, and fails closed. The migration window was given a checkable exit condition, and the framing corrected: neither membership is migration-scoped, only the socket's group ownership is.

Nothing moved a socket or rewrote a plist, asserted structurally. Host carries only the intended fixture, reversible with one command. Gates: 2218 passed / 179 skipped / 0 failed, 35 hermetic enrollment tests, clippy and fmt clean, emitter equivalence clean. Code review approved with an explicit pass on the privileged surface, established by executing hostile inputs.
decisions: The per-operator range must be stored somewhere the operator it describes cannot write. The spec pins the group and its membership as root-owned state but leaves the range's phase-one home open, and the obvious candidate - a custom attribute on the operator's own group record - would let an operator widen their own range if the directory service permits self-writes. That recreates the partitioning defect with a different mechanism and the same consequence, and worse, it would look partitioned. Write-authorization must be tested as the second operator rather than inferred from the read path.

Three further properties ordered for the range's phase-one storage: it must be readable by the unprivileged daemon, since the next session derives ranges from it and a privileged read makes it unusable; it must be replaceable when the plists become authoritative later, preferring something a later session can stop reading over something it must convert; and an absent value must be a refusal rather than a default, since defaulting is the exact failure mode just removed from three call sites.

The operator keeps membership in the shared group as well as its own, and the reason is a traversal dependency rather than a redundant grant: the shared group gates the daemon socket AND owns the socket directory, so an operator outside it cannot reach any socket whatever group the socket itself carries. The per-operator group is a second group layered on top. The daemon likewise stays in every per-operator group because the gateway machine holds an interface on every slot, so a daemon outside one operator's group breaks session creation for ALL operators, not just that one.

For the enforcement session: what gets unwound later is narrower than both memberships. The durable rule is that the DAEMON retains membership in each per-operator group, because the gateway machine holds an interface on every slot. The operator's shared-group membership outlives the migration for a different reason entirely - the socket directory is group-owned and group-traversable, and the shared group is independently the daemon-socket enrollment gate. Enforcement moves the socket's group ownership off the shared group onto the per-operator one; neither membership is removed. Reading split membership as taking operators out of the shared group would break traversal for every operator at once.

Correction to the migration framing: neither membership is migration-scoped. The shared group currently plays two unrelated roles - it is the socket group named in every slot plist, and separately it is the traversal right on the socket directory plus the daemon-socket enrollment gate. Enforcement moves the first role only. The daemon's membership in each per-operator group is permanent for as long as any daemon-uid process opens a slot socket, and the operator's shared-group membership is permanent for the traversal and gating role. What actually ends is the period where assignment and enforcement disagree.

The migration window has a checkable exit condition rather than a judged one: for every slot in the pool, the socket's group names the per-operator group of exactly one operator, and that operator's recorded range contains that slot. At that point the two sources agree and the daemon should read the socket group, because that is what the kernel actually checks. Two traps for the enforcement session - the fallback must be per-slot rather than per-host, since a partially migrated host is a normal intermediate state, and a host-level migrated flag would mishandle it.

The privileged surface passes, established by executing crafted hostile inputs against the real script rather than by reading its validator: command separators, a leading dash, traversal, whitespace and backtick injection are all refused before any directory command is reached, and every mutating path routes through the same validation. Collision with reserved identities is prevented structurally by the name prefix rather than by an exclusion list, and service accounts are refused by explicit enumeration with a uid floor as an independent second gate.
discoveries: The backend guard added in the previous session fails OPEN in every defaulting path: the enum's default variant and the migration's column default both resolve to the full-backend value, and the store hard-errors rather than coercing an unrecognized string. So an unclassifiable session is included in recovery rather than skipped, which is the safe direction for that particular check. This was not established when the guard was written - it was verified afterwards, and it is the property that makes the guard defensible rather than merely convenient.

The enrollment-ordering failure was re-measured first-hand rather than cited, with a positive control on byte-identical arguments: the socket daemon refuses before the virtualization framework loads and never falls back to a default group, and a corrected retry succeeds over the stale socket left by the failed attempt, so no manual cleanup is needed between attempts. A mis-ordered enrollment therefore fails closed. Incidentally the first probe hit the platform socket-path length limit from a scratch directory, which is worth knowing before anyone builds probe topologies under deep paths.

The range attribute is not operator-writable, measured on the real account against the real group rather than inferred: six unauthenticated attempts - create, change, append, mint a fresh group, delete the group, and edit membership - all refused with a permission error, with the value and the membership verified unchanged afterwards. Covering the mint and delete paths mattered as much as the overwrite, because a design that refuses only overwrites is holed by either of the other two.

The daemon can read everything the next session's range derivation needs with no privilege at all: the range attribute, the list of per-operator groups, and each group's membership are all readable as the unprivileged daemon account. That was the property that would have disqualified this storage choice regardless of how well it resisted writes.

The refusal is an authorization boundary, not an artifact of missing credentials: an authenticated non-admin write was refused too, and the control that makes it conclusive is that an auth-only check with the same credentials succeeded first. So the boundary is admin-or-root, and the operator account is confirmed outside admin. Without that control the refusal would have been indistinguishable from a wrong password.

Reading the range attribute prints a not-found message and STILL EXITS ZERO, so exit status cannot distinguish absent from present and the text is the only signal. An absent range was consequently surfacing as the whole-pool default in two places - the status command and the installer's plan - which is the defaulting-instead-of-refusing failure this milestone has now removed from several call sites. Both refuse now, and the trap is commented at both sites.

A killed directory-delete client is not evidence the delete failed. The stalled deletion completed asynchronously once the client was killed, so the hang was in the client's wait rather than in the removal - the record was being deleted the whole time while the command never returned. Re-checking later is the cheap way to find out, and it is much cheaper than restarting the directory service, which is what the apparent failure would otherwise have justified.

Second instance of the same reading trap in one session: native directory attributes read back with a type prefix before the key, so splitting the output on the first colon leaves the key glued to the value. It was caught only because the enrollment step verifies a write by reading it back rather than trusting the writing command's exit status - which is the general lesson, and the same shape as the missing-key read that exits zero.

log.title: Per-operator vmnet pools, range derivation and quota errors
log.summary:
The daemon's slot ledger is now per-operator: a uid-keyed pool registry, ranges derived from root-owned enrollment state, a persisted field for sharding restore, and two quota error shapes. The pool's shape and its claim and release semantics are unchanged - there is simply more than one of it.

The session's central risk was inverting its own milestone's lesson. The three preceding sessions all hardened by refusing rather than defaulting, and the surrounding code now teaches that strongly - but one row of the derivation table must warn and fall back, and refusing there is a total outage on every host that exists today. Every row was given its own defined behaviour rather than one rule applied uniformly, including three cases the table does not name at all. The outage case was measurable rather than hypothetical, because the previous session left this host with one operator enrolled and the primary operator unenrolled: the legacy row is live here, and the test panics with the outage framing if that operator is ever refused.

Two interpretive calls were raised rather than silently resolved, and both were upheld. Where a one-line summary row and a detailed section disagreed, the detail governs and the row describes the end state - decisively, because the summary reading gives every slot on a current host the legacy answer, fails that row's own acceptance criterion, and would make the preceding session unobservable to its only consumer. The implementation unions both sources so the later migration changes no code here.

The best finding was not requested: legacy slots must share ONE ledger, because private pools over the same indices cannot see each other's claims - both hand out slot zero, both machines attach to segment zero, and two operators become peers on one layer-two segment. That is the isolation failure the partition exists to remove, produced by the code meant to preserve the status quo, and something the single pre-migration pool structurally could not do. The reasoning now sits at the test that pins it, written at the person who would split it.

Two measured facts that would each have caused a silent wrong answer: the group-membership call returns only supplementary members, so an account whose primary group is the one queried is absent from its own member list - the daemon account, live. And the obvious in-tree operator enumerator walks the state directory, so a newly enrolled operator is invisible to it, which is precisely the operator the absent-share error exists to diagnose.

The disclosure limit is structural rather than conventional - the holder list is built into the log and never into the response body, asserted negatively against the body itself. The full-share and full-host cases render differently, because raising the session knob has no effect on the first and cannot exceed the provisioned count anyway. Restore routes by persisted identity, falls back to the owner name, and declines rather than guessing - guessing would put a running machine on another operator's ledger, dropping would leave the pool believing an in-use slot free.

Kernel enforcement is explicitly not here: this is daemon-side bookkeeping, stated in the module docs, the commit and the guide. Two commits, 37 new tests, gates green at 2255 passed / 183 skipped / 0 failed, clippy and fmt clean, operator docs extended for both failure shapes, code review approved.
decisions: Where the plan's one-line derivation row and the spec's detailed assignment section disagreed, the detailed section governs and the row describes the phase-four end state. The decisive evidence is that the summary reading gives every slot on a phase-one host the legacy answer, which fails that row's own acceptance criterion and would nullify the entire preceding session. A reading that makes its predecessor pointless is the wrong reading. The implementation unions the recorded range with the socket group so the same path serves both phases and the later migration changes no code here.

Legacy slots must share ONE ledger rather than a private pool per operator, and the reason is not symmetry but collision: private pools over the same indices would let two operators claim the same slot and land on one layer-two segment, which the single pre-migration pool structurally could not produce. Falling back to current behaviour therefore has to mean the shared ledger. This is non-obvious enough that someone will eventually try to make it per-operator for tidiness, so the reasoning belongs at the test site.

Per-operator pools approved on independent review. The outage criterion was verified at three levels rather than one: a unit test on a fully-legacy host, a registry test proving today's concurrency survives, and a live integration test on this machine confirming the unenrolled primary operator draws a working four-slot pool rather than being refused. The shared-ledger property was traced through the single path by which any uid obtains a pool, and no two operators can hold the same index because the derivation emits at most one assignment per slot and the multi-operator case is a refusal.
discoveries: The documented build-tree exec stall arrived on schedule and was diagnosed by the runbook rather than guessed: the build directory reached fifty gigabytes with over six hundred thousand files in its dependency directory, test binaries sat at process start consuming no memory and producing no output for over ten minutes, and the control - copying the same binary outside the tree and running it there - listed its tests instantly, including the newly added ones. Same binary, different location, opposite behaviour, so the tree is the cause and not the change. The system daemons that present almost identically were correctly left alone.

The group-membership call returns only supplementary members, so an account whose PRIMARY group is the one being queried is absent from its own group's member list. Measured live: the daemon account does not appear in the shared group it belongs to. Any membership check written against the member list alone silently omits exactly the accounts most likely to matter.

The obvious in-tree source for enumerating operators walks the state directory, so a newly-enrolled operator with no state directory yet is invisible to it - which is precisely the operator the absent-share error exists to diagnose. Using it would have made a brand-new operator undiagnosable in the one case the error was written for. The enrollment record itself is the correct candidate set.

A warning belongs where the person who would break it will be standing, not where the design is explained. The shared-ledger rationale lived in a module header, which is not where someone goes to split a shared pool into per-operator ones; moved to the test that pins it and written at that reader directly, closing with what they would be turning back on. Assertion failure messages were rewritten the same way - naming the consequence, that two operators were given separate pools over the same indices and would land on one segment, rather than naming the mechanic that failed.

log.title: Brokered transport foundation
log.summary:
Rebuilt the macOS broker's control connection to carry a request and response surface roughly triple the original estimate. It previously handled one operation at a time and wedged the entire task on a stream open. Both halves of the decision shipped: pipelining by request identifier, and stream opens taken off the control loop - the second being the one the criterion is actually about, as distinct from the token-plumbing functions, and the one whose absence would have made a change that looks done and is not. An expiry or rejection now fails one operation and leaves the connection and every other operation alone.

The shared argv crate landed as a zero-dependency leaf that both the core library and the agent binary depend on, with NO edge between those two - which is what preserves the boundary, rather than a safe direction of import. Verified both ways by dependency graph rather than by inspection. It is not a placeholder: both fragments it holds were already duplicated across the boundary, including the one non-argv shape in the surface.

The concurrency audit was the highest-value part and justified being a work item rather than a claim. The agent runs on a current-thread runtime, so a blocking call stalls the heartbeat and every other operation rather than just its caller - and two handlers did exactly that. Without moving both off the runtime thread, pipelining would have delivered no concurrency whenever either was in flight: the headline feature would have shipped inert and passed its own tests. The remaining surfaces are recorded with the invariant each depends on rather than marked safe, so a future handler author meets the constraint rather than the conclusion. The artifact is tracked and self-contained.

Two changes beyond the brief, both correct and both reviewed hardest. The frame read moved into its own task because the read primitive is not cancellation-safe and the loop now polls continuously, which would have made a previously incidental partial-frame race permanent - and a truncated frame on a newline-delimited channel corrupts the next one. And liveness now measures from the last frame received rather than the last loop wake-up, which fixed a pre-existing defect: a silent agent could previously survive indefinitely as long as the daemon kept sending it work.

Tests were shown to measure the property rather than co-occur with it: with the in-flight cap set to one, exactly the two concurrency tests fail while the ordering test still passes.

CLOSING PARTIAL, BY DESIGN, on the Linux end-to-end clause. This session deliberately kept the Linux target where every other session moved to the platform-local one, because the claim it guards is genuinely cross-platform. It requires a Linux host or CI, was not substituted, and is not offered as met. Cross-platform builds and lints were verified in a pinned container instead, and two lint errors visible only with test targets were proven pre-existing by A-B against the pre-change tree rather than assumed.

Four commits, 9 new tests, gates green at 2264 passed / 183 skipped / 0 failed, clippy and fmt clean, code review approved.
decisions: The shared crate landed as a zero-dependency leaf that both the core library and the agent binary depend on, with no edge between those two. That is what preserves the boundary - not a safe direction of import, but the absence of any import at all between the two sides. Linux builds and lints verified unaffected in a container at a pinned toolchain.

A response carrying an unknown request identifier is now discarded with a warning rather than closing the connection, because this session changed what such a frame MEANS. On a serialized lane it could only be protocol corruption, so failing fast was correct; with operations now timing out individually, a late answer to an abandoned operation is a legitimate cause of a stray frame, and closing would punish operations that did nothing wrong. The property that a bogus identifier never reaches a caller is preserved and asserted more strongly than before.

The no-wedge property this session delivers covers a wedged RESPONSE, not a wedged WRITE. An agent that stops servicing its socket entirely can still stall dispatch, unchanged from before, and that is a different failure from a slow answer. Recorded at the site rather than fixed, and stated plainly here so that no-longer-wedges is not read as unqualified.
discoveries: The agent runs on a current-thread runtime, so a blocking call occupies the only runtime thread and stalls the heartbeat and every other operation rather than just its own caller. Two handlers did exactly that - a synchronous socket exchange with multi-second timeouts, and a directory-service lookup performed once per invocation. Without moving both onto blocking tasks, this session's pipelining would have delivered no concurrency at all whenever either was in flight: the headline change would have shipped inert and passed its own tests.

Twenty feature-gated items in the broker, including the entire multiplexed-stream set, are compiled by neither the hermetic tier nor the integration tier - both pass different feature flags and never that one. They are dead in both. That is worse than having no tests there, because the names create confidence nobody is entitled to.

The liveness change fixed a pre-existing defect rather than merely accommodating the new loop shape: the timeout previously reset on every loop iteration including request dispatch, so a silent agent could survive indefinitely as long as the daemon kept sending it work. Measuring from the last frame actually received means the timer tracks the agent rather than the daemon's own activity. A healthy-but-slow agent is unaffected because its heartbeats advance the same clock as its responses.

log.title: Typed Docker ops: container and network lifecycle
log.summary:
Moved the container, network, volume and image lifecycle Docker verbs onto a closed typed op set brokered to the operator's agent, so no production invocation in this family targets an operator's socket directly from the daemon. Twenty-one variants, enumerable in one enum, and the closure is enforced by the compiler rather than by tests: the wire mapping and the conversions in both directions are exhaustive matches, so a variant without a counterpart fails to build, and three independent count assertions mean an uncovered addition fails the count.

Three call sites previously took free-form input and all three were closed rather than accommodated. Shell execution became a fixed command set whose bodies are constants on the agent side, so the daemon names a component and never a shell string. Format-string inspection became a fixed format set, so it names an intent and never a template - a free template can read any field of a container's configuration. And image loading became a staged-image variant resolved by the running side, because a caller-supplied path there is arbitrary read access granted to whoever is on the socket.

The strongest property was not requested: the daemon supplies no endpoint at all. The agent derives its own socket from its own home, so the guarantee holds structurally rather than depending on every call site passing the right thing. A closed op set bounds what can be asked for, and that bound is worth exactly as much as the guarantee about where it lands, because a container daemon is a root shell on its host.

Two invariants that existed only as convention are now enforced. Gateway creation refuses the virtual-machine route, because its arguments name host paths as bind-mount sources which a machine's docker resolves against a filesystem where they do not exist - producing a container with empty mounts and no symptom. And the environment-scrubbing asymmetry became a rule with a test behind it: a route that names its target scrubs the environment, one that does not inherit it. Grounding that in code made it stronger than the anecdote it replaced - scrubbing the unpinned route would make the rootless probe report a daemon unreachable rather than unsupported, and would make the reaper enumerate an empty host and report success.

The two near-duplicate reaper funnels were unified in code with the distinction moved into the type, which states the rule once instead of duplicating an invariant across two functions. Both closed enums carry notes that adding a variant is a security change, aimed at whoever adds the sixth, with two rules for telling a real variant from a pass-through wearing an enum. Two files are deliberately half-migrated with notices saying so, because finishing them here would destroy the reviewability the split exists to create.

The measured surface came in larger than the spec records and the deltas were reported without writing corrected figures back, since replacing one stale number with a fresher one only resets the clock on the same failure.

Three commits, 56 new tests, hermetic gates green at 2321 passed / 183 skipped / 0 failed, clippy and fmt clean, code review approved across all three. The container-scope end-to-end run reproduced every projected baseline failure with identical class composition and zero regressions; its single difference was proven by a controlled rerun at the pre-session commit to predate this work, with the two runs indistinguishable at every position.
decisions: The daemon supplies no docker socket path at all: the agent derives its own endpoint as an agent-side constant. That makes the no-path-outside-the-agent's-own-home property structural rather than dependent on every call site passing the right thing - the daemon cannot point the agent at an arbitrary endpoint even in principle. Stronger than the rule it replaces, and the reasoning belongs at the constant, because the next person to parameterise it for testing needs to meet the argument first.

The two call shapes that looked like they wanted argv pass-through were closed instead: shell probes became a fixed enum whose command bodies are agent-side constants, so the daemon names a component and never a shell string; and format-string inspection became a fixed enum, so the daemon names an intent and never a format. In both cases the untrusted side chooses from a fixed set rather than supplying text, which is what makes the validator load-bearing rather than decorative. Both enums carry a note that adding a variant is a security-relevant change, because sets like these are never reopened in one bold commit - they gain one reasonable variant at a time until they are effectively open.

The two near-duplicate reaper funnels were unified in code with the distinction moved into the type rather than being kept as two functions. That is stronger than what was originally asked for: two functions carrying a duplicated invariant is precisely the drift risk the spec flags, whereas a type-level distinction states the rule once. The host route deliberately does not scrub the environment, because a rootless install publishes its socket through that environment and scrubbing would point the reaper at nothing - and because that route runs in the daemon's own context rather than pivoting into the operator's, so the inherited environment is not a privilege boundary. That asymmetry must be written as a rule with its consequence, since it is exactly the sentence a later reader deletes for consistency.

The argv crate stays literally zero-dependency, at the cost of a mirrored wire layer that duplicates its enums with serialization derives and total conversions both ways. The duplication is guarded rather than merely accepted: a test renders every variant on both sides and compares the results, and asserting the variant count means a new op fails that count before it can ship uncovered. A feature-gated dependency would have been shorter but contradicts the crate's whole reason for existing, and a gate can be switched on.

The measured surface deltas were reported but deliberately NOT written into the spec as corrected figures. The spec already instructs the reader to re-count before quoting, and replacing one stale number with a fresher one merely resets the clock on the same failure - the next reader should re-measure rather than trust the newer figure either. Recording the instruction to measure beats recording a measurement.

The closed op set is approved on structural grounds rather than on test evidence: both enums were read variant by variant, and the guards are compile-time - the wire mapping and the conversions in both directions are exhaustive matches, so a new variant without a counterpart fails to build rather than failing a test. Three independent count assertions additionally pin the variant total, so an uncovered addition fails the count. No variant carries an argv, a shell string, a format template or a caller-supplied path, and no operation can name an endpoint.

The environment-scrubbing asymmetry is now a rule rather than an anecdote: a route that names its target scrubs the environment, and a route that does not name a target inherits it. Scrubbing exists for exactly one purpose - stopping anything ambient from overriding the target flag - so it belongs precisely where that flag is load-bearing, which makes the asymmetry the rule working rather than an inconsistency in it. The sharper half is the inverse: on the pinned route the flag names a container daemon belonging to a DIFFERENT account and is the only thing that says which, so there the scrub is not optional.
discoveries: The measured Docker surface is larger than the spec records: thirty-one injection points across fourteen files against roughly twenty-eight across twelve, and fifteen top-level verbs against thirteen. All five sites the spec flagged as previously omitted are present, at drifted line numbers. A spec figure that has drifted once will drift again, so the durable instruction is to re-measure rather than to trust a corrected number.

A gateway-creation path was safe only by call-site convention: its arguments name host paths as bind-mount sources, which a virtual machine's docker resolves against a filesystem where they do not exist, producing a container with empty mounts and no obvious symptom. All four callers were verified to take the correct route before the refusal was enforced. A silently wrong result is the worst available failure shape, and convention is not a control.

Two rules now written at the closed enums for telling a real variant from a pass-through wearing an enum: name the OPERATION rather than the command - if the variant name reads like a command line, that is the tell - and carry only what VARIES, so a path or identifier is a field while a program name, flag list or shell fragment is not. Anything that lets the caller change what runs, rather than what it runs on, belongs as a constant or nowhere. The notes are aimed at the person adding the sixth variant, because sets like these are never reopened in one bold commit.

A closed op set bounds what can be ASKED FOR, and that bound is worth exactly as much as the guarantee about WHERE it lands, because a container daemon is a root shell on its host. Without the endpoint being structural, the agent only runs reviewed operations degrades to it runs them against whatever daemon it was told to, and the enum stays closed while bounding nothing that matters. The argument now sits at the constant, along with the seam a test should use instead of an override - give the test its own agent with its own home, which widens production behaviour by zero bytes.

The half-migration claim holds, but by a guard rather than by absence: one lifecycle path does still call the socket-building helper, and is safe only because the route refusal added this session means the socket is always unset there. That is a structural dead read rather than an unreachable one. Worth the distinction, because removing or weakening that refusal would silently make a lifecycle call start reaching the direct socket again - the two facts are now coupled and neither comment mentions the other.

Grounding the claim in code made it stronger than the hypothesis it replaced. The rootless probe's actual job is to DETECT rootless and REFUSE it, so scrubbing the unpinned route would not merely inconvenience such a host - the probe would fail to reach the daemon at all and report it as unreachable rather than as unsupported, converting a precise refusal into a misleading one. The reaper's equivalent would enumerate an empty host, reap nothing, and report success. Both are silently wrong answers rather than failures.

A rule with a test behind it forces a later reader to break something rather than merely contradict a paragraph. The property here could not be asserted directly because the standard library exposes no accessor for the environment-clear flag, so the test pins the observable consequence instead - which is also the right thing to pin, since applying the scrub uniformly for consistency is the specific edit the rule exists to stop.

A ten-second probe with no retry, inside a session-scoped fixture, converts a one-off transient into a total suite void: the first cross-uid exec of a freshly relinked binary exceeds that budget in platform code-signing validation, one timeout poisons the fixture, and the cached setup error is replayed for every selected test. Eighty-five errors in thirty-six seconds with nothing executed. The cost is one-time per binary identity rather than per copy - a fresh copy at a new path execs in about a second once warm - so any run that relinks the daemon can void the whole suite.

The probe's own failure message guesses the wrong cause, naming a missing privilege fragment when that fragment is present and working. A diagnostic that asserts a specific cause it has not tested is worse than one that reports the symptom, because it sends the reader to a healthy subsystem and the real cause is on a different axis entirely.

The container scope is not a useful probe of per-operator slot ranges at all, which retires a concern I raised: lite and container sessions draw no vmnet slot, and that scope creates no full-backend session, so the concurrency ceiling is never approached regardless of how narrow the range is. Two tests assert exactly that and both pass. Testing the range needs a scope that creates full-backend sessions.

The graded run reproduced every one of the thirty-five projected baseline failures, and not merely by name - the class composition matches count for count and the baseline's signature strings are all present. Zero baseline failures started passing. That makes the single new failure a clean signal rather than one difference among many, which is the value of having a catalogued baseline rather than a pass rate.

The one apparently-new failure predates the session: it fails at the pre-session commit too, same leg, same error code, same position. The two runs are indistinguishable - identical counts, identical selection order, identical outcome at every one of the eighty-six positions, and identical failure sets test for test with none unique to either side. The harness was verified byte-identical between the commits first, so the daemon binary was the only variable.

Correction to the earlier reading: the failure is not non-deterministic, it is deterministic GIVEN the container scope - same position in both runs at two different commits - and passes only when run alone. The reason the catalogued baseline appears to contradict this is that the baseline is a full-scope run where the same test sits far later behind different preceding load and passes, and where only its other backend variant fails, at a different leg with a different error code. Baseline-says-passes versus this-scope-says-fails is a scope artifact rather than a regression, which means a full-scope inventory does not project cleanly onto a narrower scope.

The harness's void-run trap has a cheap prophylactic rather than only a diagnosis: pre-build with the exact feature set the harness itself uses, so its own build relinks nothing and the staged binary keeps an identity that has already been validated, then exec that binary once across the uid boundary to warm the platform's code-signing cache. Applied deliberately, the void run simply did not occur.

log.title: Typed Docker ops: policy and egress plane
log.summary:
Moved the policy and egress-plane verbs onto typed ops - the nft rulesets, Envoy bootstrap and listener, and resolver policy that the enforcement pipeline blocks on. Reviewed as an egress-enforcement change rather than a refactor, which is why it was a separate session, and the verdict is explicit: nothing here can result in traffic escaping unenforced.

Twenty-two variants now, one new for the stdin-fed shape. Artifact identity with each generator is asserted rather than inspected across eight pairings, and kept non-tautological by extracting the production functions the call sites use so the assertion is that the bytes sent equal the bytes generated - a test comparing a rendered artifact to a locally-built expectation would have proven nothing.

The dangerous site was not the one the spec flagged. The flagged one was guarded only by an assertion compiled out of release builds, but every caller passed compile-time constants, so its real exposure was nil and the defect was that safety rested on invisible convention. Its sibling was worse: the write helper was public and re-exported, so the crate's interface accepted an arbitrary string path destined for a shell string - an open door with no caller through it. Both were removed rather than escaped: the interface now takes a closed artifact enum, so there is no string left to escape, and the check the vanishing assertion was making runs release-live agent-side on every operation, which also covers a daemon built at a different revision.

Framing on the line-delimited channel was proven against a fixture containing the frame delimiter itself and a forged protocol request, which stays inside the string rather than becoming a frame, with a hundred-kilobyte body crossing intact and no truncating cap on either read path.

Read and write authority were separated - the resolver-owned file is readable and refused for write, where read previously implied write by omission. And a read-surface hole was closed that the scope argument only incidentally surfaced: the stats endpoint takes a regex filter, so a free-form filter reads arbitrary admin state, and two readers of it existed with only one enumerated. Both now share one variant with anchored constant queries.

An introduced duplicate-test-execution bug was caught by a check worth generalising - a test-count delta that does not match the attribute delta is a defect rather than bookkeeping - and reverted, with the accounting closing exactly. The same investigation established that the two test commands run different sets, so a baseline must name the command that produced it.

Three commits, 32 net-new tests, gates green at 2357 passed by make and 2353 bare, 183 skipped, 0 failed, clippy and fmt clean. Container-scope end-to-end came in at 50 passed / 35 failed / 0 errors against a reference of 49/36 that was independently reproduced at three commits with a byte-identical failure set: zero new failures, zero regressions, one previously-failing test now passing which was deliberately not banked as a fix.
decisions: The fix removed the input rather than escaping it: both string-taking helpers are gone and the public interface now takes a closed artifact enum, so there is no string left to escape. Escaping would have preserved the hazard and added a correctness burden that must hold forever. The check the compiled-out assertion was making now runs in release, agent-side, on every operation - which also covers the case the crate's own unit test cannot, a daemon built at a different revision sending an entry the current set does not contain.

Read and write authority were separated at the same time: the artifact enum marks which files are writable, and the agent refuses a write to the one the resolver owns. Read access no longer implies write access, which was previously true by omission rather than by decision.

The duplicate-execution export was reverted rather than kept, and the cross-check moved to the side that already owns the module, held in step with the sender by a shared count assertion on both lists with each naming the other. The structural fix - having the binary consume the library's modules instead of recompiling them - would restore the export for free but is a restructuring of that crate rather than an egress-plane change, so the reason was left where the next person tempted to add that export will be standing, with the measured numbers.

The egress-enforcement pass is explicit and clean: nothing in this session's work can result in traffic escaping unenforced. All eight artifact pairings were verified to call the production generator and the production op constructor rather than a copy, so the assertion is that the bytes the call site sends equal the bytes the generator produces. Framing was confirmed against a fixture containing the frame delimiter itself and a forged protocol request, which stays inside the JSON string rather than becoming a frame, and a body of over a hundred kilobytes crosses intact with no truncating cap on either read path.

All seven previously-public argv and write helpers are confirmed absent rather than merely unused, the release-live validation runs unconditionally on every operation, and the single surviving shell interpolates only static constants with every producible body pinned as a literal in a test. The three behaviour changes were each judged incapable of weakening enforcement: a write budget where there was none can only convert a wedge into a fail-closed rollback, the environment scrub matches what the deleted helpers did manually, and creating a parent directory can only turn a failure into a success.

A previously-failing test now passes and was deliberately NOT banked as this session's fix. The session does touch the plausible surface, but every counter that would register a changed re-arm is identical to the previous run, so nothing structural moved and a known load-sensitive test simply landed on the good side once. Recorded as unresolved-but-favourable rather than claimed. Distinguishing a fix from variance would need repeated in-suite runs.
discoveries: The dangerous site was not the one flagged. The spec pointed at a shell interpolation guarded only by an assertion compiled out of release builds, whose real exposure turned out to be nil - every caller passed compile-time constants, so the defect was that safety rested on invisible call-site convention. Its sibling was worse: the write helper was public and re-exported, so the crate's public interface accepted an arbitrary string path destined for a shell string. An unguarded public entry point with no caller through it beats a vanishing guard with only safe callers.

The stats endpoint takes a REGEX in its filter parameter, so a free-form filter reads whatever it likes off the admin surface - cluster membership, upstream addresses, transport counters. Two readers of that same endpoint existed and only one had been enumerated, which is the same hazard as the free-form inspection template one endpoint over. Both now share a single variant with anchored constant queries, so neither can widen into a neighbouring counter family. The subsystem-versus-shape argument that got this taken was incidental; the real reason was a read-surface hole.

A test-count delta that does not match the attribute delta is a defect rather than bookkeeping, and checking it takes seconds. Here it caught a duplicate execution: exporting a module from the library target made that target compile and run ninety-three unit tests a second time, because the binary target already declared its own copy. Measured per-target rather than in aggregate, the accounting closed exactly - a hundred and twenty-four apparent new tests were ninety-three duplicates plus thirty-one real ones, matching the attribute count precisely.

The two test commands genuinely do run different sets - the make target passes feature flags that a bare workspace run does not, and without them a set of feature-gated unit tests compiles in neither target. The difference is four tests, not the hundred and five that prompted the check. So both facts are true and only one was the cause: quote which command produced a baseline, and do not let a real methodological finding absorb an unexplained number it does not account for.

The enforcement direction was positively confirmed rather than merely un-contradicted: all nine blocking-direction tests passed in this run and both references, and reading every one of the thirty-five failing assertions found none saying something got through that should have been blocked. The only traffic-level failure is OVER-blocking - allowed traffic failing closed, which is the safe direction. The egress plane also armed as often as before by counter, so the passes are not passes-by-absence.

One failure changed shape and was shown to be oscillation rather than novelty by finding the identical shape in the pre-previous run and reproducing the test in isolation, where it advances past the changed leg. A second test oscillated the opposite way between the same two runs. So a changed signature is not automatically a new signature, and the cheap discriminator is whether the shape exists anywhere in the run history.

log.title: The three long-lived brokered streams
log.summary:
Moved all three long-lived streams onto the brokered path - the guest-agent transport, the SSH proxy pump, and the DNS-gate bridge that opens one stream per DNS query on the egress-allow critical path, which the original issue counted as two. All three now go through one seam with a closed three-variant destination enum carrying only a container name; the destination and the socket are rendered agent-side from constants, because a stream is a raw byte pipe and a caller-chosen destination would leave the closed op set bounding nothing.

The capacity question was the session's centre and the answer is structural rather than a headroom estimate: the gate's accept loop is strictly serial per session, so concurrent opens are bounded by session count and the query rate cannot reach the concurrency cap at all. At the cap an open waits, which resolves to no listener armed, no injection performed, and the resolved address meeting the deny path. The chain was verified end to end including its one non-obvious step - the resolver does answer the query, but answering has no egress consequence because the enforcement boundary is the firewall and proxy layer, not the resolver. The exhaustion test carries its own positive control, so the absence it observes is distinguishable from a broken fixture.

The token plumbing was generalised without a variant list: both sides work from one exhaustive match, so a new operation does not compile until someone declares which side of the line it is on. The deliberately un-forked gate listener was preserved rather than normalised, with the reason recorded where an optimiser would stand - two listeners cannot both bind one path, and the unlink-early option would make the second steal the first's socket rather than fail, so parallelising the gate for throughput would break it.

The remote-shell transport was measured rather than modelled: this platform ships a different rsync implementation from the one whose splitter everyone assumes, and the two disagree in three ways. A parser ported faithfully from the wrong one was caught by probing the real binary, and the parser now models only the intersection and refuses what they disagree about. The previous test used a naive whitespace split that agreed on simple inputs and modelled nothing. A latent break was also fixed: the agent's container transport named the host daemon and would have found no such container after ownership flips.

The async-I-O carve-out survived intact, and its note was found already stale - it named a site that no longer spawns anything, which is how a later sweep removes a carve-out whose reason it can no longer see. It now names every stream and both implementations, and records that the agent's case is stronger because its single-threaded runtime means blocking stalls the heartbeat and every other operation.

Three commits, 32 net-new tests, gates green at 2389 by make and 2385 bare, 183 skipped, 0 failed, clippy and fmt clean, review approved with the fail-closed chain verified. Container-scope end-to-end came in at 50 passed / 35 failed / 0 errors - zero delta on every axis, with failure and pass sets byte-identical to the reference, every stream counter identical, and enforcement over-blocking only with no bypass.
decisions: The stream seam takes no timeout argument at all, rather than accepting one and discarding it as the one-shot path does. That is stronger than discarding carefully - there is nothing to discard - and a wall-clock budget on a stream would be a budget on the session inside it. The one-shot discard remains unowned and is tracked separately so it does not fall between sessions.

The fail-closed chain is verified end to end, including the step that needed interrogating: the resolver does answer the query, but answering it has no egress consequence because the enforcement boundary is the firewall and proxy layer rather than the resolver. The response tells a process what to connect to; the firewall decides whether it can. Those are structurally different layers and only the second constitutes egress. No injection ran, the allow-set stayed empty, and the resolved address meets the deny path.

The carve-out note was stale before this session and is now accurate: it had named a site that no longer spawns anything, which is exactly how a later sweep removes a carve-out it can no longer see the reason for. It now names four streams and both implementations, keeps one canonical rationale, and records that the agent's case is stronger than the daemon's because its runtime is single-threaded - blocking it stalls the heartbeat and every other operation rather than only its own caller.
discoveries: The gate's open rate cannot exhaust the control lane's concurrency cap, and the reason is structural rather than headroom: its accept loop is strictly serial per session, so concurrent opens are bounded by session count and not by query rate at all. At the cap an open waits rather than proceeding, which resolves to no listener armed, no injection performed, and the resolved address meeting the deny path - fail-closed on the egress-allow critical path. Asserted with a test carrying its own positive control, so the absence observed in the first half is distinguishable from a broken fixture.

This platform ships a different rsync implementation from the one whose argument splitter everyone models, and the two disagree in three measurable ways including whether a tab separates words. A parser ported faithfully from the wrong implementation passed review and was wrong for the host it runs on; it was caught by probing the real binary with a script that dumps its own arguments. The previous test used a naive whitespace split that agreed on simple inputs and modelled nothing. The parser now models only the intersection and refuses inputs the two disagree about, which is the right verdict for a fragment shared by both platforms.

The gate's serial accept loop must not be parallelised for throughput, and the reason belongs in the code: two listeners cannot both bind one path, and the unlink-early option would make the second STEAL the first's socket rather than fail. Optimising an enforcement path is where good intentions do the most damage, and this is the sentence that stops it.

A third failure shape appeared for a test already known to oscillate between two, and was correctly treated as potentially new rather than waved through on the strength of the test's reputation. Diagnosed: the preset names three domains and the propagation gate requires a cached address for each, but only two ever resolved, so the gate timed out one step earlier than the known shapes - caught earlier precisely because the domain that flaked is the one the test never subsequently fetches. Confirmed by isolation, where it falls through to the known shape. Class membership unchanged.

Two daemon-log shapes differed from the reference and both were explained rather than counted: one was this session's own rewording of an existing message with a byte-identical payload, and the other a pre-existing branch dating to May that had simply never fired in the reference run - total teardown errors unchanged, with one landing in the benign bucket instead of the noisy one. A new log shape is not automatically a new failure mode, and the discriminator is whether the branch predates the change.

log.title: In-VM limactl shell and copy operations
log.summary:
Replaced the in-machine shell and copy operations with eleven typed brokered operations - the last of four op families, and the one previously owned by no phase. Enumerable three ways with count assertions on each, so a new variant fails a count before it can ship uncovered.

The headline is a security fix rather than a refactor. The firewall baseline was previously written to a fixed path under the machine's sticky temporary directory and applied by a SECOND call, so between the two the policy sat rewritable by anything running as that machine's login user - and the shell operation hands that user out. Stickiness protects an owner from deletion by others, not from overwriting by that owner. Collapsing the two sites into one operation that streams the ruleset to standard input removes the window structurally rather than shortening it, and also removes a heredoc whose correctness rested on the generator never emitting its terminator - checked by nothing, in a document whose purpose is to change.

That change made a second one load-bearing: with the payload on standard input, a privilege escalation that decides it wants a password reads that password FROM the payload, consuming policy text as a credential attempt rather than hanging. The non-interactive flag makes it refuse instead. That invariant was initially documented and spot-checked but not enforced - found by the author self-auditing after being told nothing further was needed - and is now bound across the whole operation set by a mutation-verified test predicating on whether an operation carries a body.

Where the container families' reasoning did not transfer was recorded rather than assumed. The provisioning files must travel as content rather than paths because they live owner-only in the daemon's directory and the agent cannot read them - a correctness requirement, not hygiene.
