The file-creation mask had the opposite correct answer here, because these files are read inside the container as the session user rather than the owner, so the restrictive mask that protects keys elsewhere would have left a container unable to read its own authorized keys. And the no-shell claim does not hold on this transport at all - there is a login shell under every operation - so the narrower true claim was stated instead, with two of the author's own overstated doc lines corrected.

The count a later session depends on came back measured with sites named: one surviving ownership-blocked site, both its callers belonging to the route-helper session, and that site the sole remaining caller of the environment helper - so the later decision resolves to keep today and flips to delete the moment that session lands.

Two commits, 45 net-new tests, gates green at make 2434 and bare 2430, 183 skipped, 0 failed, clippy and fmt clean, review approved with an explicit enforcement sign-off on the combined state. Container-scope end-to-end matched the reference with set diffs empty in both directions on fully-qualified identifiers, the firewall baseline positively confirmed applied, the permission change confirmed healthy by direct capture, and no bypass.
decisions: The count owed to the later session came back as one surviving ownership-blocked site, both callers named and both belonging to the route-helper session. That site is also the sole remaining caller of the environment helper, so the later decision resolves to its keep branch today and flips to its delete branch the moment the route-helper session lands - which converts a judgment call into a consequence of already-planned work. The seam's degenerate-path implementation does spawn the binary but is deliberately not counted and has its own environment function, so the caller count stays a clean signal.

The gap is being closed as a follow-up commit rather than an amend, because a review is live against the reported hash and moving it under a mid-audit reviewer costs more than it saves. The earlier commit's message understates the closed window relative to the code documentation; that is being left rather than rewritten, because the strong statement already sits where a reader of that code meets it, and the follow-up commit's own message carries the strong version into history. Both properties without rewriting anything. The reviewer was told a follow-up is coming and that the enforcement sign-off applies to the combined state, since the invariant guarding the window is only enforced after the second commit.

The firewall-baseline operation has its explicit enforcement sign-off, and the reviewer confirmed the window independently rather than restating it: stickiness protects a file's owner from deletion by others but not from overwriting by that owner, and the owner is the login user the shell operation hands out. It also confirmed that the firewall tool commits in a single transaction after reading its whole input, so a truncated transfer is a parse failure rather than a partial policy - which matters because a default-drop chain arriving without its drop rule would be permissive.

The enforcement commit binds the two properties across the whole operation list rather than re-checking today's operations, and both escape routes are closed: a variant missing from the list fails the count assertion, and a variant on the list carrying a payload with an interactive privilege step fails the new test. The pre-existing tests were confirmed to check different things - one spot-checks a single builder, the other checks builders that carry no payload at all - so neither tied the two together. The enforcement sign-off now stands on the combined state of both commits.
discoveries: The firewall baseline had a time-of-check-to-time-of-use window on the enforcement path itself: the old shape wrote the ruleset to a fixed path under the machine's sticky temporary directory and applied it in a SECOND call, so between the two the policy sat where anything running as that machine's login user could rewrite it - and the shell operation hands that user out. Stickiness narrows the window without closing it. Collapsing the two sites into one operation that streams the ruleset to standard input removes the window structurally rather than shortening it.

Adding the non-interactive flag to the privileged in-machine steps is load-bearing rather than cosmetic, because standard input now carries the payload: without it, a privilege escalation that decides it wants a password reads that password FROM the command's standard input, which is the ruleset. The failure mode is not a hang but consuming policy text as a credential attempt. The flag makes it refuse instead. That interaction is invisible unless you know what standard input is carrying, and becomes invisible again the moment someone adds another payload-carrying operation.

The same code with the same intent had the opposite correct answer on this transport: the agent's existing operations use a restrictive file-creation mask so keys land private, but these staged files are read inside the container as the SESSION user rather than the owner, so that mask would have left a container unable to read its own authorized keys. Also, the claim of no shell does not hold here and was correctly narrowed rather than asserted - there is a login shell under every one of these operations, and what actually holds is that nothing builds a command line out of values while the tool quotes each argument so the remote shell re-parses the same words.

Documented and spot-checked is not enforced. The non-interactive-privilege invariant was written down and tested at two sites, but nothing tied CARRIES A PAYLOAD ON STANDARD INPUT to RENDERS NO INTERACTIVE PRIVILEGE STEP - so a future payload-carrying operation missing the flag would compile, pass every existing test, and silently restore the failure where policy text is consumed as a credential attempt. Found by the author self-auditing after being told nothing further was needed, which is the more valuable half of finding it at all.

The reviewer independently confirmed the spec row's caller count is one high, by grep and by adding up the row's own enumeration - the phrase naming four install steps covers three. Two independent measurements of the same figure now agree against the written one. Not corrected in place, consistent with the earlier ruling that recording the instruction to re-measure beats recording a fresher number.

The enforcement test was mutation-verified rather than trusted on a green run: the flag was dropped from the one operation that has the combination today, the test was confirmed to fail with a message naming the operation, the rendered step and the consequence, and the file was then restored with an empty diff confirmed. A guard nobody has seen fail is not yet a guard, and this is now the third session in which that check has caught or confirmed something.

The invariant was deliberately stated over the PAIR rather than as a blanket rule that every privileged step uses the non-interactive flag. A blanket rule would be true today and would not say why, which is exactly the property that goes invisible - the danger is not the privilege step alone nor the payload alone but their combination, and a rule that omits the reason survives until someone finds a counterexample to its stated form.

Concurrent agents on a shared host can void an end-to-end run without touching it: a workspace-wide test run relinks the daemon WITHOUT the harness's feature flag, which replaces the binary identity the code-signing cache was warmed for and re-arms the void-run trap mid-flight. The runner noticed two such runs live, waited for both before pre-building, and will check the binary's modification time at exit to detect a relink during the run. Worth generalising: when one agent's work depends on a build artifact's identity, another agent's routine verification can invalidate it silently.

The umask change is load-bearing rather than incidental, confirmed by direct in-machine capture rather than by absence of complaints: the staged files land world-readable under a group-writable directory, and the container runs as the operator's uid, so under the previous restrictive mask they would have been owner-only and unreadable. The corroboration that matters is that the forwarded-socket and guest-agent tests pass at all - the pump cannot succeed unless the container read the authorized-keys file the changed transfer staged.

The firewall baseline is positively confirmed applied rather than merely un-refuted: the apply counter matches both reference runs, a mid-run dump inside the machine shows the table present with its default-drop chain and closed allow-list intact, and the enforcement plane armed slightly MORE than the reference rather than less, tracking a higher count of resolver-change events. All ten blocking-direction tests passed for the third consecutive run.

log.title: Fail-closed pre-route window and durable bypass resistance
log.summary:
Closed the pre-route egress window on the lite backend, and converted a property an earlier gate could only observe as open into one the tree demonstrates. The durable bypass-resistance test now passes end to end in the suite, non-vacuously: its controls are assertions rather than diagnostics, so passing entails the route helper's route asserted present before any mutation, the allowed URL reachable through it, the bypass route installed and the gateway route confirmed absent, the container still resolving on-link while bypassed, the bypass probe failing, and egress returning on restore.

The property required THREE changes, not one, and that is a spec finding rather than an implementation detail: removing the bridge translation forces the gateway's default route onto the egress network, and that move requires the enforcement chain to admit the egress-side source, because the chain was source-scoped to the address the old route selected. The section proposing the two means did not anticipate the collision. Established by a completed matrix - each half breaks allowed egress independently, by different mechanisms with different signatures, a fast reset when the gateway's own filter refuses its source and a slow timeout when its traffic dies untranslated.

The first attempt shipped the first two changes and regressed twelve tests. That was caught by the full-scope run, and attributing it took three readings: an over-claimed attribution, an over-corrected withdrawal on a control that was not sufficient, and finally a controlled experiment - the comparator commit passing on the same host with the resolver measured dead at both ends, and the outcome alternating three times inside eighteen minutes, tracking code rather than clock. The cell that settled it was one both the implementer and I had treated as optional.

The reusable lesson is about the stand-in: the evidence that allowed egress survived was measured on a container wired to resemble production, which structurally could not carry the per-session policy chain the daemon injects into a real gateway. Its limits were labelled correctly and a conclusion was still drawn beyond them. A stand-in cannot test a property that lives in the thing it stands in for.

The enforcement edit was kept as its own commit and carried its own egress-enforcement review, with the verdict that nothing can now get out that could not before: the source predicate was widened by exactly one address, both belonging to the gateway container itself, the destination allow-set is untouched, the chain still ends in a refusal, and a test iterates every allow-set rule asserting each still begins with a source match. Persisting the egress address is load-bearing rather than tidy, because the ruleset is re-rendered every propagation pass and a pass that could not see it would have unwound the fix seconds after create.

The criterion demanding a refusal signature was amended with measurements rather than cleared, because removing the translation removes the last thing on the path capable of sending one. The other platform's check reached its negative branch - that platform's gateway has a single interface on the session bridge, so its translation carries every allowed flow - and the change is scoped accordingly. The networking document was corrected to the measured topology on both backends rather than the intended one.

Eight commits, gates green at make 2443 and clippy and fmt clean, review approved across every commit including the enforcement edit. Container scope re-cleared at 51 passed against 35 failed of 87 with set diffs empty both directions and all thirteen regressions gone; full scope at 74 against 86 of 161, the single deviation being a catalogued oscillator returning to a shape recorded in this repository before this session existed, in the over-blocking direction, with the other backend's half holding member for member for the second consecutive run.
decisions: The fail-closed change goes in at TWO sites, not one: the create path and the recreate-on-restart path. Closing only the first would make the property true until the first bounce, which is worse than not claiming it. The typed carrier for the option already existed from the container-lifecycle session, complete with a doc comment saying it exists for exactly this purpose and agent-side validation accepting it - it was simply never set. The alternative means closes the window but not the bypass, so it cannot carry the durable test.

A timeout can be made discriminating rather than being forbidden outright, and this resolves the tension between the criterion and the likely topology. The criterion forbids a bare timeout because it is indistinguishable from a broken test - a wrong address, an unbuilt container, a request never issued - not because slowness is uninformative. Pairing the same request over the same path from the same container AFTER the route is installed, and requiring it to succeed quickly, turns an absence into evidence: the request works in one state and hangs in the other with one variable between them. The paired assertion must fail if the control does not succeed, or a comprehensively broken fixture passes both halves.

The signature the criterion mandates is unachievable by this fix, measured rather than argued: with the translation rule removed the packet IS forwarded out of the machine un-translated and dies beyond it, and nothing on that path can emit a reset or an error, so a black hole is the only thing removing the rule can produce. Three measured rows separate the states - open in ninety-four milliseconds, closed at eight seconds, and closed in three milliseconds only if a refusal rule is added. The criterion is being amended with that evidence rather than cleared, because a clause the correct fix cannot satisfy is a clause to amend.

The durable test's middle leg is stronger than the bracketing I proposed and the improvement is worth naming: before-and-after controls alone leave open that the container broke between them, since a fixture that dies mid-test fails the probe and cannot pass the third leg, but nothing in the test can see the ordering of those failures. Asserting that the container still resolves names through the gateway WHILE the bypass route is installed proves liveness in the failing state itself, because resolution is on-link and does not travel the default route. An exit-code set would have been the weaker check here, not the stronger one.

The route-election knob landed as a nullary variant rather than a caller-supplied number, which is the closed-set discipline applied where it was not obviously required - a numeric priority field would have been the natural shape and would have handed the caller control over which interface wins the default route. The adjacent leg on the other backend attaches the same way and was named as an observation rather than touched, because it belongs to the routing defect that is explicitly not this session's.

That adjacent measurement was deliberately left as a lead rather than promoted to an explanation: the spec records it as measured and states explicitly that no claim is made that it accounts for the catalogued failures on that backend, which are a guest-side missing route in a different place. An adjacent measurement that looks like it explains a known defect is exactly what gets over-read later, so the restraint is the valuable part.

The version requirement is stated to its evidence rather than asserted: verified working on the installed version, documented as introduced in an earlier one, lower bound explicitly not measured. What WAS measured is the property that makes an unmeasured floor tolerable - an unsupported flag exits with an error, names the flag, and does not attach the container, verified by inspecting afterwards - so an older daemon yields a refused create rather than a session on a mis-wired network. The remaining half of that chain is labelled as a code read.

Approved on all four commits. The window closes and stays closed across a restart, because both the create and the recreate paths read from one options function - so a session whose bridge was destroyed and rebuilt cannot come back with different egress properties. The other platform's route is genuinely untouched, emitting no such option at all. The durable test's three-way bracket was confirmed to fail if either control leg fails, and to reject a resolver failure separately so a broken resolver cannot masquerade as a pass.

The full-scope run is being graded against TWO comparators of different sharpness, reported separately rather than merged. The container half has been tracked continuously across five runs with a byte-identical failure set and is sharp. The full-backend half has not been measured since the baseline eight sessions ago, so drift there is expected and is not attributable to this session - whose change is scoped to the in-machine route and cannot touch it. A single headline number over a mixed-sharpness comparison would be worse than useless.

S14's review is complete across all six commits. The loud-failure chain decomposes into three measured steps and one labelled code read, and the reviewer caught that the doc comment cites the new test for the setup function's error propagation WITHOUT claiming the handler teardown is tested - a precision that keeps a label honest as code moves around it. The sabotage analysis is the subtle part worth keeping: the recording route refuses every attach regardless of the option, so a reverted call site would still error and still satisfy the failure expectation - only the recorded-operation assertion catches it. A weaker test would have passed the revert while appearing to cover it.

This is precisely the gap the session named itself: its evidence that allowed egress survives with the translation rule removed was measured on a STAND-IN gateway wired to resemble production, not on a real session, and the author stated that limit explicitly and said a real session needs this run. So the failing hypothesis is not a surprise - it is the thing the stated limits left open, and it must not be discounted because a review approved the change. The review approved evidence that was correctly labelled as not covering this case.

S14's exit clause is NOT met and the session does not close: the change broke allowed egress on the lite path, with twelve outright regressions from passing to failing including plain allowed-domain and repository-clone tests that involve none of the new test's mutation. Attribution is unambiguous - six commits separate the comparator from the head and five are tests or documents, leaving one functional change. Direction is over-blocking rather than a bypass; no deny-side assertion fired anywhere in the run.

RETRACTION of the attribution I relayed: I called the twelve regressions unambiguously attributable to this session's one functional commit, on the grounds that everything else in the window was tests or documents. That reasoning silently assumed the environment was constant between the comparator run and today, and it was not. The counts stand; the cause does not. I amplified a grader's over-claim into a certainty and dispatched the author to hunt a defect that may not exist.

The discriminating experiment is the same failing test at the comparator commit on this host as it stands - same environment, different code - rather than repairing the resolver and re-running. Those answer different questions: repairing tests the environment and would show the resolver SUFFICIENT to cause this without showing the change innocent, since both could contribute. Repairing must also wait, because the broken state is the evidence the experiment needs. If the comparator commit fails too, the reverse control at the head is also required, since a resolver that rotates upstreams on failure can rotate back between measurements.

Attribution settled by controlled experiment, and it moved back: the change IS at fault. The comparator commit passes on this host with the resolver measured dead immediately before and after, and the pass-fail outcome alternates three times inside eighteen minutes while that resolver stays dead throughout - so it tracks the code and not the clock, which a rotating resolver cannot produce. The dead resolver is a real latent defect but is not the cause.

The fix threads the egress-side address into the enforcement rule rather than dropping the source predicate, because dropping it would let anything originating in the gateway's network namespace reach an allowed destination - trading enforcement for enforcement to make a hardening change work. Only the gateway's own processes are in that namespace today, and today-only is the form of reasoning this milestone has punished repeatedly. Two things must be established by measurement: whether both addresses are needed or only one, and what the predicate still excludes after the edit - if that cannot be stated, the edit is too wide.

The completed matrix overturns the previous conclusion: BOTH halves break allowed egress independently, by two different mechanisms, and the differing signatures prove they are two failures rather than one flaky one - a fast reset when the gateway's own filter refuses its source, a slow timeout when its traffic dies past the machine untranslated. So the route pin is not a mistake to drop. Removing the translation requires the pin, and the pin requires the enforcement chain to admit the egress-side source. All three move together or none of them do. This came from running a cell I had treated as optional.

Sequenced as two commits so the enforcement edit stays separately reviewable: first restore the already-reviewed change, then thread the egress-side source into the output chain as its own commit carrying the enforcement review the phase requires. The separation is the whole reason the implementer stopped rather than continuing, and it should survive into the history rather than being folded into a single fix. Three things must be established in that second commit: what the source predicate still excludes, whether one address or both are needed, and that the value the rule receives is the one the kernel will actually use as source rather than one that merely ought to match.

The property is delivered as three changes moving together: the translation rule removed, the route pinned to the egress network, and the gateway's own output chain given its egress-side source. The source predicate was kept rather than dropped, so the chain still admits only the gateway container's own two addresses with the destination still decided by the allow set and the chain still ending in a refusal. Both addresses were measured necessary for different legs - the session-side pair carries name resolution, the egress-side pair carries the upstream leg that the moved route now sources.

The enforcement edit is approved with an explicit verdict that nothing can now get out that could not before. The source predicate was widened by exactly one address, both belonging to the gateway container itself; the destination allow-set is unchanged; the fall-through refusal is unchanged; and a test iterates every allow-set rule in the chain asserting each still begins with a source match, so an unscoped rule cannot be added silently. The reviewer confirmed the propagation loop reads the persisted value every couple of seconds, which is what makes persistence load-bearing rather than tidy.

The container-scope clause is met: fifty-one passed against thirty-five failed of eighty-seven, exactly the target, with set diffs empty in both directions on fully-qualified identifiers and all thirteen regressions cleared. The bypass test passed non-vacuously - its controls are assertions rather than diagnostics, so the pass entails every leg including that the container still resolved through the gateway while bypassed. The enforcement chain was captured live mid-run and is measurably narrower rather than looser: the destination allow-set is untouched and only the gateway's own second address was added as a permitted source.

The full-scope clause is being MEASURED rather than argued, despite a strong composition available: the enforcement change renders byte-identically when the new field is absent, that is pinned by a test, and the field is only ever set on the lite path - so the other backend is unaffected by construction. But the criterion names the full scope, the last full measurement was of the broken commit, and this session has already demonstrated that a plausible scope argument can be wrong. Machine time is the cheap resource here; the difference between a clause met and a clause argued is not.

The single deviation does not matter, for three measured reasons rather than one argued one: the daemon side is identical to the run where it passed, down to the same compiled-policy hash; the failure is the OPPOSITE of the regression the test guards, which is broken hydration causing a denied destination to start resolving, whereas here resolution failed; and the limitation was stated honestly - because the allowed assertion precedes the denied one, the post-restart denied leg was not evaluated this run, though it was measured passing at this same commit in the container re-clear.
discoveries: The platform check reached its NEGATIVE branch, which is the check working rather than a scope reduction. On the other platform the gateway container has a single interface on the session bridge itself and the egress network does not exist there at all, so that bridge IS the uplink and its translation rule carries every allowed flow - disabling it would kill allowed egress on both backends. A green suite on this platform would never have surfaced that, which is precisely why the criterion said a suite pass is not the check.

Disabling the translation rule alone would have shipped broken, and finding out why exposed a documentation error. Attaching the session bridge MOVES the gateway container's default route onto it, so allowed egress currently leaves through the session bridge's translation rather than through the egress network - which contradicts what the networking document says the topology is. Without a companion priority pin the gateway itself loses the internet once the rule is removed. The pin was measured to restore it.

The mechanism is now stated in one sentence that will survive re-reading: removing the translation rule does not stop the packet, only the translation, so it still leaves the machine and dies where nothing holds a port to refuse it or has reason to send an error. A refusal has to be SENT by something, and this fix removes the last thing on the path that could send one. The amendment includes the row showing the mandated signature IS achievable and by what, so it reads as a deferral with a known price rather than an unreachable ideal, and closes by telling the reader not to mistake the deferral for an open bypass.

Correcting the documentation required a fresh measurement and changed what the correction says: replicating the OTHER backend's wiring showed the default-route election moves the same way there, after which its container cannot reach the internet at all because the attached network's isolation mode blocks it. So the document's route row described neither path. It was corrected to separate the topology's intent from which interface actually carries the route on each backend.

A clarity gap worth fixing was found in the test rather than the code: it reconstructs the pre-route state with a privileged exec from outside, because the session container drops all capabilities and cannot re-enter a state it was born in - but a reader can come away thinking the bypass REQUIRES privilege to exploit. It does not; the window is the state the container starts in, before any process runs. That distinction is the difference between a defect anyone hits for free and one needing root, and the second reading would undersell it to exactly the person deciding whether the fix mattered.

Pressing on an evidence label produced a measurement rather than a defence: the half that had been read was converted into a hermetic test driving the real setup path over a recording route that returns the failure, asserting the refusal propagates with both the bridge and the underlying message named. The chain now rests on one code read instead of two. The same test also pins the option at the production call site, which nothing covered before - the argument-rendering tests proved the flag renders, not that the code asking for it asks for it.

Three times today a read of the working tree was accurate when taken and falsified by the act it was reporting on - a file grepped just before its commit, a status showing modifications mid-write, a log missing a commit landing seconds later. Each time the agent's response was right: show the evidence rather than assert the state. In a tree several agents write to, a status read is a timestamp and not a state, and the durable habit is to say WHEN a read was taken rather than what is true. I have not been consistent about that and it has cost three round trips.

The cross-agent relink hazard fired for real rather than theoretically: a reviewer verifying a test with a workspace-scoped run was about to invalidate the binary identity an eighty-minute measurement depends on. The runner caught it and held rather than launching on top. Package-scoped runs do not have this effect - only workspace-wide ones relink the daemon the harness stages - so the mitigation is a scope restriction rather than a moratorium, and the reviewer was told to say if a sound check needs a workspace run, in which case the measurement moves rather than the check weakening.

The installed operator agent binary predates ten commits that touched its crate, including this session's two new wire variants - measured from the install timestamp against the log, not assumed. It is harmless today because operations whose owner uid equals the daemon uid dispatch to a daemon-local executor and the gateway machine is daemon-owned, so the in-machine operations this session changes never reach the agent at all. Corroborated empirically: the previous session also touched that crate and graded clean on this same binary. The other backend's half does route operator-uid control-plane operations through it, which is a further reason drift there is not attributable to this session.

Direct live measurement during the killed run established that the translation-rule change genuinely reaches the container daemon: three separate session bridges were captured mid-run carrying the disable option. The version explanation was also eliminated - the in-machine daemon supports the priority flag. So neither the change failing to apply nor the flag being unsupported explains the failures, which narrows the question to whether the companion pin is effective on the path production actually takes.

The other backend's half of the same run reproduced its eight-session-old baseline member-for-member across ten catalogued classes, with zero uncatalogued failures and zero newly passing. That is what makes the regressions non-environmental: a run that held seventy-four tests of one backend perfectly stable did not break twelve of the other by accident. The stale comparator turning out to be exact is also worth knowing on its own - eight sessions of expected drift did not materialise.

The failure symptom is not what a missing route looks like: a reset by peer in under half a second rather than a timeout, and not the resolver failure code. Fast reset means the session's traffic REACHES the gateway and the gateway resets it, with the control plane fully healthy - components ready, no proxy errors, no panics. Control plane up, data plane broken. Two explanations are already eliminated by measurement: the change does reach the container daemon, and the version does support the pin.

Both hypotheses about the fix are refuted by measurement. The priority pin works: the gateway container's kernel routing table on a live session shows its default route on the egress bridge, not the session bridge, and the container inspection agrees. And production does reach the pinned call site - there are exactly two connect sites, correctly differentiated, with no unpinned second path and no create-already-attached route.

The likely real cause touches none of the changed code: a plain container on the egress bridge, with no session and no session bridge in the path, reaches an IP address fine and fails to resolve a name. The machine's stub resolver has selected a non-functional address-family upstream, so it has working IP egress and no working name resolution. All twelve regressions are resolution-shaped, and this is the same failure the affected test's own docstring describes as previously fixed. The machine has been up three days and its resolver rotates upstreams on failure, so it degrades with no code change.

The cause is the route-priority pin rather than the translation-rule removal: a variant with the translation change neutralised and the pin retained still fails with the identical connection-reset signature, so the pin alone is sufficient. The apparent paradox resolves because the pin does exactly what it claims - the gateway's default route lands on the egress network, measured - and doing what it claims is what breaks it. A reset in under half a second from a fully healthy control plane is consistent with something accepting the connection and finding nothing behind it.

A durable separation worth reusing: the graded counts and the attribution are recorded as distinct sections, with a note saying the measurement of WHAT happened did not change across three successive readings of WHY. Without that fence, a correction to the cause reads as reopening the result, and each reversal costs the whole document its credibility rather than one paragraph. The evidence table for the attribution was also moved into the document rather than living only in a message, since evidence that exists only in a conversation is lost when the conversation is.

Root cause found and it is a collision, not a bug in either half. The gateway's own output chain admits originated traffic only while its source is its address ON THE SESSION BRIDGE, which holds only while its default route points there. Moving the route made the source the egress-side address, no rule matched, and the chain's fall-through refusal fired. That predicts every observation: health checks green because they go over loopback, established flows fine because they match the connection-tracking rule, and the data plane dead in whichever leg trips first - resolver failure, upstream reset, or a fast refusal on the deny path.

The two means the spec names are jointly unsatisfiable as written: leave the route alone and the gateway's traffic dies past the machine untranslated, move it and its own filter rejects it. That is a spec finding rather than an implementation defect - the section proposes both without noticing that one collides with a standing dependency in the enforcement chain, and the next person choosing between them needs to know the second has a prerequisite.

The most reusable lesson is about the stand-in: it was wired like production and pinned like production, and could not have the one thing that decides the outcome - the per-session policy chain the daemon injects into a real gateway container. Its limits were labelled correctly and a conclusion was still drawn that those limits did not support. The lesson is not to label harder; it is that a stand-in cannot test a property living in the thing it stands in for, and the gap between the wiring works and the gateway works is exactly that chain.

My proposed mechanism was measured false and reported as such: the address-discovery command returns identical ordering with and without the pin, so the value the loggers bind to does not change, and the two proxies bind elsewhere entirely. The catalogued bind-mismatch shape is real and is not what fires here. Asking for a hypothesis to be tested rather than adopted is only worth something if being told it is wrong is a welcome answer.

Persisting the egress-side address is not incidental but load-bearing: the ruleset is re-rendered on every propagation pass, so a pass that could not see the address would quietly undo the fix seconds after create. That is the difference between a fix and a fix that lasts three seconds, and it is the kind of thing that would have presented as intermittent rather than broken.

A measurement taken in the wrong state gives the right answer for the wrong reason, and it is nearly undetectable. The first capture of which source address the kernel would select landed BEFORE the session bridge was attached, so the only address present was trivially the answer - it would have read as confirmation and confirmed nothing. Re-measured in the state the gateway actually runs in, with both interfaces up and the route moved, the kernel's per-destination choice agrees with what the daemon read from the container runtime. The agreement is now measured rather than assumed, and the near-miss is the more useful half.

The address the rule receives is the address the kernel selects, and the reason is structural rather than coincidental: the gateway is started on the egress network and attached to the session bridge with a priority that declines the default-route election, so the default route stays on the egress network and the kernel sources from the interface carrying it. An unreadable address is a hard error that aborts gateway setup rather than rendering a chain missing its rule.

The void-run trap's framing has been carrying a wrong mechanism, corrected by measurement: the feature flag gates the route-helper's configuration seam, not the daemon's, which honours its environment override unconditionally. So a relink without the flag is not itself the hazard - the hazard is a relink at all, because it changes the binary identity the code-signing cache was warmed for. The trap is real and its cause is the relink, not the feature set. Worth correcting because a mitigation aimed at the wrong mechanism protects by luck.

A build system reporting everything fresh in a fraction of a second, and declining to re-place the artifact, is a state in which you cannot tell by inspection which variant is on disk. The runner stopped inferring and forced the question - touched a source file, rebuilt, and produced an artifact whose timestamp unambiguously precedes the measurement window. Freshness reported by the tool is not the same as knowing what the tool left behind.

A rebuild intended to disarm the void-run trap silently no-opped because the build tool was not on the shell's path, returning a command-not-found status the runner caught rather than proceeding on. It then verified the artifact was the intended variant by finding a feature-gated symbol INSIDE the binary rather than trusting the build's own success line. Verifying the artifact rather than the tool's report is the difference between disarming the trap and believing you did.

A host-state observation an earlier session recorded as inert for the narrower scope is NOT inert at full scope, exactly as that session predicted: the per-operator machine home has lost its base-image metadata, so the fixture that would short-circuit will instead rebuild the base image under a long budget, and a failure there converts test failures into fixture errors - a shape the comparator does not have. Flagged before the run rather than discovered as an unexplained delta afterwards.

My list of catalogued oscillators was incomplete and the grader corrected it with citations rather than accepting the brief: the flipped test is a FOURTH test on the same resolver-flake class, recorded in this repository's own handoffs before this session existed - failing in-suite with that exact assertion and passing on an isolated rerun at the same commit, and noted elsewhere as a flake that migrates between tests run to run. Under the brief's own rule it is not a previously-stable test. A brief that enumerates known noise must be treated as a starting point, not a closed set.

The other backend's half held with all four set diffs empty, member for member, for the second consecutive full-scope run. The base image did rebuild as predicted and completed in thirty-five seconds against a three-minute budget, so the fixture-error shape the comparators lack never appeared - which is why the wall clock landed within eight seconds of the comparator despite the extra work.

log.title: Typed route-helper broker operation
log.summary:
Landed the typed in-VM operation seam and then audited the security-relevant prose around it, which turned out to be the more productive half. Auditing comments against the code they describe surfaced a functional gap that a clean code review had passed: the route helper would install a default route on a caller's say-so, so it now refuses unless the gateway address sits on a subnet the namespace itself reports, and it resolves its helper binary from a fixed list rather than the environment.

The prose audit corrected several claims that were confidently wrong about kernel behaviour. The ptrace access check compares real credentials rather than effective ones; a capability held in a parent user namespace does not promote to all capabilities in a child; and the ambient-capability requirement that a dependency comment stated unconditionally holds only for a non-root parent, since a root parent receives the full bounding set across exec. Each was measured on Linux rather than reasoned about, and two of them had already reached the user-facing installation guide.

A capability check comparing getcap output by substring was fixed to compare capability sets at eleven sites across five files. It was fail-open in one direction, accepting a superset of the intended capabilities, and fail-closed in the other: against the rendering used by older libcap releases it rejected a correctly capped binary and aborted a correct install, which had not been reported before. Nine scenarios now cover it, five of them demonstrated red against the pre-fix code.

Four commits, nothing pushed. The recurring failure this session was relaying measurements without the conditions that scoped them, including a count I widened from one file to three while keeping its number.
decisions: Taking the resolver repair BEFORE any of this session's code exists, rather than after, and measuring it in isolation against a clean tree. The previous session spent significant time on an attribution bisect precisely because an environment condition and a code change were in flight together; repairing a known-broken environment on top of new code would reproduce that trap exactly. A container-scope run against a clean tree yields a delta attributable to one cause, and becomes the reference the session's own gate is compared against.

Gated the repair on a classification the agent must make before acting: state-only repairs are applied, but if the bad resolver configuration originates in tracked source - the image, a template, or emitted daemon config - the agent must stop and report rather than change it. A source fix would be undone by the next machine re-create, and more importantly it is production behaviour that belongs in a planned session with review, not in an environment-repair errand.

Redirected the in-flight measurement instead of letting it run as briefed: the before/after on the MECHANISM - what the resolver is configured with and what it actually returns, measured from inside the machine and from inside a container, captured both before and after the repair - becomes the primary deliverable, and the suite run is demoted to a gate reference with an explicitly narrow claim scope. Declined to escalate to full scope, which is where the timeout population lives, because the confound makes any movement there unattributable: roughly two hours for a signal that could not be assigned to a cause, versus a direct measurement that answers it in minutes.

Corrected my own todo's premise rather than letting the errand run on it. The item claimed the dead stub was the plausible common cause of the oscillator class; that was my inference and it is probably false. The repair is still worth doing for what it actually fixes, but the capture must cover all three resolver legs including a guest-side lookup through a live session - the awkward leg, needing a session stood up for it, and the only one on the oscillators' path. Confining the capture to the stub would demonstrate a real repair that moves nothing test-visible and invite reading a clean run as confirmation.

Required the capture to establish dead versus intermittent by repeated observation per leg with reported counts, not an adjective. A resolver that fails intermittently, sampled once before and once after, yields a before/after signature that is not real - the identical single-observation trap that has already produced one wrong diagnosis in this milestone.

PRE-REGISTERED, before the numbers exist: the post-repair container-scope run must REPRODUCE the prior re-clear exactly - 51 passed, 35 failed, 0 errors, 1 skipped of 87, with an empty set difference in both directions on fully-qualified test ids. Rationale for the prediction: the only failure positively attributed to the machine stub is an image-pull leg, that test is on the other backend half, and no container-half test touches the golden-image, rebuild or image-pull path at all. A correctly-scoped stub repair should therefore move zero container tests.

Pre-registered differential too: a deviation confined to the two known container-scope oscillators is flake and says nothing about the repair; a deviation ANYWHERE ELSE is the repair perturbing something and blocks. The prediction is void if the repair turns out to touch the per-session DNS path, the gateway image, or the container DNS server rather than the machine stub alone - and I must learn that before grading, not after.

Withholding the pre-registered expectation from the agent producing the numbers, and keeping it with the verifier that authored it. An author told the expected result can rationalise a deviation into agreement or report a match without checking closely. The producing agent is being asked only for raw counts, full id sets, and an explicit statement of what the repair touched.

Commissioned a second, independent read of the three spec passages the session's principal decision rests on, deliberately withholding the first reader's conclusions and instructing the second not to open the first's handoff until its own answer is committed to disk. The decision turns on a claim that the spec contradicts itself, which so far rests on a single reader; a second reader who has absorbed the first's framing is not a second reader. The comparison is only worth something if the independence is real.

PRINCIPAL DECISION TAKEN - the property is NOT being pursued in this phase, and the reason is now measured rather than argued. The wanted property is that an interactive shell into the machine is not by itself a route-rewrite primitive. Narrowing the dedicated grant cannot deliver it, which the spec already asserted; the measurement confirms it and goes further.

The spec's own first option is INSUFFICIENT, which the spec does not say. It proposes a distinct in-machine principal for brokered operations - a separate account plus its own identity - but the interactive login user retains blanket elevation regardless, so it could still invoke the helper directly. Delivering the property additionally requires removing that blanket right from the login user, which is impossible without relocating every privileged provisioning step - directory creation, install, mode change, capability set, and the firewall baseline load - onto the distinct principal too. The property's true cost is re-architecting all in-machine privilege, not adding an account: several phases, not a criterion.

The control that DOES land is the subnet containment check, and it is worth having on its own terms: it closes the arbitrary-address case entirely, leaving only the narrower case of an address inside the session's own small prefix. The documentation rewrite must claim exactly that and must not say the perimeter was restored, because it was not - what exists afterwards is one real check plus a stated residual.

Keeping the dedicated single-binary grant rather than deleting it, despite the measurement showing it confers nothing today, and commenting it accurately instead. Deleting it would be a behaviour change beyond this phase and would remove a safety net that becomes load-bearing the moment the provisioning model stops handing the login user blanket rights. But leaving it uncommented invites precisely the misreading this session exists to correct - a reader seeing a single-binary grant infers a control that is not there - so the comment must state that it is currently redundant and under what change it would start to matter.

Spec conflict, unresolved: §5.2 requirement 2 and §4 Phase 3 criterion 4 conflict directly and neither text establishes precedence. My working interpretation - that criterion 4 supersedes requirement 2 so satisfying a branch discharges it - is falsified: it rested on an earlier-draft/later-revision asymmetry, but §5.2 self-identifies as the later revision in the same bullet, so that premise does not discriminate. Also corrected: the three branches belong to criterion 4; requirement 2 has one branch.

Adopting the assignment reading, provisionally and pending peer rebuttal: §5.1/§5.2/Phase 3 are one requirement at three altitudes, with §5.2 explicitly assigning its perimeter list to the route-helper phase, so Phase 3's criteria are its executable form rather than a competing text. Consequence: the doc rewrite is unblocked by a RECORDED DECISION on the sudoers question, not by a sudoers code change. Decisive support: the literal reading makes the doc rewrite permanently unsatisfiable, which is almost certainly not intended.

The perimeter doc rewrite will be briefed to a DIFFERENT agent than the one implementing the containment control, and written from the landed code rather than from the implementer's description of it. Rationale: the author of a change describes what they intended rather than what shipped, and a commit correcting an overclaim is the likeliest place to write a new one.

The route-helper subnet-containment control is defence in depth, not a boundary. It binds the gateway argument to the namespace it is installed into; it does NOT establish that the address is the session's assigned gateway, because root in the gateway VM can shape what a namespace reports and a small prefix admits many candidate addresses. This limit is stated in the module doc so later readers cannot upgrade the claim.

Git-tracked spec and delivery files under .tasks/ that name now-deleted symbols will NOT be edited. They are point-in-time intent recording what the work was meant to remove; rewriting them to match the landed tree is chasing intent backward, which the planning rules forbid. Durable surfaces (source, docs/) are clean, which is the property that actually matters.

The PATH-injection escalation will be fixed in this session as its own commit, separate from the typed-op work, even though it is pre-existing and out of the session's nominal scope. It is verified, exploitable by any enrolled operator, defeats the product's central guarantee, and lives in the same binary this session already modifies; shipping a security-hardening change to that binary while leaving it open is not defensible. The fix is a list of absolute candidate paths rather than one literal, because ip(8) sits at different locations on operator hosts and in the gateway VM.

The caller-controlled audit destination will NOT be fixed in this session. It is forensic only - no enforcement decision reads it, and a write failure never denies. The fix needs a real design decision rather than a patch: the helper holds no DAC-bypass capability and runs as the caller, so no single fixed path is writable by both the daemon and arbitrary operators without a shared group that reintroduces cross-operator tampering, and the two modes live in different filesystems. Deferred with the constraints recorded.

Correcting the route-helper's false doc claims and closing the PATH-injection escalation are one change, not two, because pinning an absolute path turns several currently-TRUE hazard disclosures into false ones. A stale 'we are vulnerable to X' comment misleads exactly as much as a stale 'we are safe from X', so the code fix and the prose it invalidates land together.

Declined to widen the existing grep-blind-spot memory with the new report that the failure also fires on ordinary tracked paths. That mechanism claim is unverified, the memory already records that its own stated mechanism has been wrong three times while its conclusion held, and the remedy it prescribes (explicit paths, the negating flag, or a known-hit control before trusting a clean sweep) is unchanged under either mechanism. Folding the check into the final verification pass instead of appending an unmeasured cause.

Writing no claim beat writing a true-but-unmeasured one. After the child's environment was cleared, a comment asserting the loader-injection variable cannot reach the child would have been true, and was still declined because nobody had measured the mechanism. In a file whose whole value is that its claims can be trusted, an unverified true sentence is a liability: it is indistinguishable from the verified ones and will be relied on the same way.

Holding the next correction pass until the adversarial code verification returns, rather than editing in parallel. That agent pinned the same files by checksum; editing under it would invalidate its line references and force a re-run, and the two findings that matter most from the latest audit are contradictions BETWEEN files that have to be fixed consistently in one pass anyway.

Fixing the production installer guard in this session rather than deferring it. The dev-side guard was just made strict, and leaving the production path looser than the development path inverts the intended relationship. The fix direction is fail-safe: an over-strict guard costs a redundant setcap, while the current bug silently accepts an over-capped privileged binary.

Briefing the CLI fix to determine per-site intent before changing anything, because one of the two functions is named as a single-capability presence probe. Converting a legitimate presence check into set equality would be a new defect wearing the fix's clothes. Also requiring every new test be demonstrated failing against the pre-fix predicate, after this session already produced two assertions that could never fail.

Leaving the advisory diagnostic's capability check lenient. It uses the same substring shape and an over-capped helper passes it, but it gates nothing, carries a written rationale for its leniency, and is user-facing. Tightening a diagnostic's verdict semantics changes what operators get told and deserves its own consideration rather than being swept in at the end of a session about something else. Recorded rather than silently fixed.

Authorising the correction of the same false userns claim in a fourth location that fell outside the correcting agent's assigned files. It is committed content, every other agent has finished so there is no ownership contention, and the measurement that falsifies it is already done. Leaving one copy behind is the specific trap where a later reader sees the corrected neighbours and assumes the crate was swept.

Commissioning an independent blind verification of the newly written prose rather than accepting the correcting agent's self-review. Self-review caught two false claims it had just introduced, which is evidence the risk is live rather than evidence it is handled. The verifier is deliberately not given the earlier measurements, so agreement means independent rederivation instead of confirmation.

Fixing the production installer's capability guard in this session rather than deferring it. The defect is one class in three places; two are fixed and the third is the installer that end users actually run, so stopping now would leave the production path looser than the development path it is supposed to be stricter than. That is the same reasoning already used to justify fixing the updater, and it applies with more force here.

Correcting the false log entry by appending a retraction rather than editing the store, consistent with the earlier decision. Rewriting a past entry to look correct destroys the record of when the belief changed, which is the more useful artifact than a tidy log.

Declining to propagate a precision improvement into a fourth site whose sentence is already true, on consistency grounds. Editing correct text so a family reads uniformly is churn that risks introducing a defect into the one place that did not have one, which is how correction passes manufacture work.

The namespace-corroboration work was committed as a feature rather than as documentation. It had been characterised as comment and prose corrections, but it adds a functional control that refuses a route install when the gateway address does not sit on a subnet the namespace reports, which defends against a caller invoking the helper directly under sudo inside the gateway VM and bypassing the daemon, broker and validator entirely.
discoveries: The guest-resolver flake is TWO shapes, not one, and they separate by backend half: a fast resolve failure and a resolve timeout. A black-holing stub resolver produces the TIMEOUT shape, and the container scope contains zero occurrences of it by construction - the entire timeout population sits on the other backend. So the container-scope run cannot support or refute a claim that repairing the resolver fixed the class; it speaks only to the fast-failure half, which is one or two tests.

Resolver-dead and route-missing are CONFOUNDED in the timeout shape. A guest with no default route at all - already catalogued as its own defect - also times out resolving, producing the identical signature. So movement in that population after a resolver repair would be ambiguous between two causes, and attributing it to the resolver would be unfounded.

Counting failure shapes by grepping stderr for the curl error string systematically under-reports, because tests invoking curl in silent mode surface only a return code and emit no matching string. A real occurrence was missed exactly this way, and the miss made a false conserved-count story look supported by the numbers. Shape counting must be per-test or return-code based; the grep is not a valid instrument for it.

There are at least three distinct resolvers in this system and they had been conflated into one. The host resolver serves the daemon's policy propagation and measured healthy at 33 of 33 events across 14 domains. The machine's stub resolver serves that machine's own container daemon, and its only positively attributed failure is an image pull. The per-session gateway container's own DNS server is what guest-side lookups traverse - and that is the one the oscillating tests use. Repairing the stub therefore addresses image pulls, not the oscillators.

The decisive measurement against the conflation: in the same run where guest-side lookups for three specific hosts failed, the daemon resolved those exact three hosts successfully with non-empty address sets. The domains and at least one upstream path were healthy throughout, so the failure is specific to the guest-side path rather than to name resolution generally.

My justification for the run was factually wrong and unfalsifiable in the same breath. Wrong: an at-HEAD container reference already exists, measured at what is still current HEAD, so the run does not buy at-HEAD - it buys post-repair. Unfalsifiable: framing it as establishing a fresh reference means whatever it produces becomes the reference, so a regression introduced by the repair is absorbed as the new normal. Framing it as confirming reproduction of the known reference costs the same and can actually fail.

The spec contradicts itself on the sudoers grant, and the contradiction changes what done means for two of the six criteria. The threat-model section instructs narrowing the grant as its second numbered requirement; the phase's own criterion says narrowing cannot deliver the property an earlier draft claimed and forbids narrowing-and-ticking. The phase text self-identifies as the later revision, so it supersedes - but the numbered list was never updated, and it carries the ordering constraint that gates the documentation rewrite on that disputed step landing.

The claim the spec says appears in two files appears three times in one of them, plus a fourth related-but-distinct instance elsewhere justifying a permissive socket mode on the same single-tenancy premise. Correcting only the two cited sites would leave a third asserting a perimeter that does not exist. This is the audit-list failure mode again: a handed-over site list under-reports, so the fix has to be driven by grepping the claim's own phrasing rather than by the list.

The prior session's hand-off is confirmed by full grep: the environment helper has exactly one call site, inside the one function whose only two callers are the route-helper invocation. Both die with this change. The uid field it takes survives with six other uses, so only the function is dead - deleting the field too would be the over-reach the confirmation invites.

The phase's control is weaker than the threat-model delta it answers. The delta names two absent checks - that the address is the session's ASSIGNED gateway, and that it is even in the container's subnet - and the criterion requires only the second. Session bridges are a 28-bit prefix, so containment admits sixteen addresses where exactly one is correct. The documentation rewrite must therefore claim the property that actually landed, or 'the control was restored' will read as the stronger claim.

Every line number in the phase's file list is stale - earlier phases moved the code - while every NAME is still correct. The implementer must locate by name and re-measure, and the same applies to the citations in the recon handoff itself, which were measured at the current head and will drift as the work lands.

MEASURED: the gateway machine's login user - the same user an interactive shell lands as - already holds blanket passwordless elevation for every command, from the virtualisation tool's default provisioning. The dedicated single-binary grant the spec discusses narrowing therefore confers nothing that user lacks without it. Corroborated behaviourally as well as from config: the daemon already depends on four elevated commands inside that machine which the dedicated grant does not cover, and they succeed today, so the blanket right is measured by consequence rather than inferred from a file.

Subagents inherit this session's 1M-context model and die on 'Usage credits required for 1M context' before doing any work. Pin a standard-context model on every Agent spawn; the failure presents as an agent-type problem but is not.

curl rc=6 vs rc=28 does NOT discriminate a black-holing resolver from a fast-failing one. Measured against a certainly-black-holing stub, curl returned rc=6 five times out of five, each at 20.06s: the code reflects whether curl's --max-time beats the resolver's ~20s give-up, i.e. the test's timeout budget, not the mechanism. Any triage that infers a DNS failure shape from the exit code alone is unsound.

The gateway VM's own DNS is broken by nft rules the daemon itself emits. Lima's stock hostResolver DNATs 192.168.5.3:53 to 192.168.5.2:<high-port> in nat/output (priority -100), which runs BEFORE filter/output (priority 0); our generated output-eth0 chain is policy-drop and accepts DNS only on dport 53, so it drops the rewritten port. Measured: LIMADNS counters incremented (+1 UDP, +3 TCP) while tcpdump on host 192.168.5.2 captured zero DNS packets; control dig @1.1.1.1 answered.

The per-session guest DNS path bypasses the gateway VM's stub resolver entirely - the macOS session code pins a fixed public CoreDNS upstream - so the VM's dead stub cannot be the cause of guest-side resolution oscillators. Three resolvers are distinct: macOS host, gateway-VM stub, per-session CoreDNS.

docs/internal/macos-e2e-baseline.md is a FULL-scope reference (160 selected), not container-scope. The container-scope comparator at HEAD 392cb6d is the S14 re-clear handoff: 51 passed / 35 failed / 0 errors / 1 skipped of 87. Do not compare a container run against the baseline doc.

The sudoers narrowing is measurably a no-op under either reading of the spec conflict: the gateway VM's login user already holds ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL from the distro's default cloud-init, so narrowing a separate fragment changes no effective privilege. The security outcome is therefore identical whichever way the textual precedence resolves - the conflict changes the paperwork, not the posture.

LIVE PROHIBITION: §5.2's correction table forbids recording a gateway-axis improvement in GitHub issue #82 or anywhere else external until §1.6 ships. Internal handoffs and progress logs are fine; external surfaces are not. Absent from the recon handoff, so it can be missed by anyone briefed only from that.

§5.1 carries TWO different publication prohibitions that are easy to conflate: the logged-out delta's 'this list may be published' (lifted) and the gateway-axis prohibition (live until §1.6 ships). Reading the lifted one as general cover for the gateway axis would be a mistake.

The spec's §5.2 perimeter item 2 rests on a false description of the code. It asserts the sudoers grant installs a blanket 'ALL ALL=(root) NOPASSWD:'; the emitted line is command-scoped to the single helper binary, with the two ALLs being the user and host fields. Verified against the generator, not inferred. The spec's own line citation for it is stale.

Caller-side validation for the new typed op is deliberately shape-only, and is documented as such at four sites with an explicit pointer to where the binding check lives. This matters because the realistic future regression is not deleting the helper-side control but reading the caller-side checks, concluding the case is handled, and relaxing the helper.

A stale security doc-comment can be made MORE dangerous by a correct fix: the route-helper perimeter text was wholly false, and the containment control turns it half-true while leaving the identity claim false. A perimeter pass that diffs against landed code reads it as newly-accurate and leaves the overclaim standing, now with a real control lending it credibility. Perimeter passes must positively verify each claim against code, never diff against the change that touched the area.

The broker op protocol has no version negotiation: an older agent silently drops a line it cannot parse, so a daemon/agent op-set skew stalls to the per-op timeout instead of returning a Rejected response. Adding an op variant is therefore not safely rolling-upgradeable today.

Confirmed by review: the change that corrects a security overclaim is itself where the next overclaim gets written. While fixing a false perimeter claim, the implementer wrote a new one in the new module - 'an unrelated private address is refused' - which is false for a wide observed prefix, because inside a /8 the containment test degenerates to the private-address test that already ran. Unreachable in production (/28) but unconditional as written.

Single observation, mechanism not established: a reviewer subagent spawning kio-qa-test-runner had it decline the work as an unverifiable injection because it could not resolve the spawner's name in its roster. This is subagent-to-subagent dispatch, a different call path from the earlier main-to-subagent measurements where that type simply never acked, so the two observations may not describe the same failure. Treat as one data point about nested delegation, not as a diagnosis of the agent type.

Boundary addresses are RELATIVE when a namespace reports several subnets. A gateway that is the broadcast address of one observed subnet is an ordinary host on another, and containment accepts if any observed subnet contains it: observed 10.0.0.3/28 plus 10.0.0.20/24 with gateway 10.0.0.15 returns Ok, even though .15 is the /28 broadcast. So 'network and broadcast addresses are refused' is not an unconditional property of the control.

Two successive audits each found a DIFFERENT false claim in the same doc sentence - the reviewer found the wide-prefix case, the fixer found the boundary-address case while repairing it. A findings list is neither sound nor complete, so a corrected security sentence needs a fresh reader who did not write it and is not told what the earlier defects were.

A reviewer's code-pattern pointer is not evidence. The review cited a fake-executor pattern at two line numbers in the gateway Lima module; those sites are op-construction, not fake executors. The workspace's real pattern lives in the DNS gate bridge module. The implementer checked rather than followed, and said so.

The stale-perimeter defect class here was not crediting a caller-side check as a control - no comment did that. It was crediting the ENVIRONMENT as one: comments asserted the VM boundary was itself the authorization gate, when the VM provisions passwordless sudo to its login user and lite sandbox containers run inside that same VM, so an in-VM caller reaches the capability-bearing binary directly as uid 0.

Doc-claim audits keep finding that a named step number or flag does not exist: a comment credited a --audit-log flag the argv parser never had, and attributed the containment check to step 6, which is a different function testing a users.conf CIDR that does not exist inside the VM. Cross-references to step numbers and flags rot silently because nothing validates them.

Verified by execution on Linux: the route helper raises CAP_NET_ADMIN to the AMBIENT set before exec'ing a bare-name ip(8), so the first ip on the caller's PATH runs with effective CAP_NET_ADMIN inside the entered container netns. A decoy binary created a netdev there and the helper exited 0; the same user with empty cap sets gets EPERM. The installed binary is 0755 with file caps, so any operator enrolled in a users.conf pool can exec it directly and satisfy the pair-check with --for-user defaulting to themselves. This is a privilege escalation that reaches the egress-enforcement layer itself.

LD_PRELOAD and LD_LIBRARY_PATH are already neutralised on that path because a file-caps binary is a secure-exec process and glibc scrubs LD_* from its environment - measured, the child saw no LD_PRELOAD while PATH survived intact. That is what makes absolute-path pinning a sufficient fix rather than a partial one; without checking it, fixing PATH alone could have closed the visible half of an env-hijack hole.

The injected child receives only CAP_NET_ADMIN, not CAP_SYS_ADMIN or CAP_SYS_PTRACE, which bounds the escalation: the code cannot setns back out of the container netns. Severity is high because CAP_NET_ADMIN inside that netns is exactly the privilege needed to rewrite routes and nft rules and defeat egress policy - the blast radius is the product's central guarantee rather than the host.

Four separate false doc claims shared one root: the numbered step list describes an intended order the code does not implement - argv parse actually runs before caller-identity resolution, not after. Every downstream reference to 'steps 1-4' and 'step 6' inherits the off-by-one. Patching the sentences individually would have left the generator live; the list is the fix.

A blind audit of prose that had just been carefully rewritten still found four false and six partially-true claims. Correction text is the least-reviewed text in a change, and its author cannot audit it - the reviewer who reads the diff sees only that the old wrong sentence is gone. An independent reader who is told nothing about the prior defects is the only pass that catches this.

Measurement overrules inference on the LD_PRELOAD question. One agent inferred from AT_SECURE semantics that LD_PRELOAD reaches the child of the helper's exec; another had already measured the child seeing no LD_PRELOAD while PATH survived. Both are consistent: the variables are stripped at the HELPER's own exec because it carries file capabilities, so they are absent from the environment it passes on. The inferred claim must not be written into the docs.

The route-helper install probe tests getcap output for one capability name out of the three it installs, so a partially-capped binary is reported already-installed, provisioning is skipped, and the failure surfaces later as EPERM at setns - precisely the late failure the caps probe exists to prevent.

The shell grep on this host is a ugrep wrapper that honours ignore-files, so a recursive search from the repo root can return ZERO hits for a string that is definitely present while the same search one directory down finds it. Repo-wide sweeps come back falsely clean rather than erroring. Use 'command grep -rn' for any sweep whose conclusion is an absence.

Correcting a wrong count is not enough when the count was unqualified: the measured figure held only for a namespace reporting a non-boundary host address, becoming a different number when the reported address is the network or broadcast address, or when two addresses are reported. The qualifier is the part a fix-the-number pass omits, and its absence is why the original wrong figure survived unchallenged as prose.

The route-helper PATH escalation was fail-OPEN, not merely a privilege gain: with a decoy earlier on PATH the helper exited 0 having installed no default route. The caller was told the sandbox was configured while its egress route was absent, so the same defect handed an attacker CAP_NET_ADMIN execution and suppressed the signal that anything was wrong.

getcap prints capabilities in kernel numeric order, not in the order they were passed to setcap (measured on libcap 2.66). Any check that parses its output must be order-independent; a fixture built by echoing back the setcap argument string would pass while the real tool's output failed.

Two independent blind audits both classified the pidfd-versus-procfs TOCTOU claim as true-but-inferred, and a third pass measured it false and backwards: the procfs handle pins the namespace at open and survives the pid being killed and reaped, while the pidfd form fails. The claims that survive on plausibility are exactly the ones most likely to be wrong, because plausibility is what got them written down.

CAP_SYS_ADMIN does not implicitly promote to all capabilities inside a child user namespace. A four-arm experiment varying one factor at a time showed the real grant is the caller's euid matching the userns owner, which is why a capless child historically worked in a single-uid install and why that dependency silently fails in a multi-user deployment.

The boundary-address doc defect corrected in the containment module survived untouched at a paraphrase site in the helper's main file, and both trace to a consumed handoff plan that prescribed the wrong phrasing verbatim and instructed that the doc-comment say it in those terms. The corrected site measured and qualified the claim; the paraphrase kept the flat form.

On this macOS host, 'command grep -r --hidden --no-ignore' is a ripgrep invocation that BSD grep rejects outright, so the sweep errors rather than searching. Plain BSD 'command grep -r' does descend into the dotted coordination directory. The ugrep shell wrapper is the only thing that silently under-reports.

The production installer's capability guard uses a substring test against getcap output, so a binary carrying a SUPERSET of the intended capabilities is reported as already configured and setcap is skipped. Measured with an extra cap_chown; missing caps and wrong flags are correctly rejected, so the hole is only in the superset direction. Not an escalation vector - setting file caps already requires root - but it defeats the tightly-bounded-privilege property the narrow-helper model exists to provide.

This shell is zsh, which does not word-split unquoted parameter expansions. A harness that builds a command line by interpolating an unquoted variable therefore passes one joined argument instead of several, and the command fails in a way that looks like an empty-but-successful result. An agent verifying a guard hit this twice and only caught it by reading stderr. On this host a zero-length match is as likely to be harness breakage as genuine absence.

The substring capability check is a repo-wide pattern, not a single site: measured in the dev makefile guard, the production install script guard, and the CLI self-update path. The CLI instance is the highest-stakes because it runs on the end user's machine, and its unit tests cover flag spellings but never a superset, so the defect sits inside a tested region with all tests green.

The same guard family also fails in the opposite direction on an old-libcap host, where getcap spells flags with a plus rather than an equals sign. The exactly-correct capability set then fails to match and setcap re-runs on every invocation - harmless but noisy, and on a machine without passwordless sudo it means a password prompt every time.

File capabilities carry one effective bit for the whole file, not one per capability. Since both production expected sets mark their capabilities effective, a multi-clause superset of either is unrepresentable and setcap rejects it. That makes the single-clause superset the complete superset shape for the production case, so the guard verification covers the space rather than merely sampling it.

The two CLI capability checks needed opposite semantics, and the deciding evidence was downstream rather than local. The install gates must demand exact set equality because setcap replaces a file's entire capability set, so skipping on a superset leaves an over-capped binary uncorrected.
