The post-install verification must stay a presence probe because its real consumer is the daemon's own startup gate, which tests a single capability bit rather than a set; an equality check there would roll back an update the daemon would have accepted.

Which superset variant a test picks decides whether it can detect the substring defect at all. An extra capability sorting AFTER the expected names is rejected even by the buggy substring check, because the expected string still appears as a trailing substring. Only an extra capability sorting BEFORE the expected names, or one in a separate clause, exposes the bug. A plausible-looking test could have covered supersets and still certified the defect as absent.

Linting a subset of workspace crates needs --no-deps: cargo's workspace wrapper applies trailing -- arguments to every member, not only the -p-selected ones, so a targeted deny-warnings run otherwise fails on unrelated crates. Verified separately that --no-deps does not suppress the lint being checked.

The pre-existing Linux clippy breakage in the core crate is wider than the single import previously recorded: alongside the macOS-gated test-support import there are four dead-code errors in the DNS gate bridge module. Confirmed against HEAD with a control, so none of it is attributable to this session.

RETRACTION, superseding an earlier entry in this same store: the claim that holding CAP_SYS_ADMIN in a parent user namespace implicitly grants all capabilities in a child, and that rootful container layouts lack that promotion, is FALSE. Measured with a four-arm experiment varying one factor. The real rule is that the grant follows from the effective uid matching the namespace owner, and that a capability held in an ancestor namespace applies within its descendants for that one capability only. Any future reader who encounters the original phrasing in the log history should treat it as withdrawn.

Measured on Linux 6.8 aarch64, four arms varying only the ambient raise: a process holding a capability in permitted and effective that execs a file carrying no file capabilities yields a child with both sets empty, and the privileged operation then fails with Operation not permitted. Raising the capability into the ambient set beforehand is what carries it across the exec. This is unconditional, not a property of any particular container layout, which is why the manifest comment now states it without a layout qualifier.

The falsified capability claim also survives verbatim in the tracking store's own closed-session history, which now contradicts a later corrective entry in the same store. Left in place deliberately: the store is append-only by design and rewriting it would destroy the record of what was believed when. The retraction entry above is the remedy, since the store is read forward through review rather than mined by search.

getcap exits 0 with empty output for a file that carries no capabilities, so an exit-code check cannot distinguish absence from a failed invocation, and both read as success. Any check asserting that a binary is uncapped needs a positive control on a file known to be capped in the same run. This bites the install guards and any audit that concludes a binary is unprivileged.

The independent blind verification found five overstated claims in the just-corrected prose, including one in the sentence written minutes earlier by the correcting pass itself. That sentence measured the unprivileged case and stated it without qualification; the privileged case behaves the opposite way and is exactly the case the in-VM path exercises. Confirms that the correcting edit is the highest-risk place in a correction pass, and that self-review does not substitute for an independent measurement.

Another session is committing to the same branch concurrently and the working tree now holds seventeen modified files spanning both workstreams. Attribution before committing cannot be assumed from memory of what was touched; it has to be established from the content of each diff, and the check has to happen in the same operation as the commit.

The concurrency alarm was mine and it was wrong. The branch head last moved roughly a day ago, not during this session's recent work, and the other workstream has left no uncommitted edits at all. I read a reflog listing and inferred recency from ordering without checking the dates. Every tracked modified path belongs to this workstream, so the commit needs explicit pathspecs but not hunk-level staging.

The capability-guard fix was believed complete and was not. A note logged earlier in this same session had already named all three affected places, and a todo had been filed against the third; both were then passed over while the work read as finished. The evidence that the fix was partial was already in the record before the claim of completeness was formed.

RETRACTION of an entry I wrote earlier in this session: I recorded that the ambient-capability requirement is unconditional and not a property of any container layout. That is false. It holds for a non-root parent; a uid-0 parent exec'ing a binary with no file capabilities receives the full bounding set and the operation succeeds without any ambient raise. I formed the universal from a relayed measurement whose four arms had all run unprivileged, and I dropped the scope the evidence actually carried.

The retracted kernel rule also reached user-facing installation documentation, which states it as fact for readers setting up the product. A false claim in a session log misleads the next agent; the same claim in shipped docs misleads every user. Doc surfaces need to be swept whenever a mechanism claim is retracted, not just the code comments where the retraction was noticed.

I briefed a delegate that a documentation sentence was false, and it was not. The verifier who found it had supplied the scope correctly, noting the claim held within the file's cross-uid context; I dropped that scope when relaying and passed on the unqualified version. The delegate refused the framing, showed the measurement did not reach the claim as written, and fixed a different real defect instead. The qualifier was available and explicit at the source, so vagueness upstream was not the cause.

The capability guard had six sites in the installer, not the four that were handed over. The two missing ones sit inside a heredoc that generates a privileged child process, so their dollar signs are escaped and a plain search for the command does not match them. Generated-code regions are a systematic blind spot for site sweeps in shell scripts.

The model I used for which superset test can detect the substring defect was wrong, and it was wrong because an inference was recorded at the same confidence as the measurement it sat next to. Ordering of capability clauses turns out to be irrelevant; the deciding factors are whether the extra capability occupies its own clause and whether the guard rewrites the flag separator. One of the two guards had no reachable fail-open at all.

The same guard carried an opposite and previously unreported defect: against the rendering used by older libcap releases it rejected a correctly capped binary and aborted a correct installation. A fail-closed break on older distributions, found only because the fix was measured against several real library versions instead of the one on the development host.

A count relayed between agents carries an unstated domain. I forwarded a six-site figure that was scoped to one file as if it spanned three, and the true figure was eleven across five. The delegate caught it only because the brief explicitly told it to verify boundaries against the diff rather than repeat what it was told; that one sentence is what kept a false number out of the commit message.

A capability check on this host cannot verify the route helper's platform-gated module, because that module compiles only on Linux and the host is macOS. The containment logic was deliberately left off that gate so its table-driven tests still execute here, but the surrounding collection and binary-resolution code stays unchecked without a Linux pass.
artifacts: 4 local commits on master (91990da, 29c9732, 8e28b3c, ae5e620); sandbox-route-helper/src/containment.rs; 9 capability-guard scenarios in tests/rich-ui-dash/harness.sh

log.title: Split the agent YAML validator by VM class
log.summary: Split the guest agent's Lima-YAML validator by VM class, using a distinct typed operation as the class selector rather than the specified name-derived one. The specified mechanism was measured to be both unsound and unimplementable: it required the selector not be daemon-supplied yet derived class from the VM name, itself a daemon-supplied wire field with the daemon inside the threat model, and separately the generated gateway template contains no occurrence of the instance name at all, so the validator's containment check would have rejected every legitimate gateway create once the interface-count rule let one through. Under the operation-based selector no wire content influences which rule runs, the session rule applies unconditionally on the ordinary create so a gateway-shaped name is rejected rather than privileged, and the two rules are mutually exclusive by entry shape. The gateway rule demands strictly more per entry than the session rule. A dedicated security review approved the set against a property pre-registered before the diff was read, with zero blockers. A false claim it found in a security comment, asserting that unknown wire fields are refused at deserialization, was measured to be untrue and corrected, and the operation enum now genuinely refuses them. Landed ahead of its caller: nothing invokes the gateway operation yet, and the daemon-side sender, the instance-name rename it must carry, and the start path are all deferred. The suite total was reconciled by name-level enumeration after three reports disagreed; nothing vanished, and the discrepancy was a missing feature pair that gates tests in both polarities.
decisions: The machine's class will be carried by a distinct typed operation rather than derived from its name, diverging from the specified mechanism on the user's ruling. The name is a wire field the daemon controls, so deriving class from it leaves the selector forgeable by the adversary the threat model names; carrying the class in the operation itself makes it unforgeable by the same closed-set property the design already relies on to bound a compromised daemon. The agent derives the instance name from its own credential and never accepts it from the wire on that operation, and the session rule is applied unconditionally on the ordinary create, so a gateway-shaped name presented there is rejected rather than privileged.

The specification is deliberately not being edited to match this divergence. Point-in-time intent stays as written and the divergence is recorded forward here, where the session report will surface it.

Gateway-class network entries are pinned to exactly the socket-plus-interface key set while session entries are pinned to socket alone, making the two rules mutually exclusive by shape rather than by convention. The gateway rule demands strictly more per entry than the session rule, including canonical slot round-tripping and interface-to-slot agreement that Lima itself does not check.

The broker operation enum now refuses unknown fields. Ruling on the objection that this widens reachability of an unbounded hang: it grants no new capability, because an actor able to send an undeclared field is the same actor that can already send an unknown variant and reach the identical hang. The new case is honest version skew, and there refusing beats an enforcement point executing a request it only partly understands. Scope was held to the operation enum; the envelope and nested enums keep serde's default.
discoveries: The spec's table of validators that block the ownership flip is short by one. A containment check requiring the instance name to appear inside the template body also rejects the gateway create, and it is mentioned nowhere in the spec. Measured by running the real generator rather than reasoning about it: Lima templates carry no instance name at all, since the name arrives as a command-line argument, so the gateway template fails that check no matter how the four documented rules are fixed.

The naming decision the class selector depends on is not implemented anywhere. The two agent-side constants still carry the form without the owner's identity, across nineteen files. The selector cannot be written until that rename lands, and both agent-side sites have to move together or the container-socket path and the selector will disagree about which machine they are talking about.

The criterion the spec singles out as what distinguishes a split from a relaxation has no test, and neither does the session-side rule it protects. No existing test exercises the multiple-interface rule with the specific key being introduced, and the nearest existing test predates the class field entirely, so it never varies the label. A test that does not vary the label cannot demonstrate the property in question.

The prescribed class selector satisfies the requirement that it not be daemon-supplied in letter but not in substance. It moves the daemon's control from one wire field to another wire field rather than removing the field. Measured: the codec accepts a gateway-shaped name, the name validator accepts every gateway-shaped spelling because it guards against argument injection rather than class, and nothing between the wire and the validator checks the name at all.

The daemon is inside the threat model by the code's and the spec's own words, and it already chooses the operator identity on the wire, so it knows the value any identity comparison would check. Comparing an embedded identity against the agent's own therefore buys discipline between operators, not unforgeability against a compromised daemon.

Implementing the split as specified would widen rather than narrow what a compromised daemon can reach. Today every machine is held to a single gateway-facing interface and the gateway machine cannot be created through this path at all; afterwards a machine named in the gateway form would be permitted four direct network interfaces, which is exactly the shape that bypasses the enforcement point. A second creation channel unrelated to sessions was also measured to accept a gateway-shaped name.

The earlier recon's identification of the blocking check was corrected by measurement. The interface-count rule fails first for every input, so the containment check it named is genuinely unmentioned in the spec but is never reached, and a name validator it omitted entirely runs ahead of both.

The generated gateway Lima template contains no occurrence of the instance name anywhere in its body, so the validator's name-containment check would have rejected every legitimate gateway create once the NIC rule passed. This is an independent second reason the specified name-derived class selector could not have worked, separate from the threat-model argument.

The base-VM-name environment override was a live escalation channel under the specified name-derived selector: the daemon's startup validation accepts a gateway-shaped spelling, and the hardened-session flag is never consulted on that path. The operation-based selector closes it because no spelling reaches the gateway rule.

The start path will need its own class treatment for a different reason than create did: the wrapper validation rejects an empty wrapper, and the gateway uses an empty one. So the ownership flip cannot route gateway start through the agent without either a distinct start operation or a class-aware wrapper rule.

A frame the agent cannot parse is logged and skipped without any response, and the daemon's send path awaits its reply channel with no bound - the timeout argument is only honoured on the degenerate direct path. So an unparseable frame pins a daemon request forever, and the heartbeat watchdog cannot see it because the agent is alive and healthy.

Twelve tests compile under neither hermetic nor integration make target: eleven integration-prefixed tests in the broker plus one in the agent binary are gated on their own crates' test-env-override features, while both targets pass that feature only for the two helper crates. They are absent from the enumeration entirely rather than skipped, so no count ever shows them missing. This is the same failure the hermetic target's own comment was written to prevent, recurring for two further crates.

Sharing a cargo target directory between git worktrees silently yields stale test binaries. Workspace path-dependency units hash to the same metadata in both trees, so they collide on one filename, and cargo's mtime freshness check then treats the older tree's sources as satisfied by the newer tree's output. Exit code zero, no warning, wrong test list. Measured by accident and then reproduced deliberately.

log.title: Route-helper operation
log.summary:
Reopened against a stale next-pointer to discharge the one exit criterion of the original run that had left no durable artifact: recording, where a future reader of the sudoers grant will meet it, the security property consciously abandoned there. That criterion is discharged, and the ruling behind it - that the ephemeral session-tracking store does not count as the place of record, because it may be rewritten or deleted while the grant it concerns lives on - is logged.

The session also produced the first authorised macOS container-scope e2e result. It is RED: 35 failed, 51 passed, 1 skipped, 82 deselected, 30 minutes, over 87 selected tests; a real run, not a preflight skip. The final exit criterion - that this tier passes - is therefore UNMET. It is recorded as unmet rather than waived or reworded, per the milestone's own standing ruling on the identical clause.

Attribution was verified independently rather than assumed. All 35 are pre-existing: set-identity against the catalogued baseline was checked mechanically in both directions, symmetric difference empty, across what is now seven runs at seven commits. None trace to this session's typed route-helper op or the preceding session's validator class split - established positively, not by absence: the 8-commit delta containing both did not move the failure set, this session's route install is exercised and working in the same run (every positive-egress assertion passes, which is impossible without a default route in the container netns), and the validator's new branch is unreachable from the daemon at this commit by design.

Three framings I had relayed to triage came back corrected, and the corrections are the more useful half. Two failures I had called structurally impossible on macOS are not - what macOS lacks is the Linux spelling of a mechanism, not the facility asserted on - and platform-marking them would have converted fixable harness bugs into permanent exclusions while burying a real product defect the same run exposed. Seven host-Docker failures will not go green as a side effect of the ownership flip, so filing them against it would have deferred a harness fix onto work that will not deliver it. The failure grouping I passed on was a lossy projection of a ten-class catalogue already in the repo.

Ten todos filed, one per verified class. Two are macOS-specific product bugs predating this milestone by months; one class is an observability gap in the egress subsystem itself, with enforcement separately green - old, but not benign. No code, test, or config changed for the triage; HEAD unchanged at f80cabb.
decisions: Ruling on where a consciously-abandoned security property must be recorded: the session-tracking store does not count. That store is explicitly ephemeral and may be rewritten or deleted between increments, so recording an abandoned property only there means it evaporates while the grant it concerns lives on. The decision must be inlined where a future reader of the sudoers grant will encounter it. This resolves the exit criterion's silence about location against the reading that treats the tracking entry as sufficient.

Closing M24-S15 with its final exit criterion - that the macOS container-scope e2e tier passes - recorded as UNMET rather than waived, reworded, or reinterpreted. The tier is red for 35 failures, every one of them pre-existing and none attributable to this session's work or the preceding one's. The milestone already rules on this exact tension for a sibling session carrying the identical clause: the clause stays as written and is deliberately not reworded into something achievable on this host, because an exit list that shrinks to fit its host is how a session declares victory over its own reduced ambitions. Blocking instead would stall the milestone indefinitely on defects that predate it by months and that five other sessions' exit lists carry unchanged. The gap is therefore recorded, evidenced, and filed as ten todos - not closed by redefinition.

How to read the milestone's recorded finding that the e2e clause is 'blocked on the authorised run and on nothing else', now that the authorised run has happened and the tier is still red for 35 tests. That sentence is not falsified: it was explicitly bounded to three bring-up requirements - vmnet pool, gateway VM, operator agent - and within those bounds it held, since the run did execute and collected a real result rather than dying at bring-up. What is false is the sentence lifted out of its bounds into 'run it and it goes green'. Anyone citing it as evidence of an imminent green tier is reading past its scope; the correct statement now is that bring-up is no longer the blocker and 35 substantive defects are.
discoveries: On this host `grep` is ugrep 7.5.0, not GNU grep: `--no-ignore` is rejected as an invalid option (exit 2, message on stderr) and the working flag is `--no-ignore-files`. The `--hidden --no-ignore` pair is ripgrep's spelling and applies only to `rg`. Repo-wide sweeps that use the wrong flag fail loudly unless the error is swallowed by `2>/dev/null` or an `&&` chain, in which case they return falsely clean.

Candidate mechanism for the 'kio agent types are dead on this host' rule, which was recorded as measured-five-for-five with no cause. A stopped kio-qa-test-runner returned failureReason 'API Error: Usage credits required for 1M context'. MEASURED: every kio-* agent definition pins an explicit 1M-context model in frontmatter, while Explore/general-purpose pin none and inherit the session model; and the recorded dead/working split tracks the pinned model exactly - kio-developer and kio-qa-test-runner both pin claude-sonnet-4-6[1m] and are the recorded-dead pair, while kio-reviewer pins claude-opus-4-6[1m] and is the recorded-working exception. INFERRED, not yet confirmed: that the sonnet-4-6 1M variant specifically is uncredited on this account. If it holds, the remedy is the Agent tool's model parameter, which overrides frontmatter, rather than avoiding those agent types entirely.

CONFIRMED by probe, superseding the recorded rule that kio-development agent types are dead on this host. Spawning kio-qa-test-runner with the Agent tool's model parameter set to sonnet produced an immediate ack and a correct git HEAD read, so the agent type works. The cause was never the type: every kio-* agent definition pins a 1M-context model in frontmatter, the account lacks 1M usage credits, and the agent therefore died at its first API call before any tool use - which presents identically to a type that spawns and never reports. The remedy is to pass an explicit model override on every kio-* dispatch; avoiding those agent types is unnecessary and has been costing the workhorse implementer and test-runner roles for many sessions.

The macOS container-scope e2e tier is broadly RED and at least partly CANNOT pass on a macOS host as currently written: 35 failed / 51 passed / 1 skipped / 82 deselected, 30 minutes, over 87 selected tests. The run was real, not a preflight skip. Two failures are structural proof rather than regression: one test reads /proc/meminfo and another shells out to getent, both Linux-only facilities absent on macOS, and neither carries a platform marker - so this scope has been collecting them on macOS since they were written. This is exactly the anti-pattern the repo's own platform-axis guidance describes. Six more fail because the harness inspects the HOST docker for a gateway container that on macOS lives inside the gateway Lima VM.

The 35 macOS container-scope e2e failures are ALL pre-existing and none trace to the route-helper broker op or the agent-YAML validator class split. Verified four independent ways: the 8-commit delta containing both pieces of work did not move the failure set; set-identity against a catalogued baseline was checked mechanically in BOTH directions (symmetric difference empty, not by count) across what is now a seven-run identical baseline; the route install is positively exercised and working in this same run (transport, TLS-verify, L3 host/method/path, SVCB, stop-start-with-networking, daemon-restart-recovery and lite-gateway-parity all PASS, and positive-egress assertions are impossible without a default route in the container netns); and the validator's new branch is unreachable from the daemon at this commit by design, since the daemon does not yet send gateway-class creates.

CORRECTION to this session's earlier discovery entry: the claim that two failures are 'structurally impossible on macOS' is wrong, and the remedy it implied - platform-marking them - would be actively harmful. What macOS lacks in both cases is the Linux spelling of a mechanism, not the facility asserted on: /proc/meminfo is read to learn host RAM, which macOS has as sysctl hw.memsize, and getent is used to resolve a hostname out-of-band, which macOS also does. Both are harness bugs under the repo's two-selection-axes rule. Marking the host-RAM one would additionally bury a real product defect - the daemon emitted 548 warnings that it could not read /proc/meminfo and was falling back to 4096 MB, which is not this host's RAM. Measured: across all ten files holding the 35, git log -S over both marker strings finds exactly one platform-marker commit, and it added macos_only tests that are not among the 35. No failing test has ever been platform-marked.

Two of the 35's failure classes are macOS-specific PRODUCT bugs, not harness bugs, and both predate this milestone by months. First: the macOS lite branch routes the create-time local: push through the direct-spawn path as the daemon user rather than the operator-pivoted helper the generic lite branch uses, because macOS has no lima-helper and the forwarded gateway Docker socket is daemon-user-only; the tests source from an operator-owned 0700 temp dir the daemon user cannot stat, so rsync exits 23. This corroborates the standing unfiled finding that local: has no sink-side path check unlike shared:. Second: git-remote-sandbox re-execs itself via current_exe(), which on Linux resolves through /proc/self/exe to the real binary but on macOS returns the symlink path, so the child's argv[0] basename re-triggers the remote-helper branch and it parses the --socket value as the URL.

Ten of the 35 failures are lost egress EVENTS with enforcement intact - the deny and fail-closed tests pass in the same run while the assertions on events reaching the per-session ring find it empty. This is an observability gap rather than an egress-control gap, but it sits in the subsystem whose correctness is the project's stated reason to exist, so 'pre-existing' must not be read as 'harmless'. Separately: seven more failures are the harness shelling out to bare host docker for a container that on macOS lives inside the gateway Lima VM. Those will NOT go green as a side effect of the ownership flip - that flip changes who owns the VM, not whether there is one, and its own exit criteria require reverting cleanly to a daemon-owned VM - so filing them against that session would defer a harness fix onto work that will not deliver it.

log.title: Per-operator gateway manager and registry, unwired
log.summary:
Built the per-operator gateway manager, its registry and the naming seam behind an off-by-default switch, and closed a privilege-escalation bypass that the work uncovered on the way.

The switch-off path is behaviourally identical to the previous tree for the manager, registry and naming work, established by mutation testing rather than by reading: hardcoding the instance name turns the switch-off test red through its switch-on half, and deleting the reaper exclusion turns the reap test red, which is the verification the exit criterion prescribes. The reaper exclusion is dormant rather than dead - no gateway name can reach it on today's inputs because the two name grammars diverge at the eighth byte - but it is genuinely guarded, and a second test pins the grammars apart so it goes red when either scheme moves rather than when the exclusion is removed. The socket-path bound is re-asserted across all three name schemes at four uid pairs, worst case eighty-one bytes against a strict hundred-and-four.

The security work was not in the session's scope bullets and changes behaviour unconditionally, by design. A guard mechanism ratified mid-session was unsafe and was rejected by its implementer with a working bypass: comparing a daemon-supplied instance name against an agent-computed one proves only that the daemon chose that value. The replacement, a typed gateway-start operation carrying neither name nor wrapper, was then found by adversarial review to leave the same bypass one operation earlier, because nothing constrained which instance sat at the gateway's name. The fix that holds is a namespace reservation at create and clone - the only two operations that bind a name, there being no rename - plus a refusal to start an instance that does not exist, which is load-bearing because starting an unknown name creates and boots a VM from the default template rather than failing.

Three claims recorded during the session were later measured false and corrected in place: the spec's account of why the gateway survives the reaper, the rationale for omitting sizing fields from the start operation, and a socket-path length comparison that was wrong in both directions. Its replacement was also wrong, in the same commit that fixed it, and was corrected again after review.

Every exit criterion is met, with one recorded exception: switch-off behavioural identity holds for the plumbing and is deliberately violated by the agent-side reservation, which means the phase's daemon-side revert must not take the security fix with it.
decisions: Reaper-exclusion placement, the choice the spec delegates to this session: take the candidate-filter placement in the reap loop, not the one that threads the VM name into the session-VM classifier. Decisive reasons: the gateway VM is not a session VM, so classifying it inside a session-VM classifier is a category error, and the loop already performs exactly this kind of candidate filtering one gate earlier, which puts both defences where they are read together. The alternative costs a public-API break of the core crate, a new decision variant, a match arm, a report field and eight call sites - a heavy price for a second defence behind a filter that already catches it. Its one genuine advantage, that the classifier's priority list stays a complete account of what happens to a VM, is bought instead with a doc-comment amendment on the classifier pointing at the exclusion site; that amendment is mandatory, not optional, because the whole problem being fixed is a protection that was implicit.

How to satisfy the exit criterion that demands the reap protection be verified by removing the exclusion and watching a test go red: write two tests, and do not let the second be dropped for failing that demand. No realistic input can make the first go red, because any VM carrying a gateway name also carries no session id, so removing the exclusion changes nothing; the red-able fixture has to pair a gateway name with a session id, a combination production cannot produce. So the synthetic test is written with its unreachability stated in the comment, satisfying the criterion literally and truthfully, and a second test asserts the two grammars stay disjoint across a uid range. That second one never goes red when the exclusion is removed - it goes red when either grammar moves, which is the actual threat. A blanket 'every new test must be red against the old code' rule would delete exactly the test that guards the real failure mode.

The wrapper-validation guard on the agent's Start path gets a distinct typed operation carrying neither a VM name nor a wrapper, mirroring the existing gateway-create op, and the general Start op keeps unconditional wrapper validation. The mechanism I originally briefed - have the agent derive the trusted gateway name itself and compare the requested name against it - is unsafe and was rejected by the implementer with a concrete bypass: the VM name on Start is a daemon-supplied wire field, so equality against an agent-computed constant only proves the daemon chose that value. Create does not constrain names, so a session-shaped VM could be created under the gateway name and then started with no wrapper, booting with an unrestricted management NIC. The rejected alternative - keep the name-derived guard and have create refuse the agent's own gateway names - is materially sound but rests on a two-op invariant nothing enforces, and would require amending the tree's written doctrine that class selection must ride the op variant and never the name. A fix that needs the stated security rule weakened to accommodate it is the wrong fix.

The gateway start operation carries only the operator uid and a timeout. The hardening flag and the memory and cpu counts are omitted because they are inert on this path, not merely unused: they reach the hypervisor solely through environment variables whose only reader is the wrapper that a gateway VM does not run, and gateway sizing comes from its template instead. Relatedly, that operation exports no wrapper variable at all rather than exporting an empty one, which makes the brokered environment identical to the direct path that starts gateways today. This supersedes an earlier inclination to omit the variable only when empty - the typed operation removes the empty case from the general start path entirely.

Correcting the ruling recorded earlier in this session that the typed gateway-start operation was sufficient. Adversarial review found the bypass survives one operation earlier: the new operation derives the instance name agent-side, but nothing constrains which instance sits at that name. The general create operation validates the name for character set only, so a daemon can place a session-shaped VM with no wrapper at the gateway's own name and then invoke the gateway-start operation; the delete operation removes any real gateway standing in the way, and clone reaches the same name. The fix is a namespace reservation at every operation that can place, clone, rename or remove an instance: names matching the agent's own gateway pattern are refusable there and claimable only through the typed gateway operations. My earlier rejection of the alternative option was right about its name-derived guard, which decides class from an untrusted string, and wrong to discard its create-side reservation along with it - that half is not a class guard, does not touch the doctrine I invoked against it, and is required regardless of which option is chosen.

Correcting the rationale I recorded for omitting the hardening flag and cpu and memory counts from the gateway-start operation. The conclusion holds - they are genuinely inert on this path - but the stated reason was wrong. It is not that their only reader is a wrapper the gateway does not run; on this platform the wrapper reads none of the three, and only the other platform's wrapper does. The stronger and simpler evidence is that the existing direct start path already passes those values as bare literals alongside an empty wrapper, so omitting them changes nothing that was ever read.

The delete operation is deliberately left unreserved, departing from the review's framing. Removing one's own gateway is legitimate lifecycle work and reserving it would require a typed delete operation that does not exist. The route deletion opens is closed at the other end instead: the gateway-start operation now refuses an instance that is not present. That check is load-bearing rather than defensive, because starting an unknown instance name is not an error - it creates one from the default template and boots it, so the permissive operation would otherwise manufacture its own target with unrestricted user-mode networking. It also closes the same hole for an honest requester that starts before creating.

The two reachability gates in play are different and must not be conflated, because conflating them yields a wrong safety conclusion. The artifact-path defect is gated by registry wiring and survives a switch flip untouched. The daemon entry-point sites are gated by the switch itself, so throwing the switch alone breaks the Docker and in-VM seams with no wiring involved. The operational consequence is that the switch cannot be flipped even as an isolated experiment until those entry-point sites are converted - which orders the remaining work rather than merely listing it.

The exit criterion demanding that behaviour with the switch off be identical to the previous session's tree is satisfied for the manager, registry and naming work, and is deliberately violated by the security work that this session also carried. The agent now refuses to bind its own gateway names on create and clone, and the general start path validates its wrapper unconditionally where an empty one previously skipped the restriction marker. Both change behaviour with the switch off and with it on, by design, because they close a privilege-escalation bypass. Recording this rather than reading the criterion as satisfied wholesale: the criterion exists to keep this phase revertible on the daemon side, and the consequence is that reverting the phase must not revert the agent-side reservation - they are separable and only one of them is meant to be revertible.
discoveries: The spec's rationale for requiring an explicit gateway-VM reaper exclusion is measured false as written. It claims the gateway VM survives the orphan reaper only because its name fails the session-id parse. In fact the reap loop filters on a VM-name prefix BEFORE any parse is attempted, and the gateway name - in both its current and its per-operator form - fails that prefix filter, so it never reaches the classifier at all. The parse-failure protection is real but unreachable: a second defence sitting behind a first one the spec does not mention. What survives of the spec's argument is that protection is still accidental, resting on two independent grammar coincidences, so the explicit exclusion is still required. What does not survive is its specific worry that a per-operator naming scheme might happen to parse - false for the scheme actually chosen.

Starting a Lima instance by a name that does not exist does not fail - it creates and boots a new VM from the default template. Measured, not inferred. This means the start path is also a creation path, which widens what an unconstrained name field on that operation can do, and it makes any test that reaches the real command capable of booting a VM.

The request-handler unit tests point at the developer's live per-operator LIMA_HOME rather than a temporary directory, and earlier unit-test runs have left YAML files behind in it. Combined with the fact that starting an unknown instance name creates a VM, a unit test that reaches the real command could boot one on the dev host. Any test around the wrapper guard has to be contained before that point.

The per-operator gateway agent has always named its gateway instance with an operator-uid suffix, unconditionally, while the daemon's direct path uses the unsuffixed constant. So the naming divergence this milestone is closing is not something the new switch introduces - it already exists, and throwing the switch is what makes the daemon agree with what the agent has been doing all along. This also answers where the naming rule must live: nowhere new. The agent needs no knowledge of the core crate's switch, because its suffix is unconditional.

The brokered gateway lifecycle is entirely unwired on the daemon side, and the create and start halves must stay unwired together. The daemon still maps a gateway start onto the general start operation, and the agent names its gateway with a uid suffix the daemon's direct path does not use, so wiring only one half would address an instance the other half never created. Compounding it: starting an unknown instance name creates and boots a VM rather than failing. Both halves belong in the same change as the naming convergence.

There is no rename operation in the agent's protocol - no handler builds that argv - so the create and clone operations are the entire surface on which a name becomes bound to an instance. That is why a single reservation function called by both is sufficient rather than a condition repeated per call site, and it is the fact that makes the reservation's coverage argument finite and checkable.

A test fixture omitted a required field, so the attack test's first red came from the request being refused for its content rather than for its name. A red for the wrong reason proves nothing, and it is indistinguishable from a real red at the level of pass or fail - only the failure reason separates them. The same distinction decided how the security assertions here are written: they assert the specific rejection reason, because asserting merely that a request was refused goes green under mechanisms that refuse it by accident somewhere else entirely.

The claim that a session VM's instance name is the longer of the two naming schemes was false in both directions, and measuring it rather than reasoning about it is what showed that. A session name is a fixed twenty bytes; a suffixed gateway name is seventeen plus the uid's digits, so the two are equal at three-digit uids and the gateway is longer from four digits up - wrong for every uid where the comparison mattered. The worst full socket path measured eighty-one bytes against a strict hundred-and-four bound. The measurement was taken by forcing the real path builders' output through a failure rather than recomputing lengths by hand, which is the only form of this check worth trusting.

The orphan reaper is platform-neutral but the gateway Lima module is macOS-only, so the new reaper-exclusion test is gated to macOS and does not run on Linux. Whether that is a real coverage loss turns on whether the property asserted - that the reaper spares the gateway VM - exists on Linux at all, where the gateway is a container rather than a Lima VM. My reading is that it does not and the gating is therefore correct, but that is inference and it is exactly the kind of platform-gating judgement this project has got wrong before by asking whether a mechanism exists rather than whether the property does. It needs checking rather than accepting.

The first-exec cost of a freshly-built test binary is paid once per binary and survives the death of the run that paid it. A workspace run killed at its timeout during the list phase leaves most binaries warm, so an immediate identical retry can complete in thirty seconds where the first attempt exceeded ten minutes. The instinctive remedy - narrow the scope and raise the timeout - was prescribed here and was wrong; it would have bought two crates of coverage for the same wall time that a plain retry spent on the whole workspace. Diagnosing the mechanism correctly and prescribing the wrong remedy from it turned out to be an easy mistake to make.

Two nft-logger tests documented as deterministically failing on this platform both passed. The runner flagged the change rather than trusting either the old note or the single new observation, which is the right call in both directions: one green run is not evidence the documented failure is gone, and a durable note asserting always-fails with no mechanism recorded is exactly the kind of rule that keeps being confirmed by never being retested.

The comment rewritten to replace a measurably false claim about socket-path lengths introduced a new measurably false clause in the same breath - it places the crossover in the middle of the uid range when the transition is actually at uid one thousand, a few ten-thousandths of a percent in, with a nine-hundred-wide equality plateau. The conclusion the clause supports is sound and the test is robust, so nothing downstream is wrong, but this is the third time the pattern has shown up: the commit that fixes an overclaim is the likeliest place to write the next one, because the replacement sentence gets the credibility of the correction and none of the scrutiny.

The census of sites still reading the fixed instance name is three, not the one previously recorded. The severe one is in the daemon entry point, where with the per-operator switch on the Docker and in-VM seams would name a socket and an instance that do not exist. The implementer's own account disclosed this accurately; my earlier note under-counted it. Separately, switch-on behaviour has never been exercised end to end - every statement about it so far derives from probing the name derivation directly rather than from running the system with the switch thrown.

The lite-image artifact path is not gated by the per-operator switch at all. The manager never derives its Lima home from the owner uid - that value arrives as a caller-supplied parameter and is stored unchanged, while the owner uid feeds only the instance name. So flipping the switch changes the instance name and the Docker socket path and leaves the artifact path byte-identical. The real gate is a manager constructed for a non-daemon owner, which is the registry being wired, and the registry has no reader yet. The defect was unreachable before this batch and is unreachable now; what the batch adds is the constructor that would make it reachable.

A delegate's final response text does reach the orchestrator, in all three shapes seen this session: a synchronous agent call, a background agent's completion notification, and a resumed background agent's completion notification. This sits against a standing note asserting that background agents' plain text does not reach the orchestrator and that every delegate must report via a message to main. Recording the observations rather than rewriting that note, because three same-session observations are not enough to retire it - but the practical consequence is live either way. An implementer that parks itself on a monitor notification and stops, trusting a side-channel message to carry its interim findings, produces nothing the orchestrator can read; the reliable instruction is to put the report in the final response and to block on long work in the foreground rather than waiting to be woken.
artifacts: Commits 170049c, b061fb0, 81c391e, 7714ba4, 2427b28, d2a6444, fddc797, 93acad9. Review handoffs under .tasks/handoffs/ dated 20260820: the gateway-start adversarial review and the registry-and-reaper adversarial review. Spec amendment in fddc797 resolving the delegated reaper-exclusion choice.

log.title: Per-operator recovery, reaping, startup and the daemon-side sweep
log.summary: Per-operator recovery, reaping and startup: every gateway singleton-resolving site now resolves per-operator, with the manager registry made the sole source of managers and the gateway instance name derived from the owner uid rather than spelled out. Recovery is scoped per owner by wrapping the store in a per-shard deps type, and the per-owner recovery latch has no uid-free accessor, so an unkeyed read is unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged. Multi-operator isolation is pinned by hermetic tests at both seams, and switch-off equivalence is pinned at the two mode-parameterised functions that decide it, each with an explicit off-mode test. Hermetic suites green on macOS (2626 passed, 0 failed, 183 skipped), clippy -D warnings and fmt clean. The macOS logged-out delta and the operator-login dependency are documented on two durable guide surfaces. Code review approved by the user. Caveat carried forward: the multi-operator mechanism is inert in this build because recovery still passes Shared ownership, collapsing every operator onto the daemon uid (todo #679); readiness for per-operator managers is likewise unaddressed (#678).
decisions: Recovery gets operator scope by sharding the session list once into per-gateway-owner partitions, then invoking recovery per shard with a caller-supplied deps impl. Rejects changing the recovery-deps trait: the partition must be a pure function so the unresolvable residual is a first-class output rather than something reconstructable only by unioning N independent invocations.

Unresolvable sessions must not silently leave recovery. Property: when exactly one gateway owner exists the session recovers as it does today; when per-operator gateways make ownership ambiguous it is declined visibly and its networking status must not claim health. Mirrors the vmnet pool's declined-restore discipline.

Add a switch-collapsing gateway-owner accessor beside the instance-name accessor, and route every wiring site through it. Without it the switch-off identity criterion must be re-established by hand at ~30 sites, and a miss is invisible to existing tests because the instance name stays correct while the Lima home and Docker route are wrong.

Session-operator resolution consults the create-time session column first, then the network record, then the owner name, with the session column winning a disagreement. Open for review: recovery is asking which gateway serves a session's egress, which is a network fact, so if the two hints can ever disagree the tiebreak may belong to the network record instead.

Reversed the session-operator precedence: the network record's uid wins, then the create-time session column, then the owner name. The network hint is re-stamped at every macOS Lima start while the column is written once at insert, so on a diverged session the column is the stale operand; and the network hint is absent exactly where the column is authoritative, since the lite path never sets it. Recovery asks which gateway serves a session's egress, which is a network fact.

The per-owner latch and the comment requiring recovery to rebuild every host slot are not independently decidable once recovery gains operator scope: a per-owner latch is exactly what would permit two recoveries to run concurrently, and if each still rebuilds every slot they would rebuild each other's. Today a single manager and a single key make it unreachable. Re-decide the two together, not separately.

The startup guard that decides which live-session set the reapers receive stays untested only because it lives inline in main(). It is the single control between a store read error and deleting every sandbox on the host, so it gets pulled out to where a test can reach it.

The scoped Lima reaper is compiler-gated to macOS rather than documented with a precondition, because measurement showed its only call site already sits behind a macOS cfg with a separate unscoped arm for Linux. Gating removes no reachable behaviour and makes the check-in premise enforced rather than asserted.

Shared ownership is an enum arm rather than a uid-collapsing function, and that is load-bearing. A function mapping operator to owner can only apply to an already-resolved uid, so a one-gateway host would have to resolve every session's operator and would strand any session that fails to resolve. Those sessions recover today. The enum arm skips resolution entirely.

Shared ownership yields exactly one shard even for an empty session set, because gateway recovery restarts the gateway before it looks at any session. Zero shards would mean a crashed gateway with no running sessions never restarts.

The ownership mode describes what the application state actually holds, not what the feature switch says. It flips to per-operator when the manager and Docker route become per-owner, not when the switch flips, because routing through the manager registry early would create the second-opinion NIC map its own documentation warns against.

The per-owner recovery latch stays, and the asymmetry dissolves rather than needing collapse. The rule both sides now state is to key the latch by the gateway the work lands on: the writer keys on its shard's owner, the monitor's read keys on the daemon uid because its re-creates run over the daemon-pinned route. Same value today, independently movable later.

A declined session currently reports healthy networking because an absent entry resolves to healthy and declined sessions never enter recovery. The established precedent pairs a silent skip with an error status and a degraded tag, and that precedent was set for a fail-closed skip; this one is fail-open, so it needs the pairing at least as much.

The per-operator ownership arm now carries the set of gateway owners the caller knows it can act on, and the shard set is the union of those with the owners sessions name. The carried half gives a gateway with no sessions its restart; the session-named half keeps every session that recovers today recovering rather than declining it for being outside the caller's set.

The production recovery call site deliberately stays on shared ownership. Recovery drives a single gateway manager, so N shards would force-stop and restart one VM N times, each shard tearing down the sessions the previous one just recovered. The manager becoming per-owner is both what makes per-operator ownership correct and what makes it necessary; they cannot be separated.

The generator of that false documentation was my own instruction. A review reported the field missing from a documentation table and I passed the request through as a doc task; neither of us checked whether the field can ever be non-empty. Asking for documentation of a field is asking for a claim about behaviour, so the reachability of that behaviour has to be established before the request is made, not after.

The proposed retry mechanism was wrong and was corrected by measurement. Making the pre-call counter reset conditional does not produce a retry, because the healthy-probe arm zeroes the counter independently and every post-daemon-check exit leaves the next probe healthy; it would also hot-loop on the single exit it does cover. The retry has to be driven by the run's outcome rather than by the probe counter.

A gateway recovery pass now returns a must-use outcome and the monitor holds a retry deadline that a healthy probe deliberately does not clear. Backoff starts at one probe threshold, doubles per consecutive failure and caps at ten minutes without ever giving up, because each attempt force-stops the gateway VM and takes every gateway container down with it, so a fault that will not clear must not trigger that every half-minute forever.

Six previously committed sites asserted that degraded sessions sit with no gateway container, which was never measured and is the exact implication that was ruled out. A container under a restart policy may outlive the fault. All six now claim only that nothing was torn down and re-created and no policy re-applied.

The corollary of a measured claim inherits its felt certainty. The implementer wrote that a failure therefore does not leave unrestricted egress, which asserts the converse of what it had measured and which this path cannot observe. Both sites now state only that the table imposes no constraint on session egress, so its absence removes none, and that this is evidence in neither direction.

The load-bearing premise behind the whole eth0 correction is that gateway-container traffic is forwarded rather than locally generated. The absence of a forward chain is measured; the routing half rests on netfilter hook semantics and no packet has been observed. It stays on the live-VM list rather than being upgraded, because kernel-semantics claims certified as true-but-inferred have measured backwards here before.

When an unmeasured premise turns out to be load-bearing, look first for a route to the same conclusion that does not need it rather than going to measure it. The milestone annotation's verdict was re-grounded on purely measured facts: no rule in that table can distinguish a container flow at all. The premise itself stays unasserted at every site.

Prose correction freezes after the current bounded set. Eight commits in, an independent pass is running against a target that keeps moving, which makes its verdicts stale on arrival, and the session's actual open risk is a measurement that needs the host to itself.

I widened a delegate's correctly-scoped statement, that it had not observed a packet, into a claim that nobody had measured the routing premise, and put that into three delegation prompts as standing fact. The project's own session log records a live break-it-and-restore-it on the running gateway VM. The verifier's verdict shape is adopted: the premise is not unmeasured, which is a weaker and more honest claim than the premise is true.

The routing question and the queued core-promise question are adjacent and distinct, and settling the first does not free the machine. Where the host namespace sees a packet says nothing about what happens when the container's own tables are gone. If anything the record makes the queued question more pressing, since it places the entire constraint in the netns a restart clears.

The routing question was never gating the core-promise measurement. Both branches agree on the case that matters, since for arbitrary-host egress over the web ports this layer does not stop it either way. The branches differ only on a port with no accept rule, so one run with two destinations answers the core promise and settles the routing question as a byproduct.

An unmeasured negative claim licenses nothing in either direction. The false review criterion is annotated rather than dropped, because removing a gate is a permissive change, and the five flat assertions of the routing premise are hedged rather than deleted, because nothing establishing a claim is not the same as the claim being false.

The egress experiment enumerates all four outcome cells before the run, including the two that mean the run is invalid, because an unenumerated outcome gets rationalized into whichever branch the author expected. Counters are reset immediately before each probe rather than diffed, both branches are given positive signatures rather than one resting on an absence, and every probe must be a fresh connection since the established-and-related accept would otherwise pass the discriminating port under either branch.

Held the second correction commit rather than let it hedge the routing claims. If the premise is measured, the three unhedged log entries are true as written, and hedging would convert correct statements into uncertainty, making a future reader more willing to treat the gateway VM eth0 table as a control over container egress. A correction pass carries momentum and cannot see from inside which direction it is moving risk.

Deferred the live two-destination measurement behind the history check, reversing the planned order. The run was designed to settle the routing premise on a booted VM; if the permanent-log record holds, a far cheaper instrument already settled it and the run would spend hours reproducing a known result. The run sheet is not discarded - it stays valid and pre-registered - but it waits on the archaeology and on the adversarial refutation attempt rather than starting the moment the tree goes quiet.

The live two-destination run is dropped rather than merely deferred. It would convert an inferred claim that construction already guarantees into a measured one, at hours of VM time on an 8 GB host, while a confirmed silent egress-enforcement failure now sits unaddressed. The hedges in the tree are accurate as written, so the run buys wording precision rather than safety.

Diagnostics reports the calling operator's gateway — not the daemon's, not all of them. Reporting all would change the response schema and disclose other operators' gateway state across a privilege boundary; with the switch off it collapses to today's behaviour.

An unresolvable session owner falls back to the daemon's gateway on teardown paths and refuses outright on setup and restore paths, because tearing down against the wrong gateway finds nothing while setting up against it puts a live sandbox behind an egress policy that session was never granted.

The probe-gateway and policy-gateway accessors take an explicit owner uid with no no-owner overload; the one caller that has neither a session nor an operator names the daemon uid at its own call site, so the collapsing choice is greppable rather than implicit.

sandbox-agent learns the per-operator mode from its own startup environment, held on its run context and never read from the wire, so no broker op gains an instance-name or path field and the closed op set is preserved.

Retire the recovery-latch class from the gateway-singleton sweep predicate rather than growing its allowlist: every remaining hit is correctly-converted code, so the class measures nothing and only forces a permanent non-zero exit.

My recovery-probability arithmetic is withdrawn as unsupported. It multiplied a single one-second observation of the unhealthy state into a per-tick rate; one observation is not a rate, and the delegate was right to flag it. No recovery-likelihood claim gets published until the distribution is measured.

Plan changed: Gateway egress enforcement is measurably fail-open across a restart on the Linux route, and this belongs to no existing milestone. A single gateway process exiting takes the whole container down by design, the restart policy brings it back into a brand-new empty netns, nothing re-injects the enforcement floor, and nothing detects the gap. Needs its own milestone rather than absorption into the macOS operator-owned-gateway work, which is orthogonal to it. (total sessions: 210 → 213)

A newtype wrapping the collapsed gateway owner uid is the durable fix for the uid-confusion class, replacing prose verification with a compiler check. Deferred deliberately: introducing it mid-conversion collides with in-flight work, and it belongs with the batch that removes the singleton field rather than any one call-site batch.

Corrections that narrow a warning are the dangerous direction because they remove protection, but a warning aimed at a failure mode that cannot occur protects nothing while generating noise. The test applied here was whether the replacement lands on something that can actually fail, not whether it is more or less permissive than what it replaced.

No repair-time estimate is to be published from the crashloop occupancy figure. The monitor tick and the restart cycle are near-commensurate, so successive ticks regress in phase by about a second and sweep the cycle over tens of ticks rather than sampling it independently; the tick length itself was never measured against a running daemon. Occupancy is solid at roughly 0.37 percent, but a per-tick probability compounded over ticks is not a valid construction here.

The final sentence of the eth0-table discovery stands as written and is now better evidenced than when recorded: the table contributes nothing to session-egress enforcement in either applied or unapplied state, so failing to apply it cannot open an egress hole. Only the middle sentence is corrected, and the correction is captured forward as a new entry rather than by editing the original.

Switch-off identity was made structural rather than argued: the daemon's own route is now derived from the same factory at the daemon's own uid, which is the identical expression the collapsing function returns when the switch is off. With the switch off the per-operator accessor does not merely equal the old singleton field, it evaluates that field's own defining expression.

Gateway-uplink measurement is scoped to the lite/SLIRP path on a freshly created vmnet-free Lima instance, never the pre-existing stopped one, and the full-backend vmnet hop is recorded as undetermined rather than inferred from the SLIRP result — slot occupancy cannot be confirmed without elevation and socket_vmnet is a switch, so a wrongly-configured second VM would perturb a running instance.

The daemon-side call-site conversion is verified with zero defects by an independent predicate the verifier re-derived after its pre-registered one was invalidated by the rename. Switch-off identity is confirmed structural on both platforms -- the daemon's own route and the off-mode collapse are the same expression, not merely equal values -- and the site set is confirmed element-wise rather than by total.

Inter-agent handoff notes stay untracked under the ignored .tasks tree; they are ephemeral coordination scaffolding, not documentation. Anything from one that must survive a clean checkout is inlined into a durable surface (a code comment at the hazard site), never force-added.

The per-operator route collapse was extracted from its AppState accessor into a free function taking the route factory, so a test can exercise the real collapse without constructing the 32-field AppState. The accessor is now a one-line delegation, which is itself untested.

Agreement between two independently-authored checks counts as evidence only to the degree their failure modes are independent. Where a shared cause is present — the same rename, the same codebase, the same briefing — agreement is uninformative and can be actively misleading, so instruments are validated separately before being compared.

The call-site invariant merges both checks rather than picking one: the handler scoping from the implementer's, word-boundary spelling from the verifier's, plus the session-registry contract that neither covered — no collapsed owner uid may reach the session manager registry.

CORRECTION to an earlier session summary in this log: the clause asserting, under a 'PROVEN LIVE on this host' header, that DNS and HTTPS work from the VM host namespace while a container still egresses via the untouched FORWARD chain is NOT established. The manual test and the six integration tests cited establish the other items under that header, not this one; none of them egress a container. The routing premise carries the same hedge as every other copy until the packet-level capture lands.

Standing practice: any negative finding requires a positive control on a known-nonzero input run through the same invocation, and the delegate must state what its control could have caught. This is briefed as discipline rather than as a catalogue of known traps, because a pasted catalogue makes every delegate's blind spots identical to the orchestrator's.

The call-site discriminator is retired rather than widened, and the durable artifact is the uid contract over the three families: gateway accessors take an operator uid, the session registry takes a raw uid unconditionally, the route factory takes an already-collapsed owner uid. That model survived a rename and an extraction unamended while every pattern implementing it rotted twice.

RED demonstrations for the call-site invariant must be constructed from contract violations rather than string violations; a clause that can only be shown to fail on a misspelling is measuring spelling, not the contract.

The merged invariant is run at the extraction commit as its first application, because that commit has so far been verified only by its own author, and this session produced two self-authored checks that certified their authors' work at a zero true-positive rate.

A function is request-serving iff a caller identity is in scope. Adopted after measurement: routing-table reachability makes twelve of fifteen legitimate survivors violations, because the reachable set spans request and background paths and the distinction is not positional. Signature shape with all spellings of a caller-identity parameter gives nine functions and zero violations across twenty-one sites.

An orchestrator's hedged suggestion carries instruction force. A qualifier attached to a task assignment reads as a considered lead rather than as uncertainty, so unmeasured leads must be labelled unmeasured explicitly; hedging language does not do that work.

Any experiment whose possible outcomes include 'no reply observed at the guest' requires a third observation point outside the guest. Two observation points would have returned a confident wrong answer here — the absence of a reply was real and the inference from it would have been false.

SCOPE, and it must travel with every mention of the SLIRP result: the rig's gateway container was a bare forwarder with the production nftables ruleset deliberately absent. Nothing measured bears on whether production egress control leaks. The vmnet hop is undetermined and nothing in the capture speaks to it.

The seven hedged sites stay hedged. The standing rule gated them on 'the capture landing'; the capture landed and answered a different question — it was run against a bare forwarder with the production ruleset absent, so by the measuring agent's own scope statement it bears on nothing the hedges are about. Restating the gate by its question: the hedges lift when a run with the production ruleset in place, carrying a positive control, shows a session-sourced off-segment packet does not reach the external interface.

The capture moved the hedges in the restrictive direction, not the permissive one. It removed a candidate reason to believe containment holds — the session subnet is unmasqueraded and the emulated stack will service an off-segment source — without supplying any reason to believe it fails under production policy. Un-hedging is the permissive move and needs positive evidence, never the mere arrival of an artifact.

The correction note retiring the compound DNS-HTTPS-and-FORWARD clause is over-broad but stays as written; nothing is restored. Recording forward that its two halves fail for different reasons: the FORWARD half asserts a mechanism, which is what the refutation attacks, while the DNS-HTTPS half asserts only a direct observation and is untouched by that critique. The latter is nonetheless unestablished — no test covers it and its sole support is two fields of a single log entry written in one act by one author, which is one witness, not two.

CORRECTION, forward, to an entry I wrote one turn ago. I logged that a session-sourced packet leaves the VM interface with the container address intact, qualified as measured on a topology built from production argv. That qualifier is true and is the wrong qualifier: the argv was production, the ruleset was not. In production an unconditional masquerade in the gateway container's own netns rewrites the source before it ever reaches the VM's nat table, so the bridge-range rule I said could not cover it does cover it. The sentence is true of the rig and false of production.

The one unverified link now decides everything else: whether the generated ruleset is actually applied inside the gateway container on this platform at session-create time. The generator and its two callers were read; application was not traced. If it is applied, the emulated-stack finding is moot for production traffic and retains only two uses — a negative control, and a description of what breakage looks like. If it is not applied, that finding is live for production.

My own framing error, and it cost the run its primary question. I handed a two-candidate choice; the answer was neither, and the correct account was already recorded in the repo. A two-option frame from the person assigning the work reads as an exhaustive partition, so the delegate's real finding arrived as a refutation of both options rather than as the answer. Ask what property is responsible, never which of these two mechanisms it is.

To test a checker's domain you cannot inject inside it. Either enumerate the intended domain independently from an authority and compare counts, or inject outside what you believe is in scope and confirm the catch. A red demonstration placed in-scope is a control for the clause and no control at all for the selector.

The prior figure of zero violations across all surviving sites does not propagate. It was zero for the wrong reason. Re-measured under corrected scopes the result still holds at both revisions — the conclusion survived, the evidence for it did not, and only the re-measured form may be cited.

Name-anchored clauses are kept as cheap backstops but labelled as measuring spelling, because the self-test demonstrates their inadequacy directly: an injected defect with every identifier correct and current leaves them green while the contract clause fires. A clause that can only go red on a misspelling is measuring misspelling.

The accepted exception is expressed as a rule rather than an allowlist: a serving function may collapse the daemon uid only to ask a host-scoped question, and the resulting handle must be used solely for reads in a named set. A negative control withdraws the carve-out when a single non-conforming use is added. The exception is re-earned per site on every run and cannot be extended by appending a line.

CORRECTION, forward. The checker run I certified last segment was of a superseded file — three demonstrations injecting at one function, against a different default revision. The rebuilt file carries five demonstrations at another function and could not have produced the output I saw. My PASS was real and certified the version that still carried both scope defects.

The detector for a collapsed scope is the denominator, reported against an external landmark. How many functions did the selector match, and does that number square with something known independently — here, the count of registered routes. Ten against roughly twenty routes is visible immediately; zero violations is not. Every census reports its denominator alongside its numerator from now on.

The accepted carve-out stands, and the test is its premise rather than its provenance. Its mechanism was written after watching the clause fire, which is structurally the allowlist-entrenchment pattern whatever the intent, and pre-registration of the site is self-attesting. What settles it is checkable independently: the carve-out is sound exactly if every query in its named set is genuinely operator-invariant. If they are, when the rule was written stops mattering; if any is not, pre-registration would not have saved it.

The extracted helper is classified into the existing first family rather than founding a fourth. The contract question is which uid class a function receives, and it receives a raw operator uid and collapses internally; being handed the factory as a parameter does not move it, because the third family is defined by receiving an already-collapsed uid. A third name in an existing family is what the documented procedure covers.

Correcting a taxonomy's axis does not make it exhaustive. The re-derived binary — identity in scope or not — is local and checkable and still lost a third category: two sites need a different SHAPE of change rather than a different value, because the health probe returns one boolean about one gateway and per-operator means N gateways and N booleans. That is a fan-out design question, and it must be sequenced behind the substitutions rather than batched with them.

The route-factory rename is approved in principle and deferred on sequencing. Its proposed suffix form is exactly the shape that inverts literal-anchored checks, so it must not land while the call-site instrument is being rebuilt and re-baselined; and the daemon-side sweep must finish first so the file is quiet. Accepted on the confusion class being live in this codebase rather than on the specific pair having been confused — the author disclosed that distinction unprompted and it belongs in the document.

The two networking helpers that do no store I/O will receive an owner uid threaded from their callers rather than resolving one internally, and this is the stronger design rather than a concession. Their callers hold a uid from the authenticated peer credential; re-deriving the owner from a stored row where an authenticated uid is already in hand is a downgrade from a kernel-supplied signal to data. The alternative considered and rejected was widening an unfiltered store accessor from crate-private to public, which is a privilege-boundary change in service of stylistic uniformity.

Ruling withheld on the unresolvable-operator policy, because the asymmetry it rests on is incomplete. Tearing down against the wrong gateway is not a no-op: the correct gateway keeps the session's rules, so a fallback leaves a stale egress permission behind on a live gateway rather than merely failing to find one. Whether that self-heals depends on whether any reconcile sweep collects orphaned rules, which is now the measurement that decides the policy.

The unresolvable case is suspected to be under-discriminated, and a policy must not be written across it until that is measured. It is reachable only when all three resolver steps fail, and the reasons differ in risk: a row predating the column belongs to the singleton gateway by construction, whereas a present-but-unresolvable owner is genuinely unknown. If both routes exist the type should carry which one occurred and the policy falls out per variant; if only one exists there is no fallback to rule on, because the singleton answer is simply correct.

The operational form: when the odd member of a bucket needs a design decision rather than a mechanical change, it leaves the batch and goes to whoever owns the design. Left inside, it is estimated as its bucket-mates and settled by whoever reaches it first — which is exactly what would have happened to the question of what a mixed health result across N gateways means.

The unresolvable variant will not be split. Both routes into it are real and neither can fire, so a split would be a type change with no behavioural difference, justified entirely by a future configuration. My own framing was the defect: I asked how many routes lead into the state, which is a question about one function, when the question that settles it is whether anything constructs the state at all. Enumerable is not reachable, and a well-executed census of the first answers nothing about the second.

The network record will carry the gateway owner uid at placement time as an optional, defaulted blob field, alongside the operator uid it sits next to. The hard ordering constraint is that it must land strictly before the per-operator switch is ever flipped: absent then reads as written-before-the-field, which reads as written-before-the-flip, which is the singleton by construction. If it lands after a flip that reading becomes ambiguous and the field cannot be interpreted at all.

The backlog item commissioning a census of that defect is dropped rather than completed.
