A multi-line sweep of the false retry-cadence phrasing found five sites where a handed list named three, both extra copies in a different file from the ones under edit. The prescribed remedy for line-oriented sweeps missing wrapped prose is now measured to work rather than merely reasoned about.

Re-applying a session's policy on the recovery path is best-effort: failures are logged and not propagated. So a completed recovery attempts the policy rather than guaranteeing it lands, and nothing at runtime re-checks the ruleset afterwards. This compounds the open question about a container that outlives its fault.

The guest-operation enum is defined twice, once in the core crate and once in the agent's own protocol module, and the duplication carries the doc-comments with it. A sweep scoped to the crate that owns a concept returns clean while the same false sentence is live in its wire twin across the crate boundary.

A false claim was standing in mirror form at three further sites, phrased from the route-install side as what the baseline forwards or drops rather than as what it governs. Sweeping a claim's own wording never reaches the copies that assert it by negation or from the opposite direction, so correcting the primaries alone would have left it live.

The generator's own doc-comment was already correct and explicit, including a section on why container egress is unaffected. Every caller's doc contradicted it from eight hundred lines away. Correctness at a definition does not propagate to the sites that call it, and the callers are what a reader reaches first.

A second multi-line sweep across every crate and the docs and planning trees found four further copies of the same false claim, one of them verbatim in a crate that does not appear in the project instructions' workspace inventory at all. Each successive sweep has found more, so a clean sweep is not evidence of completeness; what changed between rounds was the axis corrected, not the diligence.

The false claim reached user-facing networking documentation and the networking design document, not only code comments. A claim that lives in doc-comments has usually also been written for users somewhere, and the user-facing copy is the one with consequences.

A separate false attribution surfaced incidentally in the policy summary: the output chain's established-related accept was ascribed to responses re-originated by gateway containers, but those traverse the forward chain. The rule is for connections the VM's own processes open. A matching test message carried the same attribution.

History settles the generator: one commit in June introduced the wording simultaneously in the macOS design spec, a milestone acceptance criterion and the networking design doc; code copies followed a day later. Two further copies were written two months on, three days ago, while the cleanup batch was already in flight. A generator keeps emitting during its own cleanup, so a corrected copy count says nothing about whether the source is closed.

The spec sentence states a purpose and then prescribes a mechanism in a parenthetical. The purpose was built; the mechanism was deliberately not, because the prescribed chain would have interfered with Docker's NAT. Every downstream copy quoted the mechanism clause, which is why the claim survived a reviewed and closed milestone: what it asserted was never what anyone tested.

The workspace has twelve crates. The project instructions claim eight and enumerate nine, omitting three, two of which held copies of the false claim. A sweep is only as complete as the inventory it ranges over, and the inventory agents trust most is the instruction file.

A systematic sort of every added sentence into measured versus follows-from-measured found five wrong claims that had already passed the author's own review, inside commits whose whole subject was correcting overclaims. The targeted advance warning caught one sentence; only re-deriving each claim from code found the rest. Two generators beyond the consequence connective: count words, which read as hedging so nobody checks them, and universals over alternatives the author never enumerated.

The worst surviving copy of the swept claim sat in the doc-comment of the very enum the sweep was about, and one false sentence was written in the same commit that deleted the sentence asserting its opposite. A sweep's own subject is a blind spot, because attention there is on the change rather than on the surrounding text.

A multiline sweep for a wrapped doc sentence returned zero matches across the whole tree while the sentence was still present. The wrap inserts a newline, indent and comment marker between words, so a pattern containing a literal space fails even with multiline matching enabled. The multiline flag is not the remedy it was believed to be; only a direct read settled it.

The retry arms at the cost of the probe trigger: while a retry is pending the consecutive-probe-failure path cannot fire at all, so at the backoff ceiling a fresh hard crash waits up to ten minutes where a first-ever crash waits thirty seconds. Separately, a retry force-stops a healthy VM after a post-ready failure, taking down gateway containers belonging to sessions that were never part of the failed pass.

The surviving copies of the propagated false claim are prescriptive rather than descriptive: a spec implementation row and three milestone lines, one of them an exit criterion demanding an egress-enforcement sign-off. A closed session may therefore have been signed off against a criterion whose premise is false.

The record of that live measurement sits in a gitignored session log, which is prose written by an agent and never executed since, so it carries no more weight than a doc-comment. What makes it auditable rather than merely assertive is that it names a commit, a failure mode and a test count. Auditing those is far cheaper than re-deriving the result on hardware.

The session-log record of a live routing measurement does not establish it. Both halves are bullets of one untimestamped session-close retrospective, the chain state it describes exists in no commit of that file ever, and the six passing tests it cites never run a container or generate a packet. Decisively, the observation could not discriminate: the rival chain accepts the same web ports, so a container fetching HTTPS egresses under either hypothesis.

The gateway VM baseline policy text opens with a flush of its own table, and every restart path re-applies it, so any instrumentation added live to that table is deleted by the exact event an egress experiment is measuring. The deletion is silent and produces a well-formed enumerated outcome, which means a pre-registered outcome census does not catch it; only a liveness check on the instrument read in the same step as the measurement does.

The gateway VM baseline reaches nft as a single stdin payload with the flush and the re-add in one string, so there is no split-transaction window. The real window is ordering: the recovery restart force-stops the VM, starts it, polls for Docker reachability on a ninety second deadline, discovers NICs and ensures the bridge, and applies the baseline last. A reboot clears nft state, so the table is absent rather than stale for that whole span, and the interface is necessarily up throughout since the Docker poll depends on it. The general startup path has the same tail behind far longer timeouts.

The closed session's egress-enforcement sign-off does not discharge the criterion it is recorded against: its subject was a staging TOCTOU (ruleset written to a fixed path in the VM's world-writable temp dir, applied by a second call), fixed by carrying the ruleset in the typed op and streaming it on stdin. That is about how the ruleset reaches nft, not what the ruleset governs. State recorded, not resolved.

The 'on the egress-enforcement path' phrasing propagated code-to-code between sibling enum variants in a single file, via a relational 'the other half of' framing, with no spec citation in the commit. Annotating a prescription at its spec root does not contain this class of copy — sibling-to-sibling drift inside one file needs a different guard.

Two sweep hazards measured here. sandboxd/target/doc/ holds generated HTML copies of pre-fix sources, so any sweep not excluding target/ returns phantom hits that look like live sites — a false-positive failure, opposite in direction to every other sweep hazard found here, and one that would have a fixer editing generated artifacts. And //! module headers sit above per-item docs and get skipped once the items are cleared: clearing a file's members does not clear the file.

The spec's own bypass-resistance gate cannot settle the routing question it was written for: its probe fetches HTTP over port 80, and the gateway VM's eth0 output chain explicitly accepts tcp/80, so the probe returns success under both competing hypotheses. A port outside the allow-list {53,80,443} makes either outcome decisive. An experiment whose result is possible under both hypotheses records a finding while testing nothing.

The five-site list for the unmeasured routing claim was incomplete by at least five more sites in one file, including a section heading whose title asserts the claim and a copy embedded inside the generated nftables ruleset string that ships into the gateway VM as a comment. The most detailed statement sits in the generator function's own doc header and reads as the origin the shorter copies paraphrase; hedging the named sites while leaving it intact leaves the generator live.

Gateway containers are created with Docker restart policy unless-stopped while session containers get restart no. A gateway brought back by Docker's own policy runs no sandboxd code path, so nothing re-injects its nftables ruleset; the container healthcheck probes only the five pipeline processes and never the ruleset, so it reports healthy, and the gateway monitor triggers only on NotRunning or Unhealthy. If a policy restart yields a fresh netns, that is a silent indefinite loss of egress enforcement. The netns-survival premise is the one unmeasured link.

The permanent log records what looks like a live measurement of the routing premise from four milestones back: an earlier baseline set the forward chain to policy drop with no accept for the re-originated path, and the observed consequence was that Docker container traffic could not egress. That outcome is impossible if container traffic traverses output rather than forward. The session had been treating the premise as never observed on this host.

For a JSON artifact, text search is the wrong instrument regardless of flags. A delegate reading the progress file for premise assertions reported one site; a structured parse over the same file found three in one pass, and cannot fail on line wrapping, gitignore scoping, shell-function substitution, or regex dialect. Parse structured data rather than grepping it.

grep and rg in these shells are shell functions, so any exec-wrapper silently substitutes a different program: timeout, xargs, env, find -exec, sudo, or a non-interactive script. Wrapped, grep becomes BSD grep and rg becomes exit 127 because no rg binary is on PATH at all. The grep function also pre-applies basic regex, so an alternation written in extended syntax returns zero hits with no error. A positive control certifies the invocation as run; wrap the control and it certifies the wrapper instead.

The per-session policy ruleset is rendered with format! and session-controlled values do reach its text, but the safety property on that path is typing rather than escaping: the element joiner quotes nothing, and what holds is that the compiler binds only the parsed-CIDR destination variant. A parsed CIDR cannot render an nft metacharacter. The guarantee is real today and has no guard behind it.

The extended claim sweep found eight sites across three files, two of which were outside the file everyone had been searching. The protocol enum is defined once per side of the broker channel and the second definition carries a mirrored doc comment asserting the same claim, so a sweep scoped to one crate reports clean while the duplicate is live.

Grading a specific commit by sweeping the working tree is void when a later commit has landed on top, and it fails clean: the sweep reads the newer commit's fixes and reports every site already correct. The grader caught this on itself mid-grade, noticed the line numbers had moved, and redid the derivation with git grep pinned at the target SHA. For any claim about what a commit did, the instrument must be pinned to that commit, not to HEAD of the tree.

The gateway VM's eth0 baseline never declared a chain on the forward hook in any COMMITTED version: string-search over the generator's full 35-commit history returns zero against three positive controls. That scope limit is load-bearing and was initially overstated as never existed - commit-history search cannot see an artifact that lived only in the working tree, which is exactly what a live bring-up debugs. The contemporaneous review attributes the observed breakage to VM-host-namespace traffic and labels the routing claim as the developer's reasoning, so the log entry does not establish the premise either way.

The routing premise is established structurally rather than by measurement: session and gateway containers are both attached to a Docker bridge network and neither is ever given host networking, so their egress enters the VM host namespace on a bridge port and is routed onward, which by netfilter hook semantics traverses forward and never output. Output applies only to locally generated packets. The rival branch was therefore never live for this traffic, but this is inference from measured flags rather than an observation, so the hedges saying nothing on this host has measured it remain true.

Two verification angles aimed at the same premise turned out not to be independent: an artifact hunt over repository history expects to find nothing under BOTH hypotheses, because the disputed chain was never committed either way. An empty result from that angle therefore corroborates nothing. Check that each angle's possible outcomes actually differ between the hypotheses before treating agreement between them as confirmation.

The gateway container's PID 1 is the entrypoint shell, a sixth process beside the five it supervises, and its monitor loop exits non-zero on the first death of any of them by explicit documented design. Both gateway creation paths carry restart unless-stopped, while session containers carry restart no. So a single crash of Envoy, mitmproxy, CoreDNS or either nft-logger drives a Docker-policy restart, which is the path that discards the network namespace and the injected ruleset with it. Readiness-probe timeouts under errexit and a failed bridge-IP discovery reach the same exit.

Nothing in the daemon can observe the resulting state: no production code reads RestartCount, no production code verifies the nftables ruleset is present (the sole non-test caller is a pre-apply rollback snapshot that treats an absent table as normal), and every health probe on both the container and daemon side checks process liveness only. The gateway monitor continues past both Healthy and Starting, so only NotRunning or Unhealthy reach the teardown-and-recreate path that would re-inject the base ruleset.

The base ruleset is injected only at gateway creation, from four production call sites inside the create and macOS setup functions. The policy-distributor and DNS-propagation injectors write policy tables rather than the deny-all and DNAT floor, so no periodic or event-driven path reinstates the floor after it is lost.

The structural asymmetry behind this defect: the egress-enforcement floor is installed from OUTSIDE the namespace that owns it. The daemon injects deny-all and DNAT via docker exec after docker run, so the container's own startup establishes no floor and a namespace the daemon did not create is open by default. A container that installed its own deny-all floor during entrypoint startup, before any traffic-carrying process launches, would fail closed on every fresh namespace by construction, with the daemon layering per-session allowances on top. That inverts the default from open-until-told-otherwise to closed-until-told-otherwise.

restart unless-stopped on the gateway actively races the daemon's own recovery. The monitor already implements the correct repair — full teardown and recreate, which re-injects the floor — but it only reaches that path on NotRunning or Unhealthy. Docker's restart policy wins the race and produces a running container that the monitor then reads as fine, so the policy converts a failure the daemon handles correctly into one it cannot see. Session containers carry restart no and would route into the monitor's path instead.

Measured on both container shapes with the genuine entrypoint as PID 1: a policy restart after a real supervised-child death does not return a healthy gateway. The Envoy bootstrap lives in a tmpfs and is written by the daemon after docker run, so the restart finds it absent, the first readiness gate times out at 30s, errexit fires, and the container cycles with a ~31s period. The externally-injected nftables tables are gone every cycle and only libnetwork's own nat table remains. The Linux shape behaves identically: its bind-mounted listener survives as designed, but that is the second readiness gate, and the first one is the tmpfs bootstrap.

The crashloop is the only thing standing in for a missing security check, and it is an accident of file layout rather than a control. The container healthcheck asserts five process-liveness conditions and never inspects the nftables ruleset. So any change that lets the Envoy bootstrap survive a restart — baking it into the image, moving it to a bind mount or volume, or synthesizing a default in the entrypoint — converts this availability failure into a silently unenforced gateway that reports healthy. The obvious fix for the visible bug is the one that arms the invisible one.

Sampled at one-second resolution across two full crashloop cycles, the container reports running with health starting for about 97 percent of the period and touches restarting/unhealthy for roughly one second per cycle. The gateway monitor polls on a 30s interval and continues past both Healthy and Starting, so it will almost never observe the unhealthy window and will not trigger recovery. A permanently dead gateway is operationally indistinguishable from a slow-booting one.

The netns inode number is not a reliable same-namespace discriminator here: across a restart the SandboxKey changed and every injected table was gone while readlink on the net namespace returned an identical inode, because nsfs reused the number. Container Pid, RestartCount and SandboxKey are the reliable discriminators. This does not disturb the earlier netns finding, whose conclusion was that the namespaces differ — reuse can only manufacture a false same reading, never a false different one, and the pin blocked reuse in that run.

The crashloop is not the safe branch, and my read of it as an availability failure was wrong. The open window is the up phase, not the down phase: forwarding needs only the namespace and ip_forward, both present from the first instant, while Envoy, CoreDNS, mitmproxy and both loggers start only after the readiness gate that never passes. So the container spends roughly 33 seconds per cycle forwarding with zero nftables tables and about a tenth of a second down. It is a mostly-open square wave, not an outage.

With no base chain registered on the forward hook the hook is not consulted at all, which is the opposite of an empty chain with a drop policy. The session's default route lives in the session's own namespace and points at the gateway address, which is static across restarts, so nothing in the gateway ruleset is needed for a packet to arrive and be routed onward. On the Linux route Docker's own source-subnet-keyed masquerade then completes the path to the internet. On the macOS routes the gateway emits an off-segment private source and the question becomes whether the VM's own uplink NAT rewrites it, which is unsettled.

The escape from crashloop into a healthy unenforced gateway runs through the ordinary policy shape, not an edge case. Policy distribution injects nftables only when the compiled rule set is non-empty, and it is empty for deny-all, deny-only and domain-only allowlists — pinned by three tests. Only CIDR rules generate nftables. So re-applying a typical domain-allowlist policy to a crashlooping gateway writes the Envoy bootstrap, unblocks the readiness gate, brings all five processes up, passes the healthcheck, and leaves the nftables state completely empty. Restoring a session is enough to trigger it.

Four in-repo comments assert that the deny-all floor is unconditionally in place from the first instant, and one of them is the stated justification for demoting the Starting state to Healthy in the monitor. The claim is true at create time and false on every restart, so a false comment is currently justifying the code path that makes the failure invisible.

On macOS a lite session is excluded from the gateway recovery arm even when the verdict is NotRunning or Unhealthy, because the backend match arm for the container kind continues without acting. So for lite sessions the recovery machinery is unreachable regardless of what the health verdict says, not merely narrow.

The search-wrapper boundary is exec of a new program image, not depth. Pipelines and both subshell forms keep the shell functions; what loses them is bash/zsh/sh -c, xargs, find -exec, env, timeout, sudo and script files. I had been briefing agents that a pipeline stage loses the wrapper, which is wrong, and it would have voided a cross-tool control that is in fact sound.

A third command is shadowed besides the two known ones: find at top level is bfs, not the system find. Neither prior agent recorded this, and one of them prescribed a find-based recipe specifically for the nested context while measuring it at the top level against the wrong find. The recipe happens to survive, but nothing in that document established it.

The whole top-level search rule is conditional on the per-session shell snapshot that installs the shadows, and neither agent varied that factor. The rg wrapper is defined only when no rg binary is on PATH, and both wrappers fall through to the real binaries when the helper is not executable, in which state the rule inverts completely. A one-line type grep check decides which half of the rule applies and costs nothing.

Exclusion spelling is not interchangeable across the three greps present here: the bare basename binds on all three, a trailing slash silently no-ops on BSD grep, and a leading dot-slash silently no-ops on all three at rc=0 with empty stderr. GNU grep is also available as ggrep and completes a repo sweep in about a second against BSD's twelve.

The gateway-singleton sweep predicate can never exit zero: its recovery-latch class matches correctly-converted code under the same field name, and the script the verification criterion cites was never committed to the repo.

The orphan reaper's per-gateway-owner pass is the already-shipped reference implementation for per-owner iteration, and the sweep predicate matches neither it nor its call site — a site can be fully in scope for this work and invisible to the instrument.

Owner enumeration for background tasks comes from the agent registry's connected-uid seam, not the GatewayLimaManager registry, which exposes no enumeration API and is lazily populated so iterating it would iterate only owners someone happened to look up.

GatewayLimaManager exposes no DockerRoute accessor, and the shipped per-owner precedent hands work a route factory closure instead — a factory cannot pair one owner's manager with another owner's route, an accessor can.

Three session-networking helpers carry a caller-username parameter that names who invoked rather than who owns the session, so it is a trap rather than a shortcut when resolving which gateway to act on.

The gateway-Lima module root doc asserts a daemon-scoped routing invariant that the registry path already violates, and it contradicts a doc 120 lines below it in the same file, so a top-down reader learns the wrong invariant.

Daemon-side and agent-side gateway instance names agree only with the per-operator switch off; sandbox-agent cannot read the switch because it deliberately does not depend on sandbox-core, so mode delivery is a privilege-boundary design question rather than a wiring detail.

Measured, not inferred: during the gateway's post-restart empty-ruleset window a session container reaches the public internet on TCP/443, ICMP and UDP/53, five open windows out of five, with the same far-end address an ordinary bridge container sees. Egress enforcement fails OPEN on the Linux route.

The escape path is Docker's own host-namespace masquerade keyed on the session subnet, not anything inside the gateway netns — the in-netns nat table only redirects the embedded resolver and carries no SNAT at all. Discriminated by counter deltas, not by reasoning: exactly three flows per open pass and zero per blocked pass.

Forwarding is live from the instant the netns exists because ip_forward is set at run time, while every enforcement process starts only after a readiness gate. So the dangerous case is restart rather than first boot: on first boot no session container has joined the network yet, but on restart they are already attached.

The container healthcheck probes five processes and never inspects the nftables ruleset, so any change that makes the Envoy bootstrap survive a restart converts a loud crashloop into a healthy, silently unenforced gateway. The crashloop is an accident of file layout, not a control.

Two registries expose get_or_create with opposite uid contracts: the gateway manager registry takes the collapsed owner uid, while the session-VM manager registry takes the raw operator uid because session VMs are per-operator unconditionally. Fourteen production call sites of the latter are correct as they stand; a check or conversion keyed on the method name would turn all fourteen into real defects.

A text-property check anchoring its enclosing-function regex at column zero makes every impl method body resolve to 'no enclosing fn', which such checks treat as allowed. The hole sat exactly over the code the check existed to guard and produced no visible output difference, so it was findable only by controlling the instrument, never by reading its results.

A taint trace over uid sinks reported bad=0 unresolved=17 good=0 and read as clean while resolving nothing: most matched sinks were type declarations rather than value flows. An instrument whose unresolved count equals its input count has measured nothing, and its zero-bad line is not evidence.

The gateway manager accessor is macOS-only, so converting a call site without the right cfg gate compiles on this host and breaks the Linux build. No check in the current verification set is behavioural or cross-platform, so nothing downstream catches it.

The macOS-only gateway singleton field is itself cfg-gated, so every existing use is already inside a macOS-only region and swapping one macOS-only expression for another in place cannot break the Linux build. The real hazard is narrower: eight call sites sit in ungated fns gated by an inner region, where the house style of resolving the gateway once at the top of a handler hoists a macOS-only call out of that inner gate.

A false warning whose only effect is defensive extra code that still compiles is close to undetectable downstream. This one had already been relayed to an implementer as fact before it was refuted, so it had stopped being a document line and become an instruction acting on a tree.

A container's unhealthy status is written by container exit, not by the healthcheck retries path. Measured on purpose-built control containers: one that Docker had just judged healthy with a zero failing streak reported unhealthy the instant it exited, so the configured retry count cannot have been reached. A third arm with no healthcheck declared confirmed the sentinel fires when the health object is genuinely absent.

During a crashloop the healthcheck state machine never advances past a failing streak of one against a retry threshold of three: exactly one probe completes per cycle after the start period elapses, and the restart resets it. Reasoning about that state machine is therefore correct about the mechanism while describing something other than what actually writes the status field.

The severity phrasing changes from never recovers to recovers only if a poll lands inside a roughly 0.12 second window per 31 second cycle. A stopped container reports unhealthy with its health object intact rather than an empty or starting field, and a crashlooping container's down-gap presents as restarting rather than exited.

Correcting the middle sentence of the earlier eth0-table discovery. That entry states unconditionally that sandbox egress is re-originated by the gateway container and traverses forwarding and container NAT. That holds only in the healthy state. In the empty-ruleset crashloop state nothing re-originates: the packet is plain-forwarded through the gateway container, whose forward hook has no base chain registered, and is then NATed by Docker's host-namespace postrouting masquerade rather than by any container NAT. The entry's conclusion survives because both states put the packet on the forward path, but a reader briefed by it would wrongly assume re-origination is guaranteed.

The measured forwarding fail-open does not bear on the eth0-table claim at all: zero table overlap. The claim concerns a macOS-only inet table generated for the gateway VM's host namespace, while the measurement concerns a deny-all table in the gateway container's namespace and a masquerade rule Docker installs in its own host namespace. The measurement also ran on Linux, where the claim's table is cfg-gated out and does not exist.

The eth0 table still declares exactly two base chains, output and input, with no forward, prerouting or postrouting hook and no nat-family chain or masquerade statement anywhere in the emitted ruleset. A pickaxe search reports it has never declared a forward chain at any commit, and an in-VM dump captured during a live run byte-matches the generator output.

A discriminating observation for the no-forward-chain reasoning now exists and was previously believed absent: on the macOS container backend a UDP round trip to an external time service completed while the eth0 table was live with a drop policy and no accept rule for that port. Under the rival hypothesis the packet dies at the default drop and the test fails one assertion earlier, with textually distinct output; the recorded failure text is from the later assertion, so the round trip had already succeeded.

The collapsing accessor is macOS-only, so three cross-platform call sites cannot name it inline. The conversion therefore moved the collapse inside two state accessors rather than writing it at each site, matching the shipped collapse-inside-the-callee doctrine. Consequence: absence of a bare operator uid reaching a route or manager no longer discriminates converted from unconverted code, because every converted site now passes that uid into the accessor by design.

The workspace does not build on Linux at the current commit, and the break predates this work. Two argv crates are declared under a macOS-only target dependency table while cross-platform code in the daemon binary references one of them, producing two unresolved-module errors. Verified pre-existing by an identical control build of the parent commit.

An unresolved-module error aborts compilation before type-checking, so a control build that fails identically on parent and child proves only that the failure is pre-existing, not that the child's cross-platform edits are sound. Establishing the latter needed a third build against a scratch tree carrying a control-only dependency-table patch, which then completed clean.

macOS session-bridge NAT is deliberately off (BridgeMasquerade(false) pushed only for DockerRoute::Vm) while the sandboxd-egress bridge is created with Docker defaults, so its masquerade is on but matches only its own subnet. A session-sourced packet forwarded out via the egress bridge therefore matches no masquerade rule — an off-segment source exists only once a session bridge and a container on it exist, so a bare gateway VM measures nothing.

The gateway VM's user-mode uplink is SLIRP (-netdev user), which terminates the guest connection and re-originates from a host socket rather than forwarding and rewriting a header. Asking what source address it rewrites to is a category error; the answerable question is whether SLIRP services a datagram sourced off its own segment and returns the reply. The eight socket_vmnet NICs are a separate mechanism belonging to the full backend.

Three sandboxd state trees coexist on this host: uid 309 (_sandboxd-test, lima dir drwx------ so unreadable without sudo), 310 (root), and 501 (owned by the login user, with a stopped gateway instance and pre-staged image tarballs). Work in the 501 tree needs no sudo and no image pull, which removes the sudo constraint from macOS-side measurement work.

A warning that shrinks from broad to specific reads as the product of scrutiny even when nothing was measured. Both the broad claim about cfg gating and its narrowed 8-site replacement fired on nothing; the sites are let-binding initializers with no top-of-handler to hoist to. Narrower is not a synonym for checked.

The forward-path dispute is two objects, not one. The narrow claim -- that the two quoted log entries measure the routing premise -- is refuted and stays refuted; the wider generalisation that nothing on this host has measured it is contested by a concurrently-written document neither author read. The two artifacts were created 41 seconds apart. Briefing the wider one as though the narrow refutation supported it is the live risk.

At least one unidentified source-rewriting step exists on the macOS session-egress path. A recorded UDP/123 round trip to a public anycast address drew a reply, but nothing masquerades a session-sourced packet on macOS, so an RFC1918 source could not have been answered. Two candidates -- the gateway container re-originating, or SLIRP rewriting at the eth0 boundary -- and the forward-not-output conclusion survives under either. The discriminator is the source address observed on the VM's eth0.

The tree and the log currently ratify opposite sides of the forward-path question: seven in-tree sites carry hedge prose asserting the reasoning is unmeasured, while the more recent log entry records that the hedge is stale and that promoting it is a permissive change needing a deliberate pass rather than a sweep. Neither surface is wrong about its own scope; they were written from different evidence.

The Linux crashloop rig ran Docker-default masquerade, matching the non-VM route, so its bypass-completion mechanism has no macOS counterpart and must not be carried across platforms. That document also discards its own docker-events histogram because the positive control failed, so the event stream from that run should not be cited by anyone.

The ruling that an unresolvable session owner falls back on teardown and refuses on setup has no call site in the landed conversion, so it is untested by it. The implementer used the always-present kernel-supplied caller uid rather than the nullable stored owner, and session lookup is owner-scoped in SQL, so the two coincide wherever a caller exists. The ruling only bites where no caller exists -- startup restore and reaper paths -- which are in the remaining batches.

A verification predicate anchored on literal substrings inverts across a suffix-extending rename: the old identifier is a proper prefix of the new one, so every converted site matches and the check reports failure permanently while appearing to track real work. Caught only because a second check over the same property used word-boundary anchoring and disagreed. Redundant checks at differing matching strength are worth their cost.

A git pathspec is resolved relative to the current directory, not the repo root, and a pathspec matching nothing makes git diff exit 0 with no output rather than erroring — so a diff-then-grep leftover-check run from a subdirectory returns empty for 'no data' and is indistinguishable from empty for 'no leftover'.

Two independent arithmetics for the daemon-side call-site residual reach the same total from different operands; the measured residual is six sites, not five, because one function carries two and one is foreground work the brief bucketed as background.

The implementer's withheld verification check and the verifier's own independently-authored check contained the identical substring-prefix defect, because both were written against the same rename-by-extension. Measured on the converted commit, the implementer's check has a 100% false-positive and 0% true-positive rate: every site it flags is code the conversion created.

A rule about the daemon's own docker field is only expressible when scoped to request-serving handlers, because that field legitimately survives at fifteen non-handler sites. Scoping is what makes the prohibition writable at all; without it no whole-file rule about that identifier can be stated.

An unsupported claim placed inside a list of supported ones, under a strong header, inherits the authority of its neighbours — the false item is laundered by the true ones. Session summaries are the copy later agents quote, so a summary is the worst place for such a list and the first that should be corrected.

The archaeology's single point of failure was tested and holds: the assertion-text row is byte-exact, and a full census confirms it is the only record preserving verbatim assertion text for that test — every other tuple-bearing record is a different test or a different backend.

The argument pinning which assertion fired has two halves — the trailing protocol suffix in the recorded tuple, which only the allow-event message produces, and the measured absence of all four early-assertion signatures from every run record. Either half relayed alone is materially weaker than it sounds; they travel together or not at all.

A name-anchored call-site predicate fails in both directions from one root cause: too loose and it matches the converted code, too tight and a shape change makes real call sites invisible. Requiring method-call syntax hid every free-function site after an extraction. Under-reporting is the dangerous direction because a clean census reads as reassurance and has no natural detector.

A check whose predicate is the code's own contract cannot drift from it; a correlated proxy can. The adopted handler definition works because a function holding a caller identity can ask the accessor and must, while one without has nothing to ask with — the same rule the accessors themselves encode.

The call-site invariant checker builds its RED demonstration in rather than transcribing it: a self-test injects a synthetic violation per clause into a throwaway extraction, never the repo, and the plain run prints that a clean result is meaningful only if the self-test passes at the same revision. Verified independently at the anchored commit — self-test PASS, plain run clean, tree untouched.

SLIRP does not drop an off-segment connection: it opens a real host socket to the destination and drives it to ESTABLISHED from the host's public address, while zero frames from the destination reach the guest interface. Serviced externally and lost on the return path. Guest-side capture alone is indistinguishable from a drop; only a host-side socket enumeration in the same run makes the distinction visible.

Measured on a real topology built from production argv: the VM's nat table carries POSTROUTING rules for the egress bridge and docker0 subnets only. The session subnet has none, and the egress rule cannot cover it because it matches on the bridge source range, so a session-sourced packet leaves the VM interface with the container address intact.

An instrument produced a false zero by pkill matching its own SSH command line and killing the shell before the probe ran; the tell was a preceding echo that never printed. The false zero pointed toward the tidier hypothesis, which is the direction that ships. Putting the logic in a script file makes the command line the script path and removes the self-match.

A bash tool call whose pipeline ends in tail reports the exit status of tail, not of the command under test. A cargo run that died at 101 was surfaced as exit code 0; only an explicit REAL_EXIT capture before the pipe showed the failure. Any run whose verdict depends on an exit code must capture it before the output is piped anywhere.

The failure was a bug in the control patch, not in the code under test, and it presented as the code failing on Linux. When a control run goes red, the control is the first hypothesis, not the subject — the instrument is the newer and less-exercised of the two.

A recorded grep baseline is meaningless without the invocation that produced it. The audited pattern contains a dot, so the literal count in the daemon binary is 87 while the same pattern as a regex yields 143 — the extra matches being an underscore spelling and English prose. A later census that retypes the pattern without a literal flag reads a 60 percent regression that does not exist. Baselines are recorded as number plus invocation or not at all.

The platform-gated composition test was verified by build-and-run on both platforms rather than by reading its attribute: the Linux binary compiles 127 tests and contains zero occurrences of the test name, the macOS one 189. The absence of a dead-code warning for the extracted helper on Linux is the corroborating signal that it is genuinely reached there rather than gated out.

The PROVEN LIVE header is not eight independent facts. Four of its clauses are assertions made inside the six integration tests whose pass is the eighth clause, so they are entailed by it rather than beside it — if that run is wrong they fall together. Six of the eight rest on one unrecorded live run. Read as a list of witnesses the header overstates its evidence by roughly fourfold, and the entailment is invisible in the prose form.

Two items on the header carry scope narrower than their wording. NIC discovery on real interface output was run against a two-slot gateway while production uses eight, so the broader claim is untested above two. Idempotent policy application was tested only in the sense of not erroring on re-application; that the resulting ruleset converges is a sound inference from a deterministic generator plus flush-then-re-add, but it was never asserted.

A fourth copy of the disputed claim set exists in the same log entry's decisions field, quoted by neither cross-check document. It is the most evidence-bearing of the four and supports both readings: it attaches an allow-list qualifier to the host-namespace probe while attaching no port or destination to the container clause, and four of its five observations survive independent examination. Not adjudicated.
Log entry 159's completed field is a list of 27 single characters spelling a timestamp — a string iterated into an array by whatever wrote it. Other entries may share the defect; the census is unrun.

progress.json line numbers are unusable as citations: the same header moved through three different line numbers during one session because the file is appended to while work proceeds. Cite by JSON path instead.

The source-rewriting step is an unconditional masquerade in the postrouting chain of the gateway container's netns, carrying no source or output-interface qualifier and no platform gating. Two stages: the session address is masqueraded to the egress-bridge address, which then matches the VM's bridge-range rule and reaches the external interface on-segment. The emulated stack services that and the reply returns — which is why egress works at all on this platform.

That masquerade is load-bearing and its failure mode is silent. With an identical topology minus the ruleset, four runs out of four completed at the far end while the guest saw only timeouts. A flushed or misordered rule does not present as a block; it presents as connections that succeed externally and hang internally.

A counter measurement was refused for three independent reasons, any one sufficient: the table lives in the VM host namespace and is installed by the daemon, which the rig never ran, so it did not exist; that table has no forward chain while the flow traverses forward, so a zero would mean not-matchable rather than not-dropped; and the probes ran on a port the table explicitly accepts. A zero would have read as evidence while carrying none.

The claim that container traffic traverses the forward hook rather than output is now inferred from measured premises rather than asserted: the captured packet carried a source no interface in that namespace holds, and a locally-generated packet cannot. The stated assumption is that nothing there used a transparent or raw socket. This is stronger than the repo's current very-likely-true position and weaker than a counter, and the production form requires substituting the masqueraded address, which survives but is one step further from what was seen.

A verification self-test validates the predicate, not the domain. I ran this checker myself, injected three defects, saw all three go red and the self-test pass, and concluded the daemon's request-serving code was clean. The scope selector was meanwhile near-inverse to what it claimed: it matched a bare typed parameter and missed the extractor form every actual HTTP handler uses, selecting 10 functions where the corrected version selects 27. My injections landed inside the 10 and so confirmed only the region already in scope.

Half of one clause was dead: an alternative spelled the registry access as a direct field call when the real spelling goes through an accessor method, and it matched zero sites at both revisions. Two sites were unchecked while the clause reported clean. Third instance this session of a check reporting zero for the wrong reason, all three in the under-reporting direction.

The checker truncates at the first test-region marker, so a test block placed near the top of the file would silently hide most of it behind a clean result. At the current revision the new test sits far down and the hazard did not fire, but it is latent and checked manually rather than guarded.

Re-running a check reproduces its scope, including a collapsed one. Independent re-runs establish reproducibility and exit codes, never that the clause searched the set it claimed — everyone re-running selects the same functions. This is agreement-is-not-evidence one level down: not two checks agreeing but one check agreeing with itself, and no number of repetitions can detect it.

The predicted rot did not materialize and the prediction named the wrong mode. Free-function call sites were expected to go invisible to a matching-strength requirement; measured by direct injection, the contract clauses catch the free-function shape in both argument forms and stay clean on the correct call. The matching-strength requirement lived only in instruments since retired or deferred. Both rots that did occur were scope defects — predicting the next failure mode from the one last seen is its own trap.

A taxonomy keyed on what a function is FOR is not checkable per site, and its connotation overrides the code. Two reads were filed as background with no operator context; the function's own parameter carries an owner uid and already uses it twenty-two lines below. The label named the role, the work depends on what values are in hand, and 'recovery loop' sounding like background was enough to make a uid sitting in the signature read as absent. Derived split is four with an identity in scope and two without, not five and one.

A literal-name sweep over-reports here by more than twofold, measured: fifteen hits for the route-factory field, seven in radius. Eight are a homonym — a zero-argument function of the same name in a different crate's integration test, which takes no uid and cannot express the contract at all. Renaming on the literal rewrites all eight as diff noise that reads as part of the change.

The rename's only silent hazard is invisible on this host. The macOS arm and the cfg-gated non-macOS arm hold two separate locals, and the Linux-side site is field-init shorthand — so renaming the field plus the macOS local leaves macOS building clean while Linux fails. Any execution of it is gated on the Linux cross-check, not on a green local build.
Intra-doc links are checked by nothing in this workspace: no crate denies broken_intra_doc_links, so a rustdoc link naming a renamed item dangles silently through build and test.

The session record does carry an operator uid, contradicting an earlier report that it held only a username. The absence was reported from a partial read — sixty lines into a hundred-and-forty-line struct, with the field sixty-nine lines below where reading stopped. The resolver already encodes network-record uid, then session operator uid, then username lookup; name resolution is its third step rather than its first.

Threading the uid into teardown also removes a hazard that could not be ruled out by inspection: whether teardown ever runs after the session row is deleted. A helper that takes the uid from its caller cannot produce an unresolvable operator on a deleted row, so the question stops mattering on the one path where it was suspected.

The fan-in count that justified resolving internally counted textual call sites rather than decisions. Fifteen teardown call sites live in exactly three functions, all three already holding an operator identity, and the DNS-gate helper has one caller — four functions, every one already carrying the value, and no new resolution decision introduced anywhere.

A second independent measurement that the loose anchor over-reports: dropping the word boundary from the field-read selector adds nine hits, all of them already-converted sites carrying the new name as a prefix. The boundary is load-bearing, and this is the prefix-inversion trap arriving on a different instrument in the same day.

A classification's arity is fixed before any member is examined, and it never surfaces as a claim anywhere. That is why a missing category is undetectable by review: a miscategorised item looks wrong where it sits, whereas the item that would have occupied an absent bucket gets filed somewhere plausible and nothing looks wrong at all. Checking the count of buckets has to be a scheduled step at the end of every classification, for the same reason a denominator does.

The unresolvable-operator state is unreachable in the shipped configuration. Its producer has exactly one non-test caller, inside the per-operator arm of the recovery partition, and the per-operator ownership value is constructed at exactly one site in the workspace — inside a test module. Production constructs the shared arm unconditionally, with no feature branch. There is no policy to write for the state today, and when the switch flips only one of its two routes will matter.

Name-to-uid resolution has no retry while its mirror direction has three attempts with backoff, and the codebase documents exactly why that guard exists — transient empty results for a valid uid under host load, from concurrent passwd readers and NSS cache eviction. The unguarded direction also collapses a genuine error and a genuine absence into the same value, so it can report an existing account as unresolvable and succeed on the next pass. This is the live defect in that area; it needs one function and no type change.

Nothing collects orphaned gateway rules. The single enumerate-and-reap machine excludes gateway containers structurally through a name parse that cannot match their prefix, deliberately deferring to a reconciler that a code comment says was never built; and every gateway-removal call site is driven by a session row, so a session with no row is visited by none of them. The stale-rule leak does not self-heal.

The per-owner orphan sweep that does run in production reaps three of the four per-session resources in a gateway VM — the sandbox container, its home volume and its network — and excludes the gateway container, which is where the enforcement rules live. The one uncollected resource is the enforcement plane.

Gateway placement is recorded nowhere. The network record names the operator, and the gateway owner is a mode function of it — returning the daemon uid while the per-operator switch is off and the operator uid while it is on — so placement is recoverable only by re-evaluating the switch at read time, which is exactly the value that can have changed since the write. Flipping the switch therefore makes every previously-placed session's rules unreachable, on a gateway that nothing collects.

The macOS reconcile pass is not a repair for the stale-rule case and would become a new instance of the original defect. It skips the lite backend entirely and uses the daemon's own route, so under per-operator gateways it would target the wrong VM for every operator-owned session; converting it helps only for stopped Lima rows, never for a removed row and never for lite. A site classified as low-priority on the conversion axis is a correctness bug on the axis that matters.

Append-only growth inverts a durable record's information order, structurally rather than by lapse. Understanding deepens over time and files are read top-down, so the most transferable sentence is always written last and therefore always sits at the bottom, under the anecdotes that prompted it. A reader arrives, meets three or four instances of a specific case, and never reaches the claim that generalises. The remedy is to restructure on each addition rather than append, and to check that the index line carries the mechanism rather than a corollary downstream of it.

RETRACTION, forward. An earlier discovery entry in this session's log states that a completed field holds a list of twenty-seven single characters spelling a timestamp, and that a string was iterated into an array by whatever wrote it. Every clause of that is false. The field holds the ordinary timestamp string; nothing iterated it; a print loop in an ad-hoc dump script displayed it one character per line and I read the display as the data. A full census of the store found zero entries with the shape, because the shape does not occur.

A repo-wide sweep returned five clean zeros because the invocation was dead, not because the tree was clean: a ripgrep-only flag was passed to GNU grep, which rejected it and printed usage to stderr, and stderr had been redirected to the bit bucket. The guard this yields is narrower and more useful than keeping a control — do not silence stderr on a search whose emptiness you intend to rely on. The dead invocation announced itself clearly and the announcement was the thing suppressed.

The fabricating pattern has zero instances in the tree, established on a denominator rather than a bare result: three hundred and twenty-two iteration sites enumerated through a syntax parser rather than a text search, partitioned completely by iterand form with the partition summing to the total. The Go half is immune because ranging a string yields a distinct static type, and the Rust bulk is immune because a string slice does not implement the iteration trait at all.

The null in that census is unusually strong because it is not on the axis the selector tests. The selector looks for loop bodies that tolerate a single-character item and it found eighteen, so it is demonstrably live on this tree; the zero comes from a second independent axis applied afterwards by hand, namely that every one of those eighteen is fed by a locally-constructed list. A selector that returns zero on its own axis proves much less than one that returns a healthy count and is then filtered by a different property.

Those eighteen sites are one helper refactor away from the defect, and they sit in assertion-message construction — code that runs only when a test is already failing, which is the moment a reader is most credulous about output and least able to cross-check it. Fabrication in a failure message is the worst placement of that class.

The defect's actual population is not the tree. Zero instances are committed; the one that occurred lived in an ad-hoc analysis script run inline and never written to disk. That population — throwaway measurement scripts — has no review, no tests and no persistence, and it is the population from which every reported finding arrives. A clean tree-wide census is therefore weak reassurance about the channel that actually failed, and could not have caught it.

The unretried name-to-uid lookup is live and is not a fallback. It has one caller outside the unreachable gateway-ownership resolver, in the macOS vmnet pool restore, which runs at every daemon startup independent of the gateway switch. A complete census of non-test network-record literals found three: both Lima paths store the operator uid, and the shared allocator stores none — and macOS lite reaches only the allocator, with nothing filling the field in afterwards. So on lite the name lookup is the only path, taken for every running session at every startup.

What makes that a defect rather than a style point is an asymmetry inside one file: the uid-to-name direction carries a three-attempt retry with backoff and an explicit rationale about transient name-service misses, and it runs once per accept. The name-to-uid direction has no retry and runs across every persisted session at startup. A transient miss declines the entry, so a running session's capacity token is not re-registered and stops counting against its operator's quota, and the decline message instructs the operator to stop the session — correct for a genuinely deleted account, wrong here.

Asking what the retired recovery pins stood in front of, rather than whether their assertions still passed, found a third owner-keyed sink that nothing checked: the gateway-recovering latch. Both of its sites are correct today and both were uncovered by every existing clause. The failure it admits is silent in the worst way — writer and reader key the same map under two different uids, so the latch is never observed, the monitor never skips a session under recovery, and nothing errors; recovery simply races.

That makes a third thing the gateway-ownership switch breaks on flip, alongside the orphaned egress rules of already-placed sessions and the gateway container the per-owner sweep does not reap. All three share one shape: correct today because a single expression is used on both sides, and silently divergent the moment that expression becomes a function of operator. The pre-flip ordering constraint now has to cover all three.

The scope guard was validated against the real historical failure rather than a hypothetical: restoring the original collapsed selector yields zero of seventeen registered route handlers and four matched functions in total, while every clause stays green because almost nothing is left to be green about. A guard proven on the actual defect it exists to catch is worth more than one proven on a constructed input, and this one also states its coverage as a floor with the two handlers that legitimately carry no caller identity measured, not assumed.

With three delegates whose replies were lost while their work landed, the reliable liveness signal turned out to be side-effect artifacts rather than the message channel or idle notifications: a bytecode cache directory's modification time shows an instrument was executed minutes ago, which distinguishes a delegate actively working from one that has silently stopped. Idle notifications reported neither correctly.

The vmnet pool registry is the sole authority on slot occupancy at allocation time: the claim path reads three in-memory mutexes and consults no store, filesystem, hypervisor or socket. And a slot is not merely a segment — the address derivation is a pure function of the slot index producing a slash-29, so two sessions on one slot share a socket daemon, a segment, and the identical VM address. One tenant per slot is not a convention layered on the pool; the address math has no room for a second, and the pool is the only thing enforcing it.

The restore path's own doc comment names the exact hazard thirty-five lines above the line that commits it: it justifies the decline policy by saying a silent drop would leave the pool believing a slot genuinely in use is free, and then a let-else silently drops on a different trigger. The prose is correct and the code contradicts it, which is the opposite of the usual defect where the comment has gone stale.

The decline guard buys visibility, not occupancy safety: declining and silently dropping leave the pool in the identical state, because neither re-registers the claim. So the never-guess policy is sound on the attribution axis and does nothing on the occupancy axis, while reading as though the failure was handled. A guard correct on the wrong axis is worse than no guard, because it advertises that the case was considered.

The existing leak detection cannot surface this class and its metric moves the reassuring way under it. The cross-check computes registry-minus-store — a slot claimed for a session that no longer exists — while this defect is store-minus-registry, a live session whose slot is unclaimed. The reverse direction is unmonitored, and when it occurs the reported claimed-slot count gets smaller, which is the direction that reads as healthy.

The per-session slot pool is the sole mechanism keeping two macOS Lima sessions off one L2 segment. Every other candidate layer either presupposes the disjoint-subnet contract the pool provides, is a pure function of the slot index rather than independent of it, or protects a different adjacency.

The module doc disclaiming 'bookkeeping, not access control' disclaims kernel-side protection against connecting to a slot socket directly, and explicitly claims that the daemon will not hand out another operator's slot. That claimed property is exactly what a lost claim breaks, so the disclaimer is the finding's charter rather than a deflation of it. Partition (whose ledger) and slot uniqueness (one tenant per segment) are separable, and only the second is at issue.

macvlan private mode is deployed on every per-session network with a comment naming slot reuse as the case it defends. Whether it reaches VM-to-VM traffic is inferred from macvlan sub-interface semantics, not measured, and two agents reading it the same way is agreement rather than independent evidence.

The call-site checker verifies a proxy - zero self-dereferences - for the property it exists to enforce, which is operator-invariance of a host-scoped query. With one member the gap is coverable by hand; it opens at the second, when a green result will be read as an admission decision. The qualifier belongs on the admission rule, not on the descriptive sentence.

A per-clause census's first version carried the exact defect it was built to detect: an un-incremented counter simply did not print, so absence read as nothing. Pre-seed every counter to zero in any instrument that reports counts.

The gateway policy addon fails OPEN. An exception raised anywhere in the addon's request hook before the deny response is assigned converts a deny into an allow, silently, leaving only an 'Addon error' line in the container log. Measured from the bytecode shipped in the pinned image, not from upstream source: the addon manager's safecall catches every Exception that is not AddonHalt or OptionsError, logs, and returns None, and the kill check tests only flow.error, which a swallowed addon exception never sets.

The image ships mitmproxy as a stripped PyInstaller onefile bundle with no Python source at all, so the prescribed 'read it out of the image's site-packages' method was impossible. The module lives inside the binary as compressed bytecode; version is recoverable from the bundle's own version module rather than from the build arg, and both current image tags share one mitmproxy layer digest.

The deny path emits its event between deciding to deny and enforcing the deny, so any exception escaping event emission turns the deny into an allow. It is defended today only by the event writer's own exception handling in a different file, with nothing at the call site expressing that dependency.

The event writer justifies its own defensiveness twice, and both times names the wrong consequence - a 500 to the caller, where the truth is the request reaching the origin server. The code is correct and its stated reason understates the stakes, so a future reader simplifying it would be trading against a fiction. The deny-path reorder is precisely the edit that would expose it.

Four instrument deaths across two delegates tonight, every one caught by a control rather than by inspection. The hardest was a probe that returned zero for every string it looked for, because a zero that refutes your own finding reads as intellectual honesty and is the least likely result to be challenged. The other direction was a count reporting total failure that was the harness's own attribute error - printing the exception text rather than the count is what caught it.

Containment holds under the real production nftables ruleset for both TCP and UDP, with two positive controls green in the same pre-registered run: a session container's packet to a denied destination never reaches the VM's external interface, zero packets, while an allowed one does and its reply returns. The pre-registration was timestamped 86 seconds before the first arm and included the commitment that both controls failing means concluding nothing.

The discriminator for the off-segment SLIRP behaviour is the absence of a postrouting masquerade, not the protocol. A three-arm A-B-A on one UDP flow differing only in that rule reproduces and repairs it. Protocol was a confound of two rigs. Production has no such path at all: UDP is masqueraded before leaving and TCP is never forwarded, since allowed TCP is redirected to Envoy which re-originates and denied TCP is redirected to the deny logger.

Loading sandboxd's baseline external-interface ruleset breaks host-namespace name resolution inside the gateway VM, permanently and A-B-A reproducibly. Lima's own guest nat chain rewrites a query to the configured nameserver into one aimed at an ephemeral high port, and nat output runs before filter output, so the policy's port-53 accept never matches. Queries survive briefly on pre-existing conntrack entries and then stop forever. Inferred to apply to production and explicitly not verified on a manager-created VM.

Two observability defects in the gateway event stream. Denied TCP produces no record at all, because the deny logger binds the address it discovers at container start, before the session bridge is attached, while the redirect targets the session-bridge address. And the allow logger reports denied DNS as an allow, because port 53 is redirected to CoreDNS unconditionally so a conntrack entry always exists. Containment is unaffected in both cases; what is affected is any audit that reads those streams.

A delegate's chosen positive control tested the wrong layer: both the allowed and the denied UDP arm were intercepted by an unconditional DNS redirect before policy was reached, so neither exercised the path under test. It was caught because the answer was implausible rather than because the instrument announced anything - a resolver returning NXDOMAIN for a name it would have answered. Reported rather than quietly replaced.

The gateway ruleset is delivered at session-create, traced end to end on both macOS backends with no platform gate excluding it, no swallowed error, and a failed nft aborting creation rather than yielding an unprotected session. Traced by reading, not confirmed at runtime. Better still, the masquerade whose absence produced the leaky arm is unconditional at generation and ships in the same nft input as the chain it protects, so no configuration installs one without the other. Two independent grounds rather than one.

Session-create and apply-policy install two different rulesets with two different failure modes. A freshly created session runs deny-all plus a redirect chain with empty allow sets, so everything falls through to the deny logger or drops. Fail-closed, and it is exactly what a rig looks like before the policy artifacts are seeded.

The unreachability of the unresolved-operator arm rests on a database invariant, not a type invariant: a one-time migration deleted the offending rows but the column is still nullable, so nothing prevents a future write path from reintroducing the state. The arm must stay live rather than becoming an unreachable assertion. Its earlier withdrawal ground - a single production consumer - is itself destroyed by the very change now being made, which adds ten more.

Seven instrument failures across four agents in one session, none caught by inspection, and three caught by luck rather than by any planned control - a line still on screen, an implausible answer, a negative control run for an unrelated reason. Two reusable heuristics: when a census returns zero for every member of a set, the uniformity is the signal; and when a selector returns empty, re-run at lower matching strength rather than re-reading the same query, because an empty grep and an absent call site are the same output.

The mitmproxy addon fail-open is latent with a stated boundary rather than latent unqualified: 158 raise-capable operations enumerated in the addon file and cleared, but only 28 percent were exercised against real imported functions and six cross-boundary subtrees were never opened. The most security-relevant operations - the request properties parsing the agent-controlled Host header, which run first and before any try block - were absent from the coverage table entirely and had to be found by censusing its complement.

Retiring a check by asking what region it guarded, rather than whether its assertion was true, found a third owner-keyed sink that neither the retired check nor any of its replacements covered. Correct at HEAD and entirely unchecked. Its failure mode is silent in the worst way: writer and reader key the same map under different uids, so the recovery latch is never observed, the monitor never skips a session under recovery, and nothing errors - recovery just races.

A violation count reported without its denominator is unfalsifiable by construction, since a correct tree and a dead clause both print zero. The fix that worked: a landmark derived from different syntax than the selector reads - route registrations rather than parameter shapes - with the acceptance floor validated against the real historical collapsed selector, which scores zero of seventeen while every clause stays green. Re-running a check cannot detect this, because every re-run reproduces the same scope including a collapsed one.

Half of one clause had been dead for some time because the spelling it matched never existed in the tree, and the two sites it nominally covered were unchecked in silence while the clause total looked healthy. Counting each alternative of a pattern separately is what made it visible. Related: a hand count run as a control on an instrument found none of the instrument's real defects and contributed eight errors of its own, so the two are independent instruments rather than one checking the other.

JSON1 functions are available in the SQLite this build actually links: the bundled amalgamation is compiled with the enabling flag passed explicitly in the sys-crate build script, verified against the lockfile rather than inferred from upstream defaults. A one-statement json_set backfill is therefore viable; no repo SQL used a JSON function before, so availability was load-bearing and unproven.

The persisted owner field serializes as an explicit null rather than being omitted when unset, so a single json_extract IS NULL predicate covers both pre-field and post-field rows. Backfill reaches Linux rows too, which falsifies a rustdoc claim that the field is macOS-only; traced as harmless because the fallback resolver step yields the same answer.

Red-injection verification cannot exercise acceptance terms. An acceptance suppresses a violation, so the site stays green and no injected defect reaches it; the self-test passes whether the acceptance works, is too broad, or is dead. Acceptances need a green/red pair on one real site. A redundant acceptance and a dead one produce identical output on every run.

A third owner-keyed sink was found by asking what a check stood in front of rather than whether its assertion held: writer and reader key the same map under two different uids, so the latch is never observed and nothing errors — recovery just races. Both sites pass every existing check.

The proxy-hook fail-open scope is bounded but not closed: 158 in-file raise-capable operations enumerated and cleared, 28 percent exercised and 72 percent read only, six cross-boundary subtrees unexamined. The most security-relevant operations — parsing the agent-controlled Host header before any try block — were absent from the coverage table entirely and cleared only by the complement pass.

None of the gateway's five health probes inspects nftables — they check processes and HTTP only. The gateway exists to enforce egress and no health check can observe whether it is enforcing. Every recovery trigger keys on NotRunning or Unhealthy, so a gateway that comes back with no rules reports Healthy, no trigger fires, and nothing re-delivers. Independent of any restart question.

Gateway bring-up order is deny-all, then DNAT plus masquerade in one transaction, then forward-allow. Forwarding is enabled only after the masquerade is in, so there is no window during setup where the gateway forwards a session packet unmasqueraded. Unreachability by ordering rather than by timing luck.

No production path pulls the gateway or lite image by name on any platform. Images move as a staged tarball streamed over the broker into docker load, with no name resolution anywhere in the sequence; every docker pull in the repo is in a test file. This removes the concrete harm that motivated the in-VM resolver check.

A macOS lite create carrying a policy distributes the full artifact set during create, fatally. The earlier claim that a freshly-created session always runs deny-all with empty allow sets is false for that path. The error was enumerating one function's call sites and not asking who called those — a call-site census is only as deep as the hop it stopped at and reads as complete at every depth.

Policy re-delivery after a gateway restart covers the per-session artifacts only; deny-all, DNAT and masquerade return solely on a full gateway re-create. On macOS the monitor skips container-backend sessions entirely, so a lite gateway found not-running is rebuilt only at daemon startup.

The unfiltered session-lister's doc block contradicts itself within twelve lines: the summary paragraph is the FILTERED sibling's documentation, asserting per-caller isolation on a function that takes no caller argument and whose SQL has no WHERE clause. The correctly-documented sibling has no doc comment at all — the paragraph migrated. Nothing in the build checks a doc comment against the item it is attached to, which is the shared cause behind all three prose defects found on this boundary.

Production bug reaching the end user's machine and no other: the gateway VM's own nft baseline breaks DNS in the VM host namespace, because Lima's DNS chain in nat OUTPUT rewrites the destination port before filter OUTPUT runs, so the ruleset's own port-53 accepts never match the packet the filter hook receives. Both image loaders succeed silently when the staged tarball is absent and nothing passes an explicit pull flag, so an unstaged host falls through to Docker's default pull policy into DNS the daemon has already broken earlier in the same bring-up. The operator sees a registry timeout where the code's own comment promises an actionable no-such-image error.

The masking is structural: a staged host has the image present, never pulls, and never sees the DNS break. Only an unstaged host — which is every end-user machine — reaches it. The dev-setup step that makes it invisible is the one the end user does not run.

Measured: a restarted gateway container comes back with its nftables ruleset gone. Three triggers agree (manual restart, stop+start, and a policy-fired restart under an auto-restart policy, the last run twice), each arm carrying a positive control that voids it if the marker table failed to load beforehand.

A network namespace's inode number is RECYCLED across container restarts and is not an identity test: it was identical before and after in every arm while the namespace was in fact destroyed and rebuilt. ifindex is namespace-local (first non-lo is always 2) and equally useless. The signals that work are the veth MAC and the embedded resolver's ephemeral ports, both freshly drawn from a large space.

That restart measurement was taken with the gateway image's entrypoint overridden, so it cannot speak to whether the real entrypoint reinstalls any base ruleset at container start. The claim it supports must be scoped to the daemon-installed rules until the image's entrypoint is read.

Measured: docker's default 'missing' pull policy does make a registry round-trip on an absent image (the failure is a registry's 'pull access denied / repository does not exist' answer, not a local lookup). With --pull never the error is verbatim 'No such image: <tag>' - which is exactly the string the lite image loader's doc comment promises operators. The comment accurately documents the behaviour of a flag the code never passes.

Lima's shipped default.yaml sets hostResolver.enabled to null with a builtin default of true, and a provisioning script embedded in limactl creates the LIMADNS chain and its port-53 DNAT gated only on the host DNS port being non-empty and non-zero. It uses iptables, which is iptables-nft on the guest, so the rules surface in nft list ruleset. sandboxd never sets hostResolver anywhere. The DNS-break mechanism is therefore traced end to end by reading, not inferred.

A ruleset dump taken inside a container cannot see VM-host-namespace tables - a container has its own netns, so the dump shows only container tables plus docker's embedded resolver. This is why a rig that ran inside a colima container had adjacent evidence about DNS but could not answer a question about the VM host namespace.

The deferred-todo backlog is 236 items, and 152 of them come from just two sessions - 103 from the session currently in progress and 49 from an earlier one.
