The migration freeze binds on every applied migration, not on the four files the bulk edit happened to touch. Two consequences are permanent and unfixable in place: a false forward-compat premise, and five milestone tags that the project's own no-tags-in-source rule can therefore never satisfy.

A deliberate guard against routing an unowned value through shared state protected the finished value while its factory sat two fields over, and the automated checker matched only invocations so a borrow was silent. Guards on a dangerous value must put producers of that value in scope.

The container network's operator identity is in-memory registry state, not a persisted column. Comments attributing it to a session row are wrong about the cause, not merely stale, and asserting the row's non-null guarantee there would make them worse.

Phrasing-grep builds correction site lists that miss reliance sites. The guest-side uid fallback depends on the operator-uid guarantee and calls unwrap_or(0) without restating the premise, so it never appeared in a phrasing-derived list.
The git remote helper re-execs through current_exe(), which on macOS resolves to the symlink name and re-enters the remote-helper branch, so the child parses the socket value as a repository URL.

The macOS e2e suite currently runs 35-red, so it is an instrument that has stopped reporting rather than a weaker green. The remote-helper case executed and failed on every recorded macOS run; it was never a case of the test not running.

The gateway route factory escapes its holder in exactly two places: one wrapped in a collapsing resolver and safe by construction, one bare and defective. The four other producer fields are call-only. The proxy fix plus the widened checker clause therefore closes the class rather than being one of N.

A guard keyed on one spelling of consumes and a census keyed on one spelling of produces are the same instrument failing at opposite ends of one seam. The census failure is worse because it reports a number, and a wrong denominator containing no defects reports identically to a right one.

Restoring the old uid fallback did not merely build a route from uid zero: the guest round trip completed and the row was served. Whether that is a robustness defect or a reachability one is unmeasured, and the startup null-operator count is its denominator.

A second commit in the same sweep family exists and its own message declares it partial with a promised follow-up; every damage-population figure gathered so far is scoped to the first commit alone and needs that qualifier attached.

Per-site provenance testing — does this exact line exist in the damage commit and not in its parent, with a known-introduced control reading 1/0 — separates real damage from false positives more cheaply and reliably than reading the sites.

A selector keyed on the residue a deletion leaves behind can point one line off the actual damage: a citation deleted from the end of a wrapped line leaves its residue on the following line, so the neighbour must be tested before ruling a site pre-existing.

The git-status block in this session's context is a start-of-session snapshot and is now hundreds of commits stale; every agent spawned here inherits it, so any commit hash cited from it names a months-old tree.

A checker that can report 'decided nothing' distinctly from green carries information a binary red/green cannot: an undecidable verdict identified a wrong input commit that both a red and a green would have silently validated.

A checker aimed at prose/code disagreement is structurally blind to the normal case: a doc written from the field's name is wrong in the same direction as the name, so nothing disagrees. 0 of 203 candidates real; the one true defect in the tree is invisible to the instrument built to find it.

Damage from a bulk comment sweep does not need reconstructing: the pre-image commit holds every original sentence. Repair is 'restore from pre-image, remove the tag properly', not 'infer the missing clause from surviving context' — which is how a repair manufactures a plausible sentence nobody downstream can distinguish from the author's.

A green e2e test can be the worst instrument in a red suite: the sole end-to-end pin for the workspace-teardown path passes because the daemon fails earlier for an unrelated reason and never reaches the injected condition. Red tests announce themselves; this one reports healthy while carrying no information.

Content stripped by the bulk comment sweep is not lost — every pre-image is recoverable verbatim from the damage commit's parent, including sites previously catalogued as permanently unrecoverable. Comparison must use authoritative diff hunks: comparing the same line number across two revisions returns unrelated text that reads like a plausible pre-image.

The most dangerous residue of the sweep is a document-to-code substitution family: 'the spec doesn't constrain that' became 'the migration doesn't constrain that', converting a claim about a document's silence into an unverified, checkable claim about behaviour that reads as already-verified beside the code.

Selectors anchored on the marker a damage commit removed cannot see files where every marker was removed; anchoring on the phrase the commit inserted found ten further sites. Third instance of one root cause — enumerate from what the commit added, since what it deleted is enumerable from nothing.

Migration-freeze mechanism verified empirically rather than inferred from library source: five pre-registered outcomes all matched, with a rerun control and a byte-restore attribution step, confirming a one-character edit inside a comment and a single appended newline are each fatal.

git check-ignore silently declines to answer on tracked paths — exit 1 with no output, byte-identical to a genuine 'not ignored'. --no-index forces a real answer. A third-outcome collapse in a first-party porcelain command, which is harder to catch than the same defect in a hand-rolled script because nobody audits git for it.

A false clause bundled into a sentence with verified ones inherits their credibility and goes unexamined precisely because it was never the point of the sentence. The measured half came from git ls-files and was sound; the decorative half rode along and was wrong.

With the per-operator gateway switch at its unset default, the route resolver returns the daemon's own uid for every operator uid, so passing a substituted uid and the true one yield identical routes. The uid is consumed but its effect is collapsed — any test asserting uid-dependent routing on that path is zero-variance and cannot fail while the switch is off.

The Lima helper rejects op-uid 0 outright, so a uid substitution is loud on that path and silent on the container path. The two backends fail in opposite directions for the same defect, which is why a single-backend measurement cannot characterise it.

V009 deletes NULL operator_uid rows and adds no constraint; the column remains nullable from V008 and SQLite cannot add NOT NULL in place. New NULLs are prevented by daemon write paths stamping the peer credential, not by the schema — confirming the frozen migration header's conclusion describes only the rows alive when it ran.

The git-remote re-exec failure is macOS-only because current_exe() appears to return the unresolved symlink there while Linux's /proc/self/exe resolves it, so the child re-enters remote-helper mode and parses the socket path as a URL. The tell was in the error text all along: the unparseable URL is a socket path, which only occupies argv[2] in the re-exec's own argv.

A parametrized test across two backends gives a free differential: the same function with the same fault injection passed eight times on one backend and failed on the other. One backend announces the gap the other conceals, which is stronger evidence than any argument from reading the code.

The in-tree comment recording the macOS events-transport gap narrowed during this session — it once named the listener and events host directories, now only the listener. A known gap is becoming an unknown one by sentence erosion, with nothing deleting the gap itself.

A function named in two source comments, including a broken intra-doc link, does not exist in the tree; it was cited as evidence in a report before being caught. cargo build, clippy and fmt are all green with broken intra-doc links, so nothing in the standard chain sees this.

The git apply --cached + bare-commit hunk-isolation technique reintroduces the cross-author commit bug one layer down: the index is a single process-wide object, so a bare commit takes any concurrently-staged work from another agent. The staging window is the exposure. Guard is an empty staged diffstat immediately before staging, in the same invocation.

Build-level instruments cannot detect cross-author contamination in a shared tree: check, clippy, fmt --check and the full 2623-test suite were all green on the union of two agents' uncommitted work, because two individually coherent changes compose coherently. Ownership must be established from diffstat-versus-remembered-edit, not from a clean build.

git notes are the wrong carrier for a commit-message correction here: git push does not push refs/notes/* without an explicit refspec, and this repo is pushed manually, so the note would be left behind by the very operation that publishes what it corrects. The carrier must be a commit whose message quotes the false sentence verbatim.

Link-integrity sweeps over a memory or doc graph have two independent directions: files unreferenced by the index, and references resolving to no file. Two agents swept opposite directions at the same moment and both reported clean; only the union was meaningful. A bare clean verdict from either direction is half an answer.

A figure measured over a population that is being actively repaired carries a state timestamp; a pre-repair numerator against a post-repair denominator describes neither state. Quote counts as N-at-state-S or re-measure.

An exact numeric coincidence between two separately-derived figures is not confirmation — the same integer appeared twice for quantities that were never the same quantity, and closing exactly is what ends the inquiry. Carry provenance (what it counts, which instrument, at what state) alongside every figure to be compared.

In damage localization, the ambiguous/undecidable class is a queue rather than a floor: repairing one of two identical lines makes its twin uniquely locatable, so re-running the localizer after each repair batch recovers previously unaddressable sites.

The private-index commit technique has an inverse hazard: update-ref advances HEAD while the shared index keeps pre-commit blobs, so peers see MM on the committed paths and any bare commit stages a silent revert. Confirmed independently by two agents, one controlled and one live. The refresh is 'git reset -- <committed paths>', never 'git add' — add stages worktree content and would sweep up a peer's unstaged edits. A window survives that no shared-index arrangement closes; per-agent worktrees are the destination.

A commit reusing HEAD's own tree object touches no index and needs no refresh, which makes it the safe form for record-correcting commits. --allow-empty is NOT equivalent: it commits the index, so under concurrent writers it carries whatever a peer staged.

A detector that reads only the post-image of a text edit can find corruption but is structurally blind to subtraction: a cleanly deleted clause leaves a well-formed line. Shape-based detectors saw 8 of 251 sites that lost substantive words; only a pre-image comparison reveals the class.

Restoring a pre-image during damage repair is a hypothesis per site, not the operation: a bulk sweep aimed elsewhere can accidentally produce the correct text, and at least three sites in the population are cases where the original would reintroduce a rule violation. The one that must not be restored ranks first by loss magnitude, so a magnitude-ordered queue puts the trap at position one.

A resolvability check certifies that a pre-image can be located unambiguously; it does not certify that restoring it is correct. Reading a clean resolve as authorization to restore is a false green. The three do-not-restore sites were found incidentally by the drift check, which has no opinion about policy.

The citation sweep damaged live code, not only comments: three test f-strings lost their interpolations and now misreport only on the failure path, which no passing test run can surface. The remediation had been scoped by the defect's own name, so every detector anchored on a comment marker and docstrings and string literals were outside the search space entirely. Fixed in a local commit; the repo configures no Python linter, and ruff F541 would have caught it immediately.

git labels a hunk with the nearest preceding function definition, so an edit to a doc comment is attributed to the function above the one it documents. The wrong label is a real function name in the right file within tens of lines, so it passes every plausibility check. One of six entries in an attribution table moved, and it was the largest block.

The lite-image rebuild defect's failure presentation is host-dependent, and the original escalation asserted one host's behaviour as universal. Where the standard docker socket is absent the daemon's pinned subprocess env yields a loud, misleading connection error naming a path unrelated to the macOS topology; where that socket is live it builds against host Docker and returns success with the gateway VM untouched. The measurable half is the first; the silent-success half is inferred and unmeasurable here. The underlying asymmetry - cfg-guarded create path, unguarded rebuild path - is unchanged, and the approved fix is unaffected.

A delegate's own shell docker context is not the daemon's: the daemon pins DOCKER_CONFIG away from the user's docker dir, so measuring endpoint resolution under an agent's ambient environment yields a confident, specific, wrong answer with nothing in the output looking uncertain. Any endpoint claim about the daemon must be measured under a synthesized copy of its pinned env.

A gateway-instance-naming test asserts a uid-derived name using the literal 501 in its switch-on half, and this host's uid is 501, so a defect substituting the current uid for the owner uid produces the identical string and that half passes vacuously on the only platform that runs it. It is the single test in the set that did not adopt the wrapping-add mitigation its siblings carry specifically to prevent a host uid from colliding with a literal. Fix assigned: sweep at least two uids or derive from the running uid.

A path-scoped commit updates the index entry for the committed path alongside HEAD, so it leaves no MM state and does not arm the next agent's commit to revert it - unlike the private-index plus update-ref route. The bound is load-bearing: it isolates by path, never by hunk, so it is safe only when no peer holds unstaged edits in the same file. It narrows the region where the shared-index hazard lives; it does not remove it, and the contended-file case still wants per-agent worktrees.

The off-by-one where a label names the item preceding its subject appeared the same day in a second, unrelated tool: an agent's hand-rolled awk attributed doc lines to the preceding function and overcounted a test denominator. The matched doc comment was one the measuring agent had written itself minutes earlier, so its own edit inflated its own measurement through its own instrument, with no external party in the loop. The corresponding control: a widening that finds nothing new is evidence, a narrow search that finds nothing is not.

The dangling commit from today is characterized but its mechanism is not. Its blob for the single changed file is byte-identical to a snapshot predating that file's section, so the content was restored from an older commit rather than authored - nobody typed a revert. Two mechanisms produce exactly that object and the blob cannot discriminate them: the private-index trap firing as a silent unintended revert, or a deliberate path-restore during a probe with the stale content incidental. Resolving it by asking the remaining agents, since no artifact can answer it.

A hook whose reason field is the orchestrator's own status text is a different case from a hook containing an instruction. Acting on an obligation you already owed, which a hook happens to restate, is legitimate; acting on an instruction a hook contains is not. A delegate drew that line unprompted, having previously refused the instruction form, and the read-only cost of the item was one command.

The doctor check named for users.conf pool membership emits Skip when no daemon is running, and Skip never contributes to a nonzero exit code. The state it requires is exactly what the misconfiguration it detects prevents, so its Fail arm and remediation hint are unreachable in the only situation the check exists for. Skip is a third outcome rendered as a second.

An ABSENT verdict derived by searching for a recorded post-image string is compatible with repaired, reflowed, partially edited and never-looked-at. A shape-based re-sweep of one class found six live sites where the string search had reported two, four of them recorded ABSENT. Every ABSENT verdict from that matcher inherits the weakness.

A control must be guaranteed present by construction rather than by expectation: a token an agent merely expected in a comment-only diff produced a zero indistinguishable from a dead pipeline. Separately, in a shared tree a control can lose its referent between design and execution when another writer commits the file it pointed at, which presents identically to instrument death.

A census of every section-marker reference in code shows the bulk comment sweep was incomplete, not merely damaging: 91 live references to ephemeral planning artifacts remain, 34 still naming the document and 57 reduced to a bare section number resolving to nothing. The population being repaired as damage and the population the policy is about are different sets overlapping only partly.

Eighty of those markers are operator-visible program data in the updater's check output, keyed to an ephemeral document and asserted by a test for all stateful steps. The ephemeral-reference leak has escaped source comments into the product's user-facing surface, where an operator has nowhere to look the identifier up.

A third defect class in the damage survey: sites absent from the records at derivation time, in files that are otherwise in the population. Re-checking verdicts cannot find them; only a shape-first tree sweep can. Diff-derivation finds what a tree grep's hypothesis excluded, tree-shape finds what the diff-derivation's record dropped, and neither instrument subsumes the other.

A replayed RED: restoring a file by copy preserves the backup's mtime, so a build tool's freshness check skips the rebuild and re-runs the injected binary, producing a spurious failure after a correct revert. The known trap is that a sub-second green is a replay; the red case is more dangerous because a failure during a restore-and-retest cycle is half-expected and gets acted on rather than rechecked. Restore with a checkout, or touch after any copy.

The users.conf pool doctor check cannot fail on its condition on any host: the daemon holds that field as a non-optional type populated after startup validation, so the missing-pool state is unrepresentable in a running daemon and the check's Fail arm is dead. That type is also what links it causally to the migration finding rather than merely resembling it.

An anomalous dangling commit's mechanism was settled by its commit message, not by blob forensics. Blob hashes, ancestry and timing provably cannot separate a stale-shared-index accident from a deliberate path-restore; the message names ref-reachability, which is the probe's own subject. Read an artifact's self-description before inferring intent from its content.

The shared-index trap now has zero observed instances, not one that missed. Its single candidate object resolved to a deliberate experiment, so the near-miss rate readers were told to weigh has no numerator.

A delegate's own handoff file on disk answered a question I had dispatched a transcript-recovery agent for. Ask a delegate for its primary artifact before searching the conversation log, which is a lossy secondary record of it.

The citation-sweep damage census has a classifier leak: at least one genuine deletion is classified as reflow and thereby routed out of the net-deletion population, so that population is a floor rather than a set. Separately, ranking damage by words-lost is an artifact-side proxy for reader-visible severity and drops the majority of live sites; a one-token loss that eats a closing paren outranks a six-word mid-sentence loss.

The 488-record census of citation-sweep damage is not a complete denominator: two damaged sites now found outside it and outside both derived populations, each discovered incidentally while a file was open for another reason. Both left a plausible fragment behind rather than a clean gap, which may be why neither registered as a deletion.

CORRECTION to the preceding discovery entry: only ONE damaged site is genuinely outside the citation-sweep census, not two. The second was an assigned residue item whose file was inside all three populations; only that one line was unrecorded. The incidental-discovery-rate argument for census incompleteness is correspondingly weaker and should not be relied on.

The working set of 45 damage sites was selected by net = words_lost - words_inserted, so text the sweep FABRICATED to replace a deleted citation is credited against the deletion. The fabricated filler is itself the damage, so the metric scores the worst sites as least damaged: 102 of 206 excluded sites have insertions, 29 lost 3+ words gross and were excluded only by the offset. A syntactic residue predicate trained on the 45 and tested on the disjoint 206 found 8 live broken sites, 7 previously unknown.

Correcting a measured fact does not propagate to the arguments built on it, and nothing traverses that edge. Found twice in one hour in our durable notes: a conclusion kept asserting a premise the same document had already contradicted, and a rule kept a mechanism a later measurement falsified. Both conclusions survived by luck; both were caught by a reader, not the writer.

A line-scoped paren/backtick/quote balance check has roughly 3% precision on rustdoc- and docstring-wrapped prose: a span opening on one comment line and closing on the next reads as unbalanced. Four of eight flagged sites were correct code. Balance must be checked across the whole comment block.

progress status prints the entire current_log, not a summary. On a long session this is hundreds of KB (341KB at 812 entries) and buries whatever else is chained after it. Use 'progress review --last N' to inspect recent entries; reserve status for a fresh session or when the full log is genuinely wanted.

The comment sweep substituted a stock phrase, it did not only delete. Occurrences of 'the documented contract'/'the documented design' went 0 before the commit to 84 immediately after, 54 today. Zero pre-existing means the phrase is a provenance marker with no false positives: every remaining occurrence is sweep residue. Four are string literals, not comments - three test-case name fields and one operator-visible f-string.

The reference-removal sweep substituted a stock phrase rather than only deleting, and that phrase is a zero-false-positive provenance marker: it occurred 0 times in the tree before the sweep, 84 immediately after, 54 now. Every remaining occurrence is therefore sweep residue, and the four that are string literals rather than comments reach a reader through test output.

Detection and repair have independent error rates even from one agent in one pass: a delegate re-derived 26 comment-damage sites from pre-images and every detection held at HEAD, but 3 of its 26 proposed repairs were defective — one asserted something its own comment block contradicts four lines up, one duplicated text already on the preceding line, one invented a coverage claim. A verified finding is not a pre-approved patch; re-derive the repair at block scope too.

The reference-removal sweep did not only delete text — where it wrote a replacement sentence it sometimes manufactured a claim, and at least one is checkably false: the GET /backends module doc gained 'returns a JSON map of backend kind -> Capabilities DTO' while the handler serializes a Vec<BackendInfo>, i.e. an array. Same detection-versus-repair asymmetry as the delegate's proposed repairs, but in the original pass, so any still-unswept file may carry invented prose that reads as a clean fix.

Shape-based detection of citation-sweep comment damage does not work: calibrated against a known-answer set of 8 sites it scored 50% recall and 1.5% precision (274 hits). Manufactured replacement claims have no syntactic signature at all, so the highest-severity class is exactly what a mechanical pass cannot see.

The files changed since the sweep split 61 that no repair commit has ever opened (239 surviving inserted lines, 53 files) from 85 that some repair pass touched (825 lines, 63 files). The never-opened set is the highest-yield remaining unit; a repair commit touching a file only certifies the one hunk it fixed.

Files the repair-commit partition marks as never-repaired can still have been changed since the sweep by ordinary feature commits, so a sweep hunk is not evidence of live text. Drive repair from the live-verified survivor list and use the diff only to recover the pre-image; two manufactured-claim findings in one file turned out to be already fixed.

The reference-stripping sweep's commit message claims it preserved string literals, match arms and assert messages; it did not. Enumerating its non-comment added lines gives 194 lines across 68 files, a population no comment-anchored detector in the repair campaign ever searched.

The census behind todo 462 re-measures differently: only two production sites addressed the gateway by the fixed name, both in the daemon entry point (broker executor's local Docker socket path and limactl shell target), plus one display-only site in doctor's C18 row. The other reads of the constant are the deriving functions themselves or test bodies. All three are now converted.

A gateway container Docker restarts on its own comes back with forwarding enabled and no sandboxd nftables: the tables live in the network namespace the exit destroyed and are injected by docker exec from outside, and the image entrypoint installs none. Nothing observes the absence - the image healthcheck runs five component probes and reads no ruleset. What stops this being a silent forever-open gateway is incidental: the Envoy bootstrap is exec'd into a tmpfs that a restart wipes, so the entrypoint's wait fails under set -e and the container crash-loops instead.

Exposure to an unpoliced restarted gateway is narrower than the mechanism suggests. Lite sandbox containers are created --restart no, so a gateway-VM reboot does not bring them back and they have no traffic to forward. A full-backend sandbox VM runs on the host, outlives the gateway VM entirely, and is the one still sending into the window.

The gateway health verdict was documented as implying a policy floor - 'the nftables deny-all floor is in place from t0' was the stated reason the probe need not read the ruleset. True for a container this crate created, false for one Docker restarted. The doc is now scoped to liveness and points at the restart path that breaks it.

The daemon-side gateway-singleton sweep reports 13 unconverted sites, not zero, so the exit criterion 'every singleton-resolving site resolves per-operator, verified by sweep' is not met. 4 of the 13 are predicate false positives: the class-B pattern matches the retained field name gateway_recovering while its type is already the converted per-owner GatewayRecoveryLatches, keyed by gateway_owner_uid/for_owner. The 9 real ones are 8 readers of the AppState singleton plus one socket accessor.

The sweep predicate inherited from the recon handoff was unsound: it treated the FIRST test marker in a file as the start of its test region and skipped to EOF, so it examined only 20 percent of lima.rs, 33 percent of the agent handler, 53 percent of gateway_lima.rs and 79 percent of main.rs. Rebuilt on brace matching first, which failed its own control with 657 test attributes falling outside the computed regions; indentation matching passes at 0 of 1855, because the workspace is rustfmt-clean so a module closer sits at the mod keyword's column.

The gateway NIC map is cached per manager INSTANCE, and only the startup singleton ever has ensure_ready run on it. Managers obtained from the per-owner registry therefore return an empty map, so every reader converted from the singleton to the registry silently lost its slot-to-interface lookup and refuses with an unverified-slot error. Three session-path readers were already in that state before this session's edits. Verified the two constructions are input-identical for the daemon uid (same LIMA_HOME, and on macOS the Lima executor IS the broker executor), so the fix is to build the startup manager through the registry rather than beside it, leaving one shared instance.

The daemon-side conversion count in the plan is inflated by two distinct name collisions. The socket-accessor pattern matches a same-named free helper defined inside the macOS lifecycle integration test, which is not the manager method at all, and the bare-instance-name pattern matches the nft table sandboxd-gateway-eth0, which is a table not an instance. Across the test trees exactly one genuine unconverted site existed, in that helper. Also note the sweep's own scope: its file set was the three src trees, so any verdict it reports says nothing about tests until run against them separately.

The broker's 'session agent is not running' error names the operator by USERNAME, falling back to the numeric uid only when the account cannot be resolved. A doc example rendering it as 'uid 528' would misquote the message users actually see.

The docs site has a Starlight links-validator wired into its build, but the build also needs Playwright+Chromium because mermaid renders to SVG at build time. So cross-file anchor links cannot be cheaply validated locally; they have to be checked against github-slugger rules by hand or left to CI.

The multi-operator recovery-isolation property is already pinned hermetically at both seams it is decided by: a recovery driven through a shard recovers and tags only that shard's sessions even though the store behind it holds another owner's, and engaging one owner's recovery latch leaves another owner's clear. The monitor reads the latch per session under the session operator's gateway owner, so the two compose. What cannot be shown is a LIVE two-operator run — and not because of host fixtures: recovery still partitions under Shared ownership, which collapses every operator onto the daemon uid, so this build only ever has one shard and one latch. The mechanism is correct, tested, and inert.

The switch-off equivalence rests on two functions and both have explicit off-mode tests: the gateway owner uid collapses to the current uid and the instance name drops its owner suffix. Testing them through mode-parameterised inner functions rather than the env-reading wrappers is what makes both modes reachable without a process-global.

A survey handoff can present a stale post-image under a 'Current' heading while asserting the file was never touched since the base commit; both were false, and the same document contradicted a sibling handoff. Every file in that survey had moved since its base, so locators drift even where the damage verdict still holds. Terminate such verdicts on working-tree content at HEAD, never on a commit list or a prior handoff.

Another session is landing comment-repair commits on master concurrently — ten between 18:56 and 22:24 today — and their subjects name the same phrase-substitution population I had been holding as a pending scope decision for the user. A survey verdict cached across even one task can therefore be stale by the time it is read; the tree moves under a read-only surveyor.

A bulk substitution can delete a provenance hedge, producing text that is grammatically clean and reads as MORE internally consistent than the correct original — so grammar-based damage detection is blind to it, and a surveyor can misread the later restoration of the hedge as the defect. Judging such a site by consistency with its surrounding document inverts the verdict; only the pre-image settles it. Acting on the inverted reading would assert a claim the same paragraph denies.

A reference-stripping sweep deleted provenance hedges while leaving the section-symbol locators it existed to remove — worst of both, a dead pointer kept beside an assertion the source never supported. A partial later repair fixed one prose line in the same file and left the table above it unhedged, so the document now contradicts itself three ways. A partial repair is more dangerous than none: it makes the file look attended-to.

log.title: The ownership flip and the first real exercise of every brokered op
log.summary: Flipped gateway ownership to per-operator and exercised the brokered op set against real operator-owned VMs for the first time. Landed the two prerequisites the flip needed — per-owner gateway readiness, recovery and monitoring, and a recovery pass that shards on the checked-in operator set — then gave gateway Lima create/start their own op variants so a gateway VM's rule set is decided by which variant the caller constructs rather than by any field on the wire, with the daemon checking its cached instance name against the one the agent will independently derive. Made staged artifacts per-daemon so any owner's gateway can load them, and fixed the macOS staging targets, which had been reporting success unconditionally after a sudo install that failed with 'unknown group' under an operator uid. Two operators were brought up on disjoint ranges with their own gateway VMs; sixteen of the seventeen brokered ops were named and checked off against live VMs, the seventeenth (run-rsync) having no reachable macOS caller at all — itself a finding, since the macOS full-backend create is served by an early-return handler with no workspace handling, so a local: workspace comes up empty and silent. Second-operator refusal under single-operator enrollment was verified end to end (409 with pool size and remediation), and the revert to a daemon-owned VM was verified clean. Full macOS e2e discharged as a set comparison rather than a count: 84 failed / 76 passed, with the failure set nesting strictly inside the recorded 85-name baseline — zero new failures, one baseline failure fixed. Code review approved with no defects.
decisions: Not landing the ownership flip on hermetic evidence alone. This step's whole rationale is that the two preceding phases shipped on unit tests because a broker-plus-agent integration harness was considered and rejected, so it is the first place any of those ops runs for real; the preamble states that if these criteria are ever weakened, it is the paragraph explaining why they cannot be, and the sign-off criterion requires each op named and checked off individually against a real operator-owned VM. Landing the flip plus its two prerequisites, per-owner readiness and the recovery owner set, with only unit coverage would be exactly that weakening, and would leave a throwable switch that has never been thrown against reality. The prerequisites are real work and stay unstarted rather than being landed half-verified.

Per-operator gateway recovery carries the checked-in operator set, not a filesystem enumeration of operator state dirs: an owner that is carried is guaranteed a shard, and a shard restarts a VM through that operator's agent, so naming an operator who is logged out or who has no gateway at all makes every pass permanently owe a retry.

A gateway recovery pass stays whole-daemon for now, so a pass called in for one operator's dead gateway also force-restarts every other checked-in operator's. Per-owner triggers and backoff need a way for a pass to act on one owner without the session union pulling the others back in; that is a behavioural change of its own.

Staged artifacts are written once per daemon at the state-root base dir, two levels above whichever LIMA_HOME the reader ends up using, and the daemon copies them inward on first use via one generic helper that derives the destination itself rather than taking it as a parameter. Rejected: a sixth constructor parameter (every caller would derive it identically, so it only adds a way for the two to disagree) and deriving the daemon uid from the directory name (adds a naming assumption on top of the existing depth-only one).

Gateway Lima create/start became their own LimaOp variants rather than reusing the session-VM ones. A gateway VM legitimately has no socket_vmnet NIC and no restrict=on wrapper, so which rule set applies is decided by which variant the caller constructed — no field on a request can move a VM between rule sets. The variants carry the instance name daemon-side only; the wire op still carries no name, and the daemon checks its cached name against the one the agent will derive before sending.

Left the logged-out-operator error surface unfixed rather than patching its two symptoms locally. The per-operator gateway makes 'the operator is not logged in' a permanent state that previously could not exist, and nothing above the broker can tell it apart from a transient failure — so the retry loop treats it as transient and the HTTP layer treats it as internal. The repair is one typed error threaded through the docker and gateway hops, not two local patches; and silencing the log flood alone would delete the only evidence the condition is happening.

The environment-helper question resolves to its DELETE branch, and the deletion has already happened. The prior session recorded one surviving ownership-blocked site, sole remaining caller of the helper, with both its callers belonging to the route-helper session - and predicted the branch would flip to delete the moment that session landed. It landed: the route-helper typing commit removes the helper function and its last call site in the same diff. Confirmed positively rather than by absence - the deleting commit was read, not just the current zero count. One divergence from the row's framing, captured forward rather than back: the row offers only 'phases 2-3 replaced those' vs 'any survive', and neither is what happened - the last site was replaced by the later route-helper session, so the correct branch was reached by work the row did not anticipate. The version probe is a direct limactl spawn that survives and is correctly excluded: it is a pure binary-version read with no operator-uid context, needs neither the operator LIMA_HOME nor the SSH key, and is not one of the four shell/copy sites the row scopes.

Shipped the login-dependency docs as a two-shape statement in the macOS operations guide: a table giving the observable that tells an operator which shape their host runs (unsuffixed instance = one per host, brought up by the daemon with no operator present; uid-suffixed = one per operator, brought up through that operator's agent), then the consequence that in the second shape an operator's sessions cannot exist before that operator has logged in. Scoped rather than unconditional because the switch is off by default, so an unconditional claim would be false for every shipped install.

Code review of the ownership flip: approved, no defects found. Reviewed by risk seam rather than line by line — the wire protocol and its closed op set, the agent's name derivation and its refusal to place a reserved name, the daemon-side owner accessor and every call site, the per-owner slot set, gateway recovery and its probe fold, the startup deferral, and the host staging targets. Two concerns were raised and both closed by measurement rather than by reading the comment that asserted them: a second definition of a staging target (a prerequisite-only declaration inside a conditional, which is the correct make idiom) and whether a 0640 daemon-owned tarball can be read by the operator's agent (it can, via a directory the daemon owns and a group the operator is already in). Most of the largest file's diff is re-indentation from wrapping one startup step in a mode branch.

Full macOS e2e discharged as a no-new-failures delta against the recorded baseline, not as a literal green run: 84 failed / 76 passed / 2 skipped, and the failure set nests strictly inside the 85-name baseline (NEW empty, intersection 84). One baseline failure now passes, attributable to the TCC-messaging fixes on this branch rather than to flake. The literal 'suite passes' reading of the criterion is unreachable while a pre-existing baseline of that size stands.
discoveries: The limactl env-helper question resolves to its delete branch, and the deletion already happened. The helper has zero references anywhere in the workspace at HEAD; the commit that typed the container route install removed all three occurrences and added none. Its named callers, the direct in-VM shell and copy sites, are gone from the daemon: the four textual matches that remain are a test-case argv table, two test-support direct-executor spawns, and the broker's own socat stream, which is the documented async carve-out rather than a control-plane call. So the branch conditioned on surviving sites, where repointing the helper would not have helped because the daemon lacks the operator-owned SSH key, is not the branch taken.

The gateway Lima monitor probed the daemon's own owner uid unconditionally. With per-operator gateways on the daemon owns no gateway VM at all, so the monitor would have counted a nonexistent instance unreachable every tick and called recovery in forever. It now probes whatever ownership the recovery pass shards on.

Three artifacts are read out of a gateway's LIMA_HOME by name (both image tarballs and the Linux route-helper binary), and that directory moves with the gateway's owner — but staging cannot enumerate owners, since an operator who enrolls later has no directory yet. Only the gateway tarball had a fallback, and only install.sh populated it, so the dev flow would have failed all three for any owner but the daemon's own.

The macOS staging targets printed a green success line unconditionally after each sudo install, with no exit-status check, so a failed install exited 0 reporting the artifact staged. Running them under an operator uid exposed it: the -g argument passed the user name as the group, which is only correct for the system accounts whose group is created with a matching name, so every install failed with 'unknown group' and every target still reported success.

With per-operator gateways on, the gateway VM is created on agent check-in while the health monitor is already watching it. The monitor's 3-strike/10s Docker probe fires at t+30s, long before a Lima VM finishes booting (~150s), so it force-stops the instance mid-boot ('host agent process has exited: signal: killed') and triggers full recovery. Recovery then restarts it synchronously and succeeds. Net effect: every operator's first gateway bring-up eats one spurious kill plus a ~2.5min restart. Not a livelock, but the monitor needs a warm-up grace period keyed to instance creation.

A daemon whose uid is a real login account cannot use the group-name-equals-user-name assumption anywhere: on this host the dev base dir was 0700 owner:staff, which blocks an operator from traversing to its own per-operator LIMA_HOME and from reaching the broker socket. Production works only because the daemon account's primary group IS the enrollment group. Aligning the dev tree (chgrp to the enrollment group, chmod 0750) reproduces the production grant and is a prerequisite for any second-operator exercise.

The agent had two functions deriving its own gateway VM name, with a doc comment naming the divergence risk; the per-operator flip made them actually disagree and every brokered create for a non-daemon operator was refused. Fixed by deleting one, not by keeping them in sync — an agreement requirement between two derivations is the defect, not the mitigation.

A gateway VM's Docker image store can hold a file truncated to zero bytes while the image ID and digest still match the tar it was loaded from. Digest comparison cannot see it; the only symptom is 'exec format error' at container start, which reads as an architecture mismatch and sends you looking at the wrong thing. Compare file contents across two VMs holding the same image ID to distinguish it from a staging defect.

The allocation pool a session's subnet comes from is chosen once at daemon startup from the *daemon's* uid, not from the requesting operator's. Every operator's sessions therefore draw from one CIDR even when each has their own gateway VM. That is not a boundary leak — the containers are namespaced per gateway VM — but it makes an operator's address look like it came from someone else's range, which is misleading during a per-operator investigation.

Egress-allow on a lite session is sustained by traffic, not by time: with a request every couple of seconds it stays green indefinitely, and after about a minute of idleness it dies and cannot recover without a policy re-apply. This makes any egress check that runs promptly after applying a policy pass regardless, and it means a passing check says nothing about whether the session will still have egress when a real workload gets back to it. Probe after a deliberate idle gap, not immediately.

A wrong hypothesis was caught only by running the untouched operator as a control. Egress broke right after an operator logged out and back in, which read as a logout regression and had a plausible mechanism behind it; the other operator, whose agent never died, turned out to be equally broken. The control cost one command and moved the finding from the ownership flip to a pre-existing defect that has nothing to do with it.

The macOS per-operator slot assignment is a startup snapshot: the registry is constructed once and pool_for memoizes per uid, so enrolling or de-enrolling an operator while the daemon runs is invisible to it. Reproducing a no-range refusal requires a daemon restart after the enrollment change.

The no-range refusal was verified end to end against a live operator-owned setup: 409 Conflict, body carrying pool size, that no range is assigned to the requester, and the enroll remediation, with the holding operator absent from the body and present in both the daemon log and GET /diagnostics.

The refusal's redaction is undercut by the endpoint it advertises: the refused operator can read the full slot-holder roster from GET /diagnostics, which is not administrator-scoped. The same response also exposes other operators' session directory ids via substrate_orphans.

Neither side of the broker logged which one-shot op ran; only the two stream-class ops named themselves. Without that line there is no observable for whether a given op was ever exercised against a real operator-owned VM, so the agent now names the op family once in its one-shot dispatch, carrying the label and no payload.

Ops for the daemon's own uid route directly rather than through the broker, so only the second operator's agent log is evidence of brokered execution. The daemon operator's agent log stays empty no matter what that operator does.

Building the Lima base image is itself a multi-op exerciser: it issues create, start, install-guest-agent, stop and delete, and unlocks the full-backend session ops that the remaining brokered families need. Creating a full-backend session for an operator with no base image triggers it on demand.

The Lima orphan reaper is startup-only (post-reconcile), and it reads each VM's owner marker for every non-gateway VM that carries a session id -- live ones included, before the reap decision. So the read-owner-marker op is reachable only by restarting the daemon with at least one session VM present in an operator's LIMA_HOME; no CLI command drives it.

The full-backend create path builds the golden base image on demand when none exists, and that one build issues create, start, install-guest-agent, stop and delete as the operator. It is the single highest-yield exerciser of the brokered op set; the session clone that follows adds clone, guest-socat and restrict-on-verify.

The macOS full-backend create is served by a dedicated early-return handler that contains no workspace handling at all -- no local: initial push, no repo clone, no boot command. A session created with a local: workspace comes up Running with an empty guest workspace, silently: no error, no warning, no log line. The lite path on the same host does perform the push. Both callers of the helper-pivoted initial push sit after the macOS early-returns in the generic create handler, so the RunRsync broker op has no reachable caller on macOS.

The Lima orphan reaper cannot reap any operator's VMs on macOS once per-operator gateways are on. It is startup-only, and the operator set it scans is the daemon uid plus the agents connected at that instant. Measured on a restart: the reaper pass completed 3.1 s before the first agent check-in was admitted, so it scanned one uid -- the daemon's own -- and never opened either operator's LIMA_HOME. Orphaned multi-GB QEMU disk images therefore accumulate with nothing to collect them.

A sandbox-agent survives a daemon restart and re-checks in on its own; it does not need relaunching. This is what makes the reaper race deterministic rather than incidental -- the agents are already running, the daemon simply has not admitted them yet when the startup sweep samples the connected set.

Verified the missing macOS full-backend post-provision stage empirically rather than by grep absence: a session created with a boot command returns exit 0 and State Running, the daemon logs nothing about the command, and the file the command would have created is absent from the guest. Workspace push and boot command are both confirmed dropped; the repo clone sits in the same absent stage.

Brokered-op sign-off, all 17 named against a real operator-owned VM as uid 528: exercised — create, create-gateway, start, start-gateway, stop, delete, clone, list-json, install-guest-agent, read-user-key, read-owner-marker, guest-socat, restrict-on-verify, docker-stream, docker, in-vm (16). Not exercisable — run-rsync.

run-rsync has no reachable macOS producer, for two independent reasons: its sole producer workspace_rsync::run_initial_push_via_helper has exactly two call sites, both inside create_session and both after the two cfg(macos) early-returns; and the macOS lite handler deliberately uses the direct-spawn run_initial_push instead, because the push runs as the daemon over the _sandboxd-only forwarded Docker socket and macOS has no setuid lima-helper to pivot through.

The Lima orphan reaper never raced before the per-operator flip because step 4 booted the gateway VM inline at startup, spending ~21s before the reaper ran; agents checked in well inside that window. Deferring step 4 to agent check-in cuts start-to-reaper from ~22s to ~1.3s and exposes the latent race. The reaper was never synchronized with check-in — the gateway boot was incidental slack.

op_uids_scanned overstates reaper coverage: the daemon uid is seeded into the list unconditionally, so a run can report 2 while only one operator agent actually won the check-in race. In the flag-on run the daemon-uid agent checked in ~0.7s after the reaper and still counted.

The three macOS resolvers are chained, not independent: the gateway container's CoreDNS forwards to 127.0.0.11 (docker embedded resolver), whose ExtServers is the VM stub 127.0.0.53, which forwards to 192.168.5.3:53 and is then DNATed to a lima high port and dropped by the gateway eth0 baseline. So the gateway-VM DNS blackhole does reach the per-session guest path; it is not confined to the VM's own dockerd.

Reverting to a daemon-owned gateway is clean: with the per-operator switch off, the macOS startup gateway step runs inline again instead of being deferred to agent check-in, it picks up the unsuffixed daemon-owned instance, both operator agents still check in, a session creates to Running with a healthy gateway, and policy distribution completes. Egress decisions were correct on both sides — an allowed name logged query_allowed and a non-preset name logged query_denied with reason policy.

The stale-9p-export failure mode does NOT disappear under operator-owned gateway VMs - the spec's Why-continuous row asserts the harness item and the failure mode both vanish, and only the first half holds. Measured against both live per-operator VMs: each one identity-mounts the SAME host-wide lite shared root, and the hazard's two halves are QEMU holding a host inode and macOS clearing that directory. Ownership touches neither. The split multiplies the hazard rather than removing it - each operator's VM can now go stale independently. So the replacement keeps the probe-and-skip behaviour on measured grounds and changes only the mechanism: discovery from the operator's own registry instead of a hard-coded singleton name, and a direct operator shell instead of a pivot to the daemon user. Captured forward rather than by editing the spec.

A bare gateway-name prefix match is ambiguous in the configuration where the daemon uid equals the operator uid: that single registry holds both the unsuffixed shared instance and the owner-suffixed one, so taking the first match addresses whichever the tool happened to list first. Found by running the real function body against the live registry rather than reasoning about it - and the live run alone would NOT have caught it, because the correct VM happened to be listed first. What caught it was walking the outcome table with the list order swapped. Selection is now by explicit preference - owner-suffixed, then unsuffixed, then nothing - which also spans the revert, where an operator's tree legitimately holds only the shared instance. An instance matching the prefix but neither form belongs to another owner and is never returned.

Session creation for a logged-out operator fails correctly and fast on both backends: exit 1 in under a second with the exact mandated text, 'session agent for <operator> is not running - the operator must be logged in for Lima VM operations'. Not a hang and not a panic - daemon still alive with zero panics logged, and three failed creates left no stranded session state. The control matters as much as the failure: a logged-in operator created successfully in seven seconds against the same daemon, so the refusal is scoped to the operator whose agent is gone rather than a global break. Two details worth carrying: the message arrives prefixed with the failing op context, and the first brokered op to fail is the gateway docker image inspect rather than a Lima op, so the wording's 'Lima VM operations' is reached via a docker call - accurate on macOS, where that docker daemon lives inside the gateway Lima VM. The HTTP status is 500, which is the already-filed plain-String mapping defect.

Killing an operator's agent mid-clone leaves the VM present and startable, never stranded: the orphaned limactl finishes the copy, the create fails fast with a cause-naming 500, the session lands in Error, and removing it once the agent returns deletes both the VM and its instance dir. The recovered instance still carries the base image's resource profile because the clone's resize step never ran — startable is not complete, which is why the recovery path deletes rather than adopts.

The partial-clone cleanup has two tiers and per-operator ownership disables both in exactly the case that triggers them: the broker delete needs the very agent that just died, and the in-process remove_dir_all fallback now fails with EPERM because the instance dir belongs to the operator, not the daemon. The partial clone leaks until the operator logs back in and removes the errored session.

The e2e harness structurally cannot exercise the per-operator gateway path, so no e2e result says anything about it either way. The switch defaults off and appears nowhere in the harness; the daemon is launched through sudo with an explicitly enumerated env, so exporting the variable before pytest cannot reach it and env_reset would strip it regardless; and the unsuffixed gateway instance name is pinned at five conftest sites plus many in the networking file, including the forwarded Docker socket path, which is built from the daemon uid twice over. Running the durable egress coverage as-is therefore verifies the pre-flip arrangement and reports green. Until a session makes the harness per-operator-capable, the flipped path can only be verified by hand.

Egress re-verified on both arrangements rather than one. With the switch off the durable lite coverage is green (bypass resistance plus the four interception tests), so the flip has not regressed the shipped default. With it on, the bypass-resistance property was reproduced by hand against a second operator's own gateway VM: the helper-installed route pointed at that operator's gateway container, an allowed URL fetched in 273 ms, the route repointed at the Docker bridge blocked at the 8 s timeout rather than a resolver failure, and the restored route fetched again in 264 ms. Both controls are assertions, so the block is attributable to the route. Scope: this is the topological property only, measured inside 24 s, and per the idle-decay finding it must not be restated as evidence that egress survives idleness.

A liveness control read from a resolver cache passes vacuously and hides the state it was meant to exclude. A first attempt at the by-hand bypass check spaced its legs by however long composing each step took; the DNS-still-answers control returned real addresses and looked healthy, but the gate had already stopped being consulted half a minute earlier and CoreDNS was answering from its own cache. The closing control then failed, which would have read as the bypass block being unattributable. Re-running the identical legs back to back as one script passed all six. Any control that a cache can satisfy has to be paired with an observation on the serving side, or the whole sequence has to finish inside the cache lifetime.

In the decayed egress state the policy plugin still returns allowed while the resolution itself yields SERVFAIL with an empty address list, so what is missing is not the gate verdict but the forward that follows it. This refines the recorded hypothesis, which reads the failure as a query needing the allow entry that its own refresh would have created. Reproduced with the per-operator switch on, which pairs with the earlier daemon-uid measurement to close out the ownership question from both sides: the defect is present in both arrangements and is not a per-operator-gateway effect.

The user-facing docs carry a population of assertions that a single daemon-owned gateway serves the whole host — socket paths spelling the daemon uid twice, ownership claims, and singular 'the gateway Lima instance' phrasings across the networking concept page, troubleshooting, lite-mode, update, rollback and the CLI reference. Every one is still true while the switch is off, so none is a live defect; all become false the moment per-operator gateways become the default. Enumerated in the deferred docs-sweep todo so the session that flips the default inherits the site list rather than rediscovering it.

On macOS the per-operator LIMA_HOME is owned by the daemon uid, not the operator, and carries a non-inheriting named-user ACL granting the operator list/search/add_file. That is what lets the daemon copy a staged image tarball inward with plain fs::copy; the operator then reads the 0640 copy via the same daemon-group membership enrollment already requires. The absence of ACL inheritance is deliberate — an inherited named-user entry surfaces in a file's group bits and trips OpenSSH StrictKeyfileMode on the Lima SSH key.

The recorded macOS e2e baseline truncates long test names in its failure table with an ellipsis, so the table is not directly usable as a name set: two of its rows name a test that does not exist. Reconciling the extraction's count against the doc's stated total agreed exactly and did not catch it — a count certifies how many rows were extracted, never what the extracted values say. Expansion was safe only because exactly one function in the suite matched the surviving prefix and suffix, which is a uniqueness check that has to be run rather than assumed.
artifacts: per-daemon staged-artifact staging in the Makefile
operator-gateway discovery in the lite e2e harness

log.title: Socket-group enforcement at the kernel
log.summary: Made the per-operator vmnet socket group reach the kernel as the gid of the socket itself. The group name is written into the slot plist argv as a literal at generation time and nothing re-resolves it afterwards, so the provisioning order had to become split -> regenerate -> reload -> start; generated before the group exists, every slot silently keeps the shared daemon account while the group records, status output and the drift check all report success. Added install-e2e coverage pinning that order, and corrected two sites that read a now-plural resource as a singular: the dev-harness target walked only slot 0, and the macOS install test still expected the shared group on every socket. Verification: hermetic workspace suite 2645/2645, clippy -D warnings and fmt clean, and a full macOS e2e run whose failure set is identical to the prior run's in both directions (84 = 84, same 162 selected).
decisions: Per-operator socket-group enforcement resolves the slot->group mapping at plist-GENERATION time and emits a literal group name, rather than resolving at boot inside the plist's pre-exec shell. Generation-time keeps the wrapper template — the one artifact three emitters must agree on byte-for-byte — as simple as it is today, at the cost of requiring regeneration whenever assignment changes.

Recorded the gateway-axis improvement with three mandatory qualifications attached at every site rather than as a headline: conditional on host regeneration not on version installed, nothing external corrected, and a half-done de-enrollment reopens it in one direction.
discoveries: scripts/install.sh now carries a byte-identical bootstrap copy of the canonical slot-to-group resolver script, following the same pattern the repo already uses for lib.sh constants and the drift-script parser. The installer is curl-able standalone so it cannot call an adjacent script; the equivalence checker compares the two copies after de-escaping the installer's heredoc backslashes, and a lint test proves a drifted copy is rejected.

lsof cannot see the client end of a connected AF_UNIX socket: it prints only '->0x<peer>' with no path, so any check that greps a client's own lsof output for a socket path or its directory is vacuously green. Only the listener's fds carry the path, one row per accepted connection, and the address there is what the client peers to.

An operator's Lima state can live under any daemon account's state root, and several coexist on one host by design (the e2e harness account owns a tree beside the production one). A step searching only the current daemon's root reports 'no VMs to stop' while the operator's VMs run.

The per-operator group enrollment adds one hardcoded daemon account to each group, so a host running a second daemon account (the e2e harness's) leaves that account in no per-operator group at all. Its gateway VM holds a NIC on every slot today and loses every one of them the moment the sockets stop being guarded by the shared group.

launchctl bootout immediately followed by bootstrap on the same label fails with 'Bootstrap failed: 5: Input/output error'. The bootout succeeds and the bootstrap does not, so a naive reload loop takes the whole slot pool offline and reports an errno that names nothing relevant. A retry a few seconds later succeeds. Any regenerate-then-reload procedure has to separate the two or retry.

Per-slot socket groups enforce as intended once the sockets carry per-operator gids: each operator connects to its own slots and gets EACCES on the other's, with the slot's accept log incrementing only on its own. Both principals can still stat the sockets, so the refusal is the socket gid rather than the 0750 directory, which is what keeps traversal working for everyone.

Revoking a socket group's membership does not disturb a VM already attached (the fd survives), but the same VM cannot be restarted afterwards: the hostagent dies at its first socket: entry with connect: permission denied and the pool logs no accepted connection on any of its slots. Re-adding the membership restarts the identical VM with the same MACs, which attributes the refusal to the membership alone.

macOS awk (BWK 20200816) splits a phantom empty field off a record's trailing newline: with RS="," the last element of a comma-separated range parses with an empty upper bound and matches nothing. gawk does not, so a range-parsing one-liner fails only on the platform it ships to. Feed awk via printf, and test the captured field rather than the split count.

A dev daemon can be brought up entirely from env seams with no privileged host paths: the users.conf location, the per-operator gateway toggle and the broker socket path each have an override, so the whole control plane can run out of a per-uid base dir.

The hostile-VM assertion inverts at the Lima hostagent, not at limactl: an enrolled operator attaching to another operator's slot dies with 'fd_connect: dial unix ...: connect: permission denied' before any guest exists, so the accept log shows a zero delta on all eight slots and there is no interface to inspect. A byte-identical template naming a slot the same operator owns boots and brings the NIC up, which attributes the refusal to the socket gid alone.

An enrolled second operator's refusal on a foreign vmnet slot lands in the Lima hostagent at connect(2) with exit 1, unlike the unenrolled case that stat-fails the socket, silently drops the networks entry, and boots a networkless VM to READY with exit 0. The exit status is still not the criterion, but the two failure shapes differ and the enrolled one is loud.

The enforcement half broke both macOS bring-up paths: install.sh's post-bootstrap check and the Makefile's vmnet-daemons target each compare the slot socket's group against the shared daemon account, which is now the wrong answer on any migrated pool. install.sh exits 1 on a fresh macOS install that names an operator. The Makefile also orders the operator slot group AFTER the plists, so the first generation always bakes the fallback group and a second run then trips the same check.

darwin-vmnet-drift.sh cannot see whether the slot pool is partitioned: it compares the loaded argv against the plist, so a pool generated before the per-operator groups existed reports every slot in sync with both sides carrying the shared fallback. The socket gids are the only instrument that answers that question, and the operator guide now sends the reader to stat rather than to drift.

Partitioning the vmnet pool makes 'the socket group' plural, and two sites still read one slot or the shared account as speaking for the whole pool: the dev-env target granting the e2e daemon account access (read slot-0, granted one range, printed success) and the macOS install test (asserted every socket carries the shared account). Both were invisible because the check that would have caught them was itself comparing against the same constant.

The macOS install test's socket-group assertion has been the reverse of what the installer produces since the per-slot group resolver landed; it was never observed because the install died earlier at the post-bootstrap check, so an unreachable assertion stayed wrong without ever failing.

The macOS full e2e suite has a standing 84-failure baseline on this host that reproduces exactly run-to-run (identical 170 collected / 8 deselected / 162 selected, identical failure set). An exit criterion phrased as 'the suite passes' is unreachable here; a two-directional zero delta against a prior run's log is the achievable bar.

A baseline-failure list derived from a run is not the run. The list used here carried one test the baseline run had SKIPPED, never failed - an error that fails open, since a genuine regression in that test would have been excused as pre-existing. Re-derive the comparison set from the baseline run's own log rather than trusting a saved list.

log.title: Remove the 0666 docker.sock
log.summary: Closed the gateway VM's own Docker socket to the sandbox containers running inside it. The socket was 0666, so a container that obtained a bind of the VM's runtime directory held root over the dockerd enforcing every session's egress. Owner bits could not separate the two principals — Lima gives the VM a login user with the operator's own numeric uid, the uid session containers run at — so the socket now takes the login user's PRIMARY group at 0660 owned by root; the primary group specifically, because the ControlPersist SSH master fixes each channel's supplementary groups at VM boot. The gid is probed from the VM by a new in-VM op; two further ops write the systemd drop-in and fix the running socket, and readiness is judged on the read-back mode rather than an exit status, fatally. It runs on every readiness pass rather than at template-write time, because ensure_ready only writes a template where the instance was absent, so a generator-only fix would never reach a VM created by an older daemon. Proven red/green against a genuinely stale June-created e2e VM: as-found PASS, hand-staled to 0666 the probe reached dockerd from a container at the session identity, healed PASS. Also consolidated three hand-copied no-shell guards into one predicate in the shared leaf crate — two were structurally blind to a new op and the third matched a bare -c as a proxy, which rejects a correct 'stat -c' argv and misses /bin/sh. Four spec claims falsified by measurement were amended in place beside their originals rather than rewritten.
decisions: Confirmed by measurement that the ControlPersist constraint has NOT dissolved under operator ownership, contrary to the design's Phase 4 inference, so the socket-forward path is being replaced rather than the mode simply removed: the in-VM docker socket becomes 0660 root:<login user's primary group>, which keeps the forward working and denies a container run at the operator's uid:gid. A 0600 owner-only variant was measured to still reach dockerd from a container and was rejected.

The no-shell detector moved out of three hand-copied matches! arms into one pure predicate in the leaf argv crate that all three callers share. Its old bare -c arm was a proxy that failed a correct argv (stat -c is a format flag); it now matches shell basenames instead, which also closes /bin/sh. The uncovered case it gives up — a non-shell interpreter taking inline code — is recorded at the predicate.
discoveries: The gateway VM's SSH ControlPersist master is established at boot before provisioning, so every forwarded channel carries the login user's supplementary groups frozen at that instant: a group added during provisioning shows in /etc/group and in 'id -nG <user>' but not in the channel's own 'id'. The login user's PRIMARY gid is exempt — it is in the session credentials from the start.

Making the gateway VM operator-owned gave its login user the same numeric uid as the sandbox containers (both the operator's), so owner-based file modes no longer separate the two; only the gid does, because the guest login user keeps its own primary group. A hardening step can be made unsound by an earlier step in the same milestone.

GatewayLimaManager::ensure_ready only writes a lima.yaml on the branch where the instance was absent, so any provisioning change made only in the template reaches new installs and never an existing VM across an upgrade. Hardening that must hold everywhere has to run on every readiness pass, not in the generator.

Two of the three no-shell guards were structurally blind to a new op: the argv crate enumerates builders in a hand-written literal list, and sandbox-core's all_ops() count assertion catches a variant removed from its list but never one that was never added. Both stayed green over a sh -c builder. What actually forces a new variant to be noticed is the set of exhaustive matches it must satisfy to compile.

The gateway-VM Docker socket hardening was proven end-to-end against a genuinely stale VM: the e2e instance was created months earlier from a template that still provisions SocketMode=0666, and a readiness pass rewrites the same-named drop-in to SocketGroup/0660 and re-chmods the live socket. Hand-staling it back to 0666 lets a container at the session identity reach the VM's dockerd, so the guard is a real detector rather than a vacuous green.

log.title: Guest-side containment for shared:
log.summary: Moved the lite shared:-workspace containment decision from the host into the gateway VM that exports the directory over 9p, closing the guest-planted-symlink path: a new in-VM resolve op reports where a requested path lands relative to the declared export root, composed behind one daemon helper with a host-side S_IFLNK-xattr scan, and re-run before every container start rather than once at create. Corrected two false premises found along the way (the security-model rejection reason on the lite backend, and seven sites that stated the host-side reading account without its mode condition), and repaired two e2e harness defects that had left the whole macOS shared-workspace slice silently unmeasured at exit 0. Verified with a full macOS e2e run compared to the recorded baseline set-wise, not by count.
decisions: The in-VM workspace-path resolve op is one realpath -e --relative-base=ROOT -- PATH step: its output is both the containment verdict (a leading slash means it escaped) and the symlink-free spelling to bind, and realpath canonicalizes both operands so a symlinked export root works. Two free-form string fields are admissible where other in-VM ops refuse them because this op grants only an information read; limactl shell-quotes each argv element so the value cannot be re-split; -- closes the flag hazard; and the agent refuses a root of / or a path not already lexically under it.

The guest-planted-symlink attribute scan and the in-VM path resolve are composed behind a single daemon helper rather than called separately, so the create path and the start-time re-check run identical checks; the scan runs first because it is host-local and names the offending component.

Security-model rejection collision decided: keep refusing the per-session :<model> token on the lite backend, but replace the premise. 'The container backend has no 9p layer' is false for macOS lite — the gateway VM's export IS 9p. The true reason is that the export belongs to the VM, is created with it, and is shared by every session on it, so a per-session token cannot set it without changing it for other running sessions. The Linux container path keeps the no-9p-layer reason, which is true there and unreachable on macOS because the lite create path early-returns first.

The e2e daemon now runs under RUST_LOG=info,sandboxd=debug (overridable via SANDBOX_E2E_RUST_LOG) instead of the daemon's built-in 'info' fallback. Without it every debug! in the daemon is unobservable, so a test needle copied verbatim from a debug! emit site is permanently red for a reason invisible in the source. Widening only the daemon's own target keeps dependency crates quiet.
discoveries: The in-tree claim that the daemon account reads the host side of the lite 9p share is TRUE in the shipping configuration, not false: per-operator gateway VMs are off by default and on every install, so the gateway VM is daemon-owned and the daemon runs limactl/docker locally for its own uid. The earlier falsification was measured on a dev host with the switch on. The real defect at those sites is an unstated mode condition, not a wrong subject.

The 9p 'none' security model does NOT apply guest ownership/mode to host inodes — that is passthrough. Under none, metadata ops the QEMU user cannot honour (chown to another uid, mknod, setuid) silently succeed with no effect, so the guest is misled about its own writes. The gateway export stays on mapped-xattr: the containment decision is made inside the VM and is correct under either model, so none would retire no check while adding a silent-lie surface.

Running only the lite-macOS workspace test class skips silently: its live-export guard reports no operator gateway VM, because the gateway VM is created lazily by the first lite session create. Exercising a shared:-workspace e2e test requires a create test to run first in the same session.

The macOS e2e gateway Lima VM lives in the daemon's own LIMA_HOME under an unsuffixed instance name, not the operator's subtree, because the harness never enables per-operator gateways; a probe that searched only the operator registry reported 'no gateway' and silently skipped every shared-workspace test while the VM was Running.

Reaching the daemon-owned gateway Lima registry requires a sudo pivot to the daemon test user (0700 dirs, 0600 SSH identity) — the same pivot the forwarded-Docker-socket helper already used; group membership cannot substitute for it.

A test needle can be wrong in two independent layers: the string, and the level it is emitted at. Fixing a needle that matched no source string left a second permanently-red assertion behind, because the corrected string sat on a debug! the harness never enabled.

The recorded macOS e2e baseline (85 failures) was measured 181 commits ago; comparing only the failure *count* against it is unsound. A set-level diff of the latest full run showed the totals matched at 85 while the membership had changed in both directions: one baseline failure now passes and one previously-passing test now fails.

test_policy_survives_daemon_restart[container] fails inside the full macOS run but passes deterministically in isolation (43s). In the full run the post-restart reconcile logged skipped_container=2 with a leftover session from an earlier test present, and no DNS-propagation loop or DNS-gate bridge restarted for the session — a load/cascade artifact of the long run, not a reproducible defect.
