Environment divergence escapes the shared-argv guarantee. The docker seam preserves the daemon HOME across env_clear on the branch taken when the route names an operator VM, so the docker CLI reads the daemon's client config when the daemon executes an op locally and the operator's when the same op goes through their agent. The shared argv crate guarantees argv cannot drift between the two sides; environment is outside it. Measurement in flight to decide whether this is live or latent.

The docker HOME divergence between the daemon arm and the operator-agent arm is deliberate and safe, NOT the config-source split recorded earlier. Both HOMEs are pinned on purpose and each is right for its own identity. What makes the divergence safe is a gate in the broker restricting the daemon's local executor to ops whose uid is the daemon's own, so the two arms never execute the same op. That condition lives one file from both arms and is referenced by neither, so nothing traverses it: dropping the never-pull policy, or letting the daemon run an op on an operator's behalf, makes it live with no comment or test at either arm to notice. Fix is to state the dependency at both arms and at the gate. Supersedes the earlier entry, whose premise was retracted by its author.

USER-FACING BUG, macOS. If one IS reachable the build succeeds, the handler returns 200 lite image rebuilt, and the image sessions actually use is untouched -- a success report for a no-op. On macOS this is the only shipped command claiming to rebuild the lite image. Diagnosed as omission on three independent pieces of history, and four of five image touchpoints in the daemon are macOS-branched. Fix now: gate it like the ensure path and error naming the tarball, converting a false success into an honest refusal. Do it once the route-resolver change has committed -- same file, currently dirty.

Updater backup/recovery has TWO invariants and only one is being closed. (a) Every file named in the recovery text was backed up - closed by iterating the backup set instead of restating it. Close the unpoliced-forwarding window a Docker-restarted gateway container opens. Per-operator gateway managers have no readiness step. ensure_ready is called only in the macOS startup block, on the manager for the daemon's own gateway owner; restart_instance_for_recovery is the only other thing that fills a manager's slot-to-NIC cache. With per-operator gateways switched on, an operator's manager is built on first lookup with an empty map, so nic_map() returns None and session create refuses the slot until a recovery restart happens to run. Turning the switch on needs a per-owner readiness path.

Gateway recovery still passes GatewayOwnership::Shared. The manager and Docker route are now selected per shard, so the per-owner arm would act on the right VM; what is missing is the owner set PerOperator carries. enumerate_operator_uids_from_fs can supply it but is not wired to the recovery path, and the switch-over needs validating against more than one live gateway.
Give the gateway Lima monitor per-owner probes, triggers and backoff so one operator's dead gateway does not restart every other operator's healthy one.

install.sh cannot stage the lite image tarball or the linux-aarch64 route helper: neither artifact is in the installer's $STAGE payload (only the gateway tarball and the host-native route helper). A production macOS install therefore leaves two of the three per-daemon staged artifacts absent. Release-pipeline gap, not fixable in the daemon.

The gateway Lima health monitor reaches its 3-strike Docker-probe threshold about 30 s into a first gateway boot and force-stops the VM it is waiting for; recovery then restarts it synchronously, so every operator's first bring-up costs one spurious kill plus a ~2.5 min restart. The monitor needs to distinguish a gateway that has never been up from one that has stopped answering — a warm-up state, not a shorter threshold.

A session VM created on the daemon's direct limactl path gets no sandboxd-owner marker file. Only the agent writes that marker, after its own successful create. The path is reached when a session VM's operator uid equals the daemon uid, so the Lima orphan reaper cannot attribute those VMs to an operator. Either have the direct path write the marker, or establish that the reaper does not need it there.

The daemon's direct limactl start accepts an empty qemu-wrapper path and silently boots the VM unwrapped, while the brokered path rejects an empty wrapper outright. No caller passes an empty one today, so the asymmetry is latent: the direct path would boot a session VM without restrict=on rather than refuse. Make the two halves agree on the refusal.

sandbox policy status never confirms propagation for a macOS lite session: it reports propagated=false with actual=- indefinitely, for both the daemon-uid operator and a brokered one, while the policy is demonstrably in force (an allowed host returns 200 and a denied one is refused). The distributor logs 'policy distribution complete', so what is missing is the reporting channel that fills 'actual', not the distribution. Not a per-operator-gateway regression — it reproduces identically on both.

A gateway VM that has been force-stopped can come back with a silently truncated Docker image layer: the image ID and digest still match the staged tar, but a file inside it reads 0 bytes, and the only symptom is 'exec format error' when the container starts. Nothing that compares digests can see this. Observed on the gateway image's entrypoint after repeated monitor-triggered force-stops; docker rmi plus a reload from the staged tar repaired it. Worth an integrity check on the loaded image, or an unclean-shutdown-triggered reload.

An operator logging out is not distinguishable from a transient failure anywhere above the broker, and two symptoms follow. (1) The macOS DNS-gate bridge re-arms on a flat 253 ms cadence with no backoff — measured, not estimated: 103 warnings in 26 s, ~14k/hour per orphaned session, indefinitely, since the condition cannot self-heal without a human. (2) A create by a logged-out operator returns HTTP 500 with the actionable sentence buried behind 'gateway: docker image inspect:', so a plain client-side precondition reads as a daemon fault. Both want the same thing: a typed 'operator agent absent' error that survives the DockerRoute and gateway hops, mapping to 4xx like RootlessDockerRefused does, and letting the bridge back off on the permanent case while keeping the tight re-arm for transient ones. Fixing either symptom alone is worse than neither — suppressing the log removes the only signal that the condition exists.

A macOS lite session's egress-allow deadlocks after roughly a minute of idleness and never recovers on its own. Measured on the daemon-uid operator's own session, so it is not a per-operator-gateway effect. Continuous traffic sustains it indefinitely (37 s of DNS+HTTP at ~2 s intervals, every probe green), but after a 60 s gap both DNS and HTTP fail and stay failed through five minutes of once-a-minute retries; a policy re-apply restores it instantly, every time. The shape suggests a cycle: CoreDNS records the resolved IP with ttl 7, the propagation loop drops it from Envoy/nft once it expires, and the DNS query that would refresh the mapping now needs the allow entry that the refresh would have created. resolved.json stops changing at the moment of the last successful lookup and the loop then correctly does nothing, which is why the daemon logs neither success nor failure. NOTE: this supersedes an earlier deferred todo that read 'propagated=false actual=-' as a cosmetic reporting gap and explicitly concluded distribution was fine — that reading was wrong; the missing hash is the symptom of this, not a separate defect.

Each policy update starts a fresh DNS propagation loop for the session without stopping the previous one, so the loops accumulate for the life of the session. Visible in the daemon log as duplicated 'rewriting Envoy listener' and 'propagating DNS-resolved IPs to nftables' pairs at near-identical timestamps after the second update — two loops doing the same rewrite microseconds apart. Every update adds another poller against the same gateway, and two writers racing the same Envoy listener file is a correctness concern, not just wasted polling.

darwin-operator-group.sh deenroll looks for the departing operator's VMs under a daemon-uid path it assumes rather than one it verifies. On a host whose daemon runs as a different uid it probes the wrong LIMA_HOME, finds nothing, and prints 'no LIMA_HOME at <path> — no VMs to stop' as a successful step, while the operator's gateway VM keeps running on the vmnet segment. Observed with the probe naming uid 310 while the live VM sat under uid 501. Stopping those VMs is the step that makes de-enrollment mean anything, and the script's own enroll-side overlap guard warns against leaving a de-enrolled operator 'on the segment with nothing detecting it' — which is precisely what this produces, with a reassuring message on top. Either resolve the daemon uid from the running daemon or its config, or fail loudly when the expected LIMA_HOME is absent.

The no-range refusal redacts the slot holder from the response body on the stated grounds that naming them would hand any enrolled operator the roster of sandboxd users on a shared machine, then points the refused operator at GET /diagnostics, which serves that same roster in vmnet_slot_assignment to the operator who was just refused. The doc-comment's premise is that the /diagnostics audience is the administrator; it is not. Either scope the field to the daemon operator or drop the redaction as decorative. The same response also leaks other operators' session directory ids through substrate_orphans.session_dirs.

After a daemon restart, session gateway containers are recreated by reconciliation but do not reach ready: both live lite sessions reported Envoy, CoreDNS and both nft-loggers unhealthy afterwards, and the agent transport reads unreachable. Determine whether this is the same idle-deadlock family as the egress finding or a distinct reconcile-readiness gap.

On macOS with per-operator gateways the daemon does not bind its API socket until startup reconciliation finishes: 95 seconds elapsed between 'sandboxd starting' and 'sandboxd listening' with two sessions to reconcile, each carrying a 45-second gateway readiness wait. A client that starts the daemon and immediately connects sees a bare 'cannot connect to sandboxd: No such file or directory' with nothing indicating the daemon is alive and working.

macOS full-backend create silently drops --workspace local:, --repo and --boot-cmd: the dedicated macOS Lima create handler has no workspace/repo/boot-command stage, so the session comes up Running with an empty guest workspace and no diagnostic. Either implement the stage or reject the flags at the daemon boundary.

The Lima orphan reaper never scans an operator on macOS with per-operator gateways: it is startup-only and samples connected agents ~3 s before check-in is admitted, so it only ever sees the daemon uid. Orphaned session VMs are never reaped. Either run the sweep after check-in settles, or make it periodic rather than startup-only.

Correct the scope claims on the gateway-VM DNS blackhole and on the three-resolver split. The blackhole todo says it affects the VM's own dockerd and NOT the per-session guest path, and the resolver-naming todo says guest-side lookups traverse only the gateway container DNS. Both are falsified by a measured chain: Corefile forwards to 127.0.0.11, the container resolv.conf names ExtServers host(127.0.0.53), the container's own getent fails, and CoreDNS logs query_allowed for an allowed name with an empty resolved_ips list while the guest reports could-not-resolve. Positive controls in the same VM: tcp 443 and tcp 80 both return 301, and a udp probe straight to the DNAT port times out.

Partial-clone cleanup falls back to an in-process remove_dir_all that cannot delete an operator-owned Lima instance dir (EPERM under per-operator ownership), and its broker-delete tier needs the agent whose death triggered the cleanup. The e2e conftest builds the gateway Docker socket path from the daemon-uid/daemon-uid tree with a hard-coded singleton instance name, which disagrees with the per-operator LIMA_HOME form it derives right beside it. Correct pre-flip, wrong once each operator owns a gateway VM.

Make the e2e harness able to run with per-operator gateways on, so the flipped path has coverage instead of hand verification. Needs the daemon-launch env to carry the switch through the sudo boundary (the env is enumerated explicitly and env_reset strips anything else), the gateway instance name discovered from the owner's registry rather than hard-coded unsuffixed at five conftest sites plus the networking file, and the forwarded Docker socket path derived from the gateway's owner rather than built from the daemon uid twice. Subsumes the socket-path item already filed separately. Sized as its own session, not a fix inside another one.

Before per-operator gateways become the default, sweep the user-facing docs that assert a single host-wide gateway. All are still true while the switch is off, so this is pre-flip work, not a live defect. Known sites: concepts/networking.md (a single daemon-owned VM hosts all gateway containers across all sessions; the forwarded-socket path with the daemon uid twice; the 0600 _sandboxd ownership claim); guides/troubleshooting.md (GW_SOCK path with the daemon uid twice); guides/lite-mode.md (a persistent gateway VM the daemon owns, twice); operate/update.md and guides/rollback.md (the gateway Lima instance, singular); reference/cli.md (doctor's gateway-instance check). guides/macos-operations.md was already brought to both shapes.

The e2e harness daemon account is in no per-operator vmnet group, so its gateway VM loses every slot once the sockets carry per-operator gids. Decide whether enrollment should take the daemon account as a parameter or the harness should run its gateway as an enrolled operator.

The gateway-VM docker.sock drop-in is written by two paths that disagree on spelling: the Lima template emits SocketGroup=<group name> (id -gn) and the daemon's readiness pass emits SocketGroup=<numeric gid> (id -g). Both are valid systemd and both fail closed, but the file content flip-flops between VM boot and daemon start. Pick one spelling (the numeric gid is the less ambiguous of the two).

macOS startup reconcile step 6a assumes the gateway VM is daemon-owned. Decide whether 6a needs an agent-gated arm (defer those sessions to 6b) instead of attempting and logging failures.

Never share a cargo target directory between git worktrees on this repo. Workspace path-dependency units hash to identical -C metadata in every worktree, so they collide on one filename in target/debug/deps, and cargo's mtime freshness check then accepts the other tree's binary as fresh. The result is a silently stale test binary: cargo nextest list returns a wrong test set with exit code zero and no warning. The tell is a test list short by exactly the tests the commit under test added. Recover with cargo clean -p <crate>. Give every worktree its own CARGO_TARGET_DIR, and treat unexplained test-count drift as this until ruled out.

Subagent dispatch here fails by MODEL PIN, not by agent type. This CORRECTS former remember item #29 (from M24-S4), which recorded kio-development:kio-developer and kio-qa-test-runner as dead 'five for five' with no cause. Every kio-* agent definition pins a 1M-context model in frontmatter: kio-developer and kio-qa-test-runner pin claude-sonnet-4-6[1m], while kio-reviewer pins claude-opus-4-6[1m] - which is the only reason it looked like the working exception. This account has no 1M usage credits, so a pinned-sonnet agent dies at its first API call before any tool use, presenting identically to an agent type that spawns and never reports. Confirmed 2026-08-20 by probe: kio-qa-test-runner spawned with the Agent tool's model parameter set to 'sonnet' acked immediately and read git HEAD correctly. ALWAYS pass an explicit model override when dispatching any kio-* agent; do not avoid those agent types. STILL TRUE and carried over unchanged from #29: background agents' plain-text output does NOT reach the orchestrator, so instruct every subagent to report via SendMessage to 'main'; ListAgents is useless as a liveness check here; the reliable probe is an explicit 'ack as your first action' instruction plus watching the filesystem.

Fresh-binary first-exec stalls at _dyld_start on this macOS host are target/ bloat, not a wedged syspolicyd. This CORRECTS former remember item #24, which prescribed 'sudo killall syspolicyd'. Measured twice: a signed binary took 23.75s to start from target/ versus 0.477s for the same binary copied to /tmp, with 789,939 files under target/debug/deps and 57 GB in target/ while the disk had 634 GiB free — so it is neither a signing problem nor ENOSPC. Diagnose by copying the binary to /tmp and running it there; if it starts fine outside target/, the tree is the problem and 'cargo clean' in sandboxd/ is the fix (reclaimed 107.7 GiB and took a workspace run from a 70-minute stall to 10.2s). Do NOT run 'killall syspolicyd' or 'pkill -9 amfid' — those are system daemons, killing them destabilizes the host, and neither has once been the cause here. Distinct from the separate ~20-minute 'make test' cost, which comes from unconditionally re-signing every test binary; that cost is paid once per binary and survives the run that paid it, so a run killed at its timeout should be retried IDENTICALLY rather than narrowed in scope.

The model-pin dispatch failure propagates one level down and my delegation prompts do not currently prevent it. A subagent that spawns its own kio-* subagent hits the same 1M-context credit error, because the override requirement lives in the orchestrator's context and is never passed on. Observed 2026-08-20: a reviewer's nested test-runner died this way mid-review. Any delegation prompt to an agent likely to spawn helpers must state the requirement explicitly: pass an explicit model override on every Agent call, and do not conclude the agent type is broken.
